en: Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya. Om, homage to the Buddha!
According to the recension of the noble Mahāsāṃghikas, the Lokottaravādins, and the Madhy’udeśikas, this is the Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya.
Thus it was: the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having accomplished the purpose for which he had come, was dwelling among the Śākyas at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Grove.

As a Teacher of gods and men, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, venerated, and respected; he had attained the highest gain and the highest fame, and was a recipient of the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick.

And there, unstained like a lotus by water, establishing beings who possess merit in merits, settling beings who possess the fruit in the fruits, and placing beings who possess latent tendencies in those latent tendencies;

distributing the nectar of immortality to gods and humans in no small measure, he leads hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings to the nectar of immortality, [delivering them] from the wilderness of beginningless birth, old age, and death, and from the treacherous pits of hell.

Having rescued them from the great precipice and established them in the secure, auspicious, level ground of the fearless state of *nirvāṇa*, he— having won over Aṅga, Magadha, Vṛji, Malla, Kāśi, Kośala, Kuru, Pañcāla, Cedi, Vatsa, Matsya, Śūrasena, Śibi, Daśārṇa, Cāśvaki, and Avanti—
has displayed his prowess in wisdom within his own realm.

Dwelling in divine abidings, dwelling in Brahma-abidings, noble abidings, and imperturbable abidings; dwelling in Brahma-abidings, noble abidings, and imperturbable abidings through constant application; the Buddha, by means of the Buddha-abidings; the Conqueror, by means of the Conqueror-abidings; the Knower, by means of the Knower-abidings; the All-Knowing One, by means of the All-Knowing-abidings—one who has attained the supreme perfection of mastery over the mind.
Furthermore, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, dwell in whichever dwellings they desire, for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are skilled in dwelling.
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with Chandā, Chandakapālā, Dāsacchandā, Chandakamātā, and five hundred Śākyan women, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One, she stood to one side. Standing to one side, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, the arising of a Buddha is rare; the teaching of the True Dharma is rare.

And now, the Blessed One has appeared in the world as a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, and he teaches the Dharma that leads to peace, to final Nirvāṇa, as proclaimed by the Sugata, for the attainment of the Deathless."
It conduces to the realization of Nirvana.
It would be well, Blessed One,
if women also could obtain the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
The Blessed One said:
"Gautamī, may it not please you [to seek] the going forth, the full ordination, and the state of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata."
Then indeed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī [thought]:
"The Blessed One truly does not grant an opportunity for women to go forth and receive full ordination into the state of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata."

Having bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One, she went together with Chandā, Chandakapālā, Dāsacchandā, and Chandakamātā to where those five hundred Śākyan women were, and having approached them, she said this to the Śākyan women: "Noble ladies, the Blessed One does not grant permission for women to go forth, to receive full ordination, and to attain the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata."

Why should we, noble ladies, ourselves shave our hair and don saffron robes, and then follow behind the Blessed One as he wanders on tour through the Kosala country in vehicles with their seats covered in cushions?
If only the Blessed One would grant us permission!

"...he will not permit us to go forth; nevertheless, O Protector, we shall practice the holy life (brahmacarya) in the presence of the Blessed One. "Very well, Noble Lady," those Śākyan women replied to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed in the city of Kapilavastu for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour through the Kośala country.
Then indeed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with Chandā, Chandakapālā, Dāsacchandā, Chandakamātā, and five hundred Śākyan women, having herself shaved off her hair and donned saffron robes,
followed closely behind the Blessed One as he was wandering on tour through the Kośala country in vehicles with their trappings bound up.
4. Then the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Kośala country together with a great community of monks, five hundred monks in number, arrived at Śrāvastī, the city of the Kośalas.
Having reached it, he stayed right there in Jeta’s Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada.
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī approached the Blessed One, bowed her head at his feet, and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, the arising of a Buddha is difficult to encounter; the teaching of the True Dharma is difficult to encounter."

And now the Blessed One has appeared in the world, a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, who teaches the Dharma that leads to peace, to final nirvana, as proclaimed by the Sugata for the attainment of the deathless and for the realization of nirvana.
It would be well, Blessed One.
"May women also obtain the going forth, the full ordination, and the state of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Gautamī, let it not be pleasing to you that women should have the going forth, the full ordination, and the state of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata."
5. Then indeed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī [thought]:
"The Blessed One truly does not grant permission for women to go forth, to receive the full ordination, within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata."
"Regarding the state of being a bhikṣuṇī.
Having bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One, she stood weeping near the gateway of the Jeta Grove monastery, scratching the ground with her big toe.
Now, a certain monk saw Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī standing near the gate-chamber of the Jeta Grove weeping, scratching the ground with her big toe.
Having seen her, he approached the Venerable Ānanda and said this to him:
"Venerable Ānanda, here is Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī standing near the courtyard of the Jeta Grove weeping, scratching the ground with her big toe."
"Go, Ānanda, and find out why Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī is weeping.
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and said this to her:
"Gautamī, why do you weep?"

When this had been said, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda: "Enough for me, noble Ānanda, with weeping; for indeed, the arising of a Buddha is so difficult to encounter, and the teaching of the True Dharma is so difficult to encounter.

Yet now the Blessed One has appeared in the world—the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One—and he teaches the Dharma that leads to peace, that leads to final nirvāṇa, proclaimed by the Sugata, for the attainment of the Deathless."
"It conduces to the realization of Nirvana.

Yet the Blessed One does not grant the opportunity for women to go forth, receive full ordination, and attain the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata. Therefore, noble Ānanda, it would be well if you were to entreat the Blessed One so that women might likewise obtain going forth, full ordination, and the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata."
"Very well, Gautamī," the Venerable Ānanda replied to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. He then approached the Blessed One, bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, and stood to one side.

Standing to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the arising of a Buddha is rare; the teaching of the True Dharma is rare. And now, the Blessed One has appeared in the world."

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha teaches the Dharma which leads to peace, to final Nirvāṇa, as proclaimed by the Sugata; it conduces to the attainment of the Deathless and to the realization of Nirvāṇa.
It would be well, Blessed One, if women also might obtain the going forth, the state of a novice, and the status of a Bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda:
"May it not please you, Gautamī’s mother, that women should receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the state of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata."
Then the venerable Ānanda thought:
"The Blessed One does not grant permission for women to go forth and receive full ordination into the state of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he approached Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and said this to her:

"Indeed, Gautamī, the Blessed One does not grant permission for women to go forth, to receive full ordination, or to attain the state of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
When this was said, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī spoke thus to the Venerable Ānanda:

"It would be well, Noble Ānanda, if you were to petition the Blessed One a second time, so that women might also obtain the going forth, the full ordination, and the state of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata."

"Very well, Gautamī," the Venerable Ānanda replied a second time to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. Having gone to where the Blessed One was, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Lord, the arising of a Buddha is rare. Thus, [having requested] everything down to the state of being a bhikṣuṇī, when this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda:

"Let it be so, Gautamī; let the mother be pleased that for women, in the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, there shall be going forth, full ordination, and the state of being a bhikṣuṇī."
"Just as, Ānanda, when a field of excellent barley is struck by a disease-king called *kāraṇḍava*, that excellent barley-field becomes defiled by a great affliction;
even so, Gautamī, in whatever teaching women obtain the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a bhikṣuṇī, that teaching becomes defiled by a great affliction."

Just as, Gautamī Mātā, when sugarcane is ripe, the disease called *mañjiṣṭhā* is called the king of diseases, and thus that ripe sugarcane is defiled by a great affliction; even so, Gautamī Mātā, in whatever teaching women obtain the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a nun, that teaching becomes defiled by a great affliction.

"Just as, Gautamī, it would please your mother, so may it please you that women receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the state of a bhikṣuṇī in the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Then, indeed, the Venerable Ānanda...
The Blessed One does not grant permission for women to go forth, to receive full ordination, and to attain the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Having approached Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, he said this to her:

"Indeed, Gautamī, the Blessed One does not grant permission for women to go forth, to receive full ordination, and to attain the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata."
When this had been said, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda:

"It would be well, noble Ānanda, if you were to petition the Blessed One a third time, so that women might also obtain the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a bhikṣuṇī within the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.

"Very well, Gautamī," the venerable Ānanda replied to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī for a third time, and having done so, he approached the Blessed One, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and [stood to one side].
Having sat down to one side, the Venerable Ānanda, seated to one side, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, how many assemblies were there for the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda, the four assemblies of the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas were as follows:
namely, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One in this way:

“Blessed One, these four fruits of asceticism— namely, the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the supreme fruit of arhatship— are capable of being realized even by a woman who dwells alone, heedful, ardent, and resolute. When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Venerable Ānanda.

"Ānanda, these four fruits of the ascetic life— namely, the fruit of stream-entry up to the supreme fruit of arhatship— are capable of being realized even by women, provided they dwell heedful, ardent, and resolute, living in seclusion. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One as follows:

Indeed, Blessed One, for the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, there were four assemblies: monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. These are the four fruits of asceticism, namely: the fruit of stream-entry, up to the supreme fruit of arhatship.
"It is possible that even a single woman from among these, dwelling heedful, ardent, and secluded, could realize [this state].
It would be well, Blessed One, if women also might receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a bhikṣuṇī in the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
[The practice of] difficult austerities..."
And Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī was the Blessed One’s nurse, foster-mother, and wet-nurse; she had passed away, and the Blessed One is grateful and appreciative toward her.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Venerable Ānanda:

"It is so, Ānanda; it is so, Ānanda. Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has performed difficult deeds for the Tathāgata: she was his nurse, his foster-mother, the one who gave him milk when his mother had passed away.
And the Tathāgata is grateful and appreciative. Moreover, Ānanda, the Tathāgata has also performed difficult deeds for Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī."
Indeed, Ānanda, it was by coming to the Tathāgata that Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī went for refuge to the Buddha,
went for refuge to the Dharma,
and went for refuge to the Saṅgha; indeed, Ānanda, it was by coming to the Tathāgata that Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī [did so].
[1] For as long as life lasts, they abstain from taking life; [2] for as long as life lasts, they abstain from taking what is not given;
[3] for as long as life lasts, they abstain from sexual misconduct.
For as long as life lasts, she abstains from false speech;
for as long as life lasts, she abstains from drinking fermented liquors, spirits, and intoxicants.
Indeed, Ānanda, it was by relying on the Tathāgata that Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī prospers through faith.
She grows in virtue, she grows in learning, she grows in renunciation,
and she grows in wisdom.
For it is by coming to the Tathāgata, Ānanda, that Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī knows suffering and knows its origin.
He knows cessation;
he knows the path.
11. Ānanda, when a person, relying on another person, goes for refuge to the Buddha,
goes for refuge to the Dharma,
and goes for refuge to the Saṅgha.
Ānanda, it is not easy for one person to repay another person, even if one were to attend upon them for as long as life lasts with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
even so, it would not be easy to repay them.
But when, Ānanda, by relying on another person, one refrains from taking life for as long as life lasts—[that is what truly repays].
For as long as life lasts, he refrains from taking what is not given;
for as long as life lasts, he refrains from sexual misconduct;
for as long as life lasts, he refrains from false speech.
For as long as life lasts, he abstains from drinking fermented liquors, distilled spirits, and intoxicants.
It is not easy for one person to repay another for this.
Even for as long as one lives, one should not serve [the teacher] with robes,
alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
even so, it would not be easy to repay [his kindness].
Ānanda, when one person, relying upon another person, increases in faith, increases in virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom— Ānanda, it is not easy for this person to repay that person,
even if they were to attend upon them for as long as life lasts with robes, almsfood, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Even so, it is not easy to repay him:
that person, Ānanda, who, by relying on another person, comes to know suffering, knows its origin, knows its cessation, and knows the path.
By this means, Ānanda, it is not easy for one person to repay this other person.
Even if one were to attend upon him for as long as life lasts with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,
even so it would not be easy for him to repay that kindness.
12. Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "If I were to reject Ānanda, the son of Gautama, even for a third time, there would be a change in his mind;
yet he has heard the Dharma."
They will fall into confusion.
My true Dharma shall remain for a full thousand years.
Let there not be any alteration in the mind of Ānanda, the son of Gautamī; let the teachings he has heard not go to ruin.
"Granted, the True Dharma shall remain for five hundred years.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:

'Just as, Ānanda, if a man were to build a dam here in a mountain gorge so that the water might not overflow, even so, Ānanda, has the Tathāgata established the eight weighty rules for the bhikṣuṇīs.'"

He establishes that those [who have performed this service] should be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by the bhikṣuṇīs for as long as they live, and should not be transgressed against, just as the tide cannot be overstepped by the great ocean.
Which are the eight? The eight weighty dharmas are the first weighty dharma.
13. Ānanda, a bhikṣuṇī who has been ordained for a hundred years must bow her head at the feet of a bhikṣu ordained on that very day.
This, Ānanda, is the first heavy rule for bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored by bhikṣuṇīs for as long as they live and never transgressed, just as the tide cannot overstep the ocean.
Guru-dharma 2: For a maiden who has reached eighteen years of age, the training prescribed for two years must be completed; only then may she expect full ordination (*upasampadā*) in both Saṅghas.
This, Ānanda, is the second guru-dharma which must be honored and revered by the bhikṣuṇīs for as long as life lasts, just as the ocean is respected by the tide.
Ānanda, the third *guru-dharma* for the bhikṣuṇīs is this:
the path of speech from bhikṣuṇīs toward the bhikṣus may be either true or false; however, the path of speech from a bhikṣu toward the bhikṣuṇīs must be true and not false.
This, Ānanda, is the third *guru-dharma* of the bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored by the bhikṣuṇīs as long as they live, and so forth.
The fourth *guru-dharma*:
regarding food, bedding, seating, and dwellings, the *bhikṣuṇīs* must receive them from the *bhikṣus*.
This, Ānanda, is the fourth *guru-dharma*, which must be honored and revered by the *bhikṣuṇīs* throughout their lives, and so forth.
Ānanda, a nun who has committed a *guru-dharma* must request a half-month period of *mānatva* from the community of nuns, as well as a formal reconciliation (*āhvayana*) from both communities.
Ānanda, this is the fifth *guru-dharma* of the nuns, which must be honored by the nuns for as long as they live, and so forth in detail.
Guru-dharma 6:
Every half-month, the bhikṣuṇīs must expect to approach the community of bhikṣus for instruction.
Ānanda, this is the sixth heavy rule for the bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored by the bhikṣuṇīs as long as life lasts, and so forth. Heavy Rule 7:
It is not permitted for bhikṣuṇīs to enter the rains retreat in a residence where no bhikṣus are present.
This, Ānanda, is the seventh heavy rule for the bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored by the bhikṣuṇīs as long as life lasts, in detail.
"Ānanda, bhikṣuṇīs who have resided for eight years must seek the invitation (pravāraṇā) from both Saṃghas.

This, Ānanda, is the eighth guru-dharma of the bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by the bhikṣuṇīs as long as they live, and which must not be transgressed, like a boundary."
By Samudra.
These, Ānanda, are the eight weighty rules (gurudharma) for the bhikṣuṇīs.
The nuns must, for as long as life lasts, honor, revere, respect, and worship [the elders], and they must not transgress them, just as the ocean does not overstep its shore.

14. "If, Ānanda, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī accepts these eight weighty rules (guru-dharma) and trains herself in the training regarding the four rules involving defeat so as not to transgress them, from this day forward, this shall be her going-forth;
this shall be her full ordination; this shall be her status as a bhikṣuṇī."
"Excellent, Blessed One! the venerable Ānanda replied, and having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he approached Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and said this to her:
"Listen, Gautamī, to the words of the Blessed One."

"Just as, Gautamī, a man might build a bridge here in a mountain gorge so that the water cannot be overstepped, even so, Gautamī, the Blessed One has prescribed the eight weighty rules for the bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by the bhikṣuṇīs for as long as they live, and not transgressed, just as the ocean does not overstep its shore."

15. Which are the eight? Gautamī, a bhikṣuṇī ordained for a hundred years must bow her head at the feet of a bhikṣu ordained on that very same day. This, Gautamī, is the first heavy rule (guru-dharma) for bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored by bhikṣuṇīs as long as they live and not transgressed, just as the ocean does not overstep its shore. In this way, all eight heavy rules [are to be observed].
That very thing was reported to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
“If indeed you, Gautamī, accept these eight weighty rules (gurudharma) and train yourself in the training so as not to transgress the four rules involving defeat (pātayantikā),
then from this day forward, this is your going forth, this is your full ordination, and this is your status as a bhikṣuṇī.”
16. When this had been said, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda:

“Just as if, Ānanda, there were here a young man of handsome appearance, having bathed his head and dressed in clean garments, who would receive upon his head a garland of blue lotuses, or a garland of campaka flowers, or a garland of white water-lilies, or a garland of *tṛṇamolikā* grass—just so, noble Ānanda, do I receive these eight weighty rules upon my head, and I shall not transgress the four rules leading to defeat.”
Training, training, I shall train.

17. Then indeed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with Chandā, Chandakapālā, the slave-girl Chandā, Chandakamātā, and five hundred Śākyan women, approached the place where the Blessed One was; having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side. 18. To the bhikṣuṇīs standing to one side, the Blessed One said this:

Therefore, from this day forward in this existence, O bhikṣuṇīs, you should pay homage to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī as the senior of the Saṃgha, the most eminent of the Saṃgha, and the elder of the Saṃgha.
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, having extended her joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, these eight weighty rules for the bhikṣuṇīs which were spoken by the Blessed One in brief—may we receive them in their detailed exposition?"
19. The Blessed One said: "It is possible.
He asked:

How then, Gautamī, must a nun who has been ordained for a hundred years perform the acts of salutation, prostration, rising to greet, joining of palms, and respectful service toward a monk who has been ordained on that very day?
From now on, a nun must not expect [to be exempt from these duties].

"When I have been ordained for a hundred years and a monk has been ordained for only one day, at that time I shall perform the acts of salutation, prostration, rising from my seat, joining my palms, and respectful service toward him.
Then indeed, all the nuns— whether elders, juniors, or those of middle standing— [must show respect] toward all monks, whether elders or juniors.
One should perform the acts of salutation, prostration, rising from one's seat, joining the palms in reverence, and respectful service toward those who are meditating.
Now, when these monks have entered the nuns' quarters,

all the nuns— whether elders, novices, or those of middle standing— must perform the acts of salutation, prostration, rising to greet, joining the palms, and respectful service toward all the monks, whether they be elders, novices, or those of middle standing.

21. Now, if a bhikṣuṇī is weak from old age or weak from illness, she should prostrate with her head at the feet of as many [of them] as she is able to reach. For the remaining ones, having placed her joined palms to her head, she should say: "I pay homage to the feet of all the noble ladies."

When these bhikṣuṇīs run out toward the bhikṣu-vihāra, they must all— whether elder, junior, or middle-ranking bhikṣuṇīs— bow their heads at the feet of all the bhikṣus, whether elders, juniors, or those of middle rank. Now, if a bhikṣuṇī is weak from old age or weak from illness, [then] as many [as there may be...]
[a] One should pay homage with the head at the feet of as many as one encounters; for the remainder, one should join the palms above the head and say:

"I pay homage with my head at the feet of all you venerable noble ones. 22. If that nun, out of contempt or disdain, addresses a monk as a "rustic monk," or as a "lazy monk," or as a "physician-monk," or as an "inept elder"—
Or thinking, "He is unwholesome" or "He is ignorant of how to respond," one does not bow the head to his feet; thus, one transgresses a weighty rule (guru-dharma).

The ṛṣi said:
"Furthermore, he should be made to understand through wisdom; if he is still young, he should be told:
'O kinsman, if you do not train now, when will you ever train?'"
But what now when you have become old, aged, advanced in years, and reached the end of your lifespan?
It would be good for you, it would be fitting, that you should teach, recite, be auspicious, virtuous, and desirous of training, and apply yourself to yoga in the teaching of the Buddhas.
85. Now, if he has become old, he should be told:
"At such a time as this, when you were once young, if you do not train yourself now, when will you ever train?"
"Now, when you have reached the entrance of the assembly hall, then you shall learn: even this retinue of yours, seeing you and following your example, will fall into ruin through improper conduct.
It is well for you, it is fitting for you, that you should teach and recite [the scriptures], being auspicious, virtuous, and desirous of training;
that you apply yourself to yoga within the teaching of the Buddhas—this is what that nun [should do]."

Whether out of knowledge or out of contempt, whether calling him a "rustic monk," a "physician-monk," or a "shaveling monk," or saying he is "unsteady, old, ignorant of proper conduct, and unskilled," if one speaks thus after having provoked him, he transgresses a rule of respect (*guru-dharma*).

86. It is not permissible for a monk to speak to a nun with the verbal path [of abuse], whether truthfully or falsely; it is not allowed for a monk to provoke a nun and say, "Shaven-headed woman! Cut-off-mouthed one! (i.e., one who has abandoned the taking of food).
If she speaks thus, she incurs an offense of transgression of discipline (*vinayātikrama*).
87. Now, if a nun is the mother or sister of a monk, and she is either flighty or arrogant;
It is not permissible to neglect her if she is still young.
She should be told:
"O relative, if you do not train now, when will you ever train?"

"What now? When you have become aged, old, and advanced in years, it would be well for you and appropriate for you that you should teach, recite, be excellent, virtuous, desirous of training, and apply yourself to the teaching of the Buddhas. 88. Now, when she has become old...
She should be told:

"O relative, you are like this now; what were you like in your youth? You do not train yourself now; when will you train? When you have reached the door of the assembly hall, then you will train. Furthermore, this assembly of yours, seeing you and following your example, will fall into ruin through such improper conduct."

"This is good for you, this is fitting for you, that you should teach, that you should recite, that you should be auspicious, virtuous, and desirous of training, and that you should apply yourself to the teaching of the Buddhas.
Gautami, this is the range of speech of the monks toward the nuns, whether it be true or false."
The path of speech for monks toward nuns must be open, based on what is true and not on what is untrue.

This, Gautamī, is the third heavy rule (gurudharma) of the nuns, which must be honored by the nuns as long as they live and never transgressed, just as the shoreline cannot be overstepped by the great ocean.

Guru-dharma 4.89: Now, Gautamī, how is it that the foremost of the alms-food, the foremost of the bedding and seating, and the foremost of the monastery must be assigned by the bhikṣuṇīs to the community of bhikṣus?
Now, if someone is providing a meal for the community of bhikṣuṇīs, he should be told: "Perform it according to the order of seniority.
If he then says, "I have no faith or confidence in that," he should be told: [to proceed as before].

"We also do not accept it. Then he said: "It was never given to the noble ones by my mother, nor by my father, nor through a connection with a social circle, nor through a connection with a guild, nor through a connection with a covenant; it has never been given to the noble ones by me."

"Alms have been prepared previously; may the noble ladies accept them. Even if one causes [the donor] to give as little as a single portion of alms-food, the community of nuns may accept food of a hundred flavors for the community of monks; there is no offense.
90. Now, what is the excellence of lodgings?
Now, if some person gives bedding and seating to the community of nuns, [the recipient] should say, "Give it according to the order of seniority.
If he then says, "I have no faith or confidence in that," [the donor] should be told: "It must be said; it must be said."
"We also do not accept it. Then he said,
"Noble lady, bedding and seating have been given to me by my mother, or [given] up to the point of being connected with the occasion, for the community of monks."

"May the noble ladies accept [this]"; even if she has given as little as a small bed for the community of monks, if the community of nuns accepts highly valuable bedding and seats, there is no offense.
91. What now is "the foremost monastery"?
Now, if someone is establishing a monastery for the community of nuns,
it should be said:
"Establish it according to the seniority of the turn."
Then he said:
"Noble lady, I have no faith there; I have no serene confidence."
"It should be said: 'We also do not accept it.
Then he said:
"Noble lady, these monasteries have been built for them by your mother or by others through a connection of kinship; may the noble ladies accept the monasteries."
"Even if one gives as little as a cow-dung hut or a flour-hut to the community of monks, if the community of nuns accepts even a seven-storied monastery, there is no offense.
92. "Those nuns, out of contempt or disdain, [address them] as 'barber-monks' or 'physician-monks'..."

If one who does not know the difference between the unqualified and the qualified, having prepared the foremost meal, the foremost bedding and seating, or the foremost dwelling, does not satisfy the community of monks, she transgresses a heavy rule (*guru-dharma*).
Thus, Gautamī, the community of monks must be satisfied by the nuns with the foremost meal, the foremost bedding and seating, and the foremost dwelling.
This, Gautamī, is the fourth heavy rule for the nuns, which must be honored by the nuns as long as they live and never transgressed, just as the shoreline cannot be overstepped by the great ocean.
Now, regarding the procedure for a nun who has committed a heavy offense (gurudharma): she must undergo a half-month of penance (mānatva) and seek reinstatement before both Saṃghas.

Now, when that nun has fallen into a heavy offense (gurudharma), she must undergo a period of penance (mānatva) for half a month within the community of nuns (bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha), as well as a formal reconciliation before both communities.
If that nun, out of contempt or disdain, or thinking "I am unskilled," does not undergo the penance for half a month within the community of nuns,
nor perform the formal reconciliation before both communities, [she commits an offense].
She transgresses a heavy rule.
This, Gautamī, is the fifth heavy rule for the bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored by the bhikṣuṇīs for as long as life lasts, just as the ocean honors its shore. This is the sixth heavy rule.

94. Why is it that every half-month the bhikṣuṇīs must expect the approach of the bhikṣu-saṃgha for instruction? On the day that the *poṣadha* occurs, on that very day the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha must go to the bhikṣu-vihāra. Now, if the entire saṃgha does not go, at least half the saṃgha must go.

If half the Saṃgha does not go, it must be accompanied by at least eight senior nuns. If those eight senior nuns do not go, they must at least take the formal consent (*chanda*) from as many as possible—down to those who have been wandering for a month or even a fortnight—and then go. If there is time, the stūpa should first be paid homage.
Having paid homage to the stūpa, the formal consent (chanda) should be given to whichever monk there is who is distinguished or well-known.
He should say: "I pay homage to the noble Saṃgha.
The noble Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, being united, bows its head at the feet of the united Bhikṣu-saṃgha."
He approaches for instruction and requests the Dharma;
he also accepts the Poṣadha.
This should be stated a second and a third time.

95. Then he said: "I am the Elder of the Saṅgha, I am the instructor there, I am the exhorter of the nuns. Having set aside these three, the remaining [monks] must give their consent (*chanda*). Having given their consent, they must go to the nuns' quarters (*bhikṣuṇī-upāśraya*).

At the time when the community of nuns (bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha) has sat down for the Poṣadha ceremony and the reciter of the Sūtras has taken up the Sūtra: "Let the noble Saṃgha listen to me. Today for the Saṃgha there is either the fourteenth-day or the fifteenth-day Poṣadha, or it is the conjunction-Poṣadha. This is the pure constellation; so much of the season has passed, so much remains. What is the prior duty of the Saṃgha?"
"The community of the Blessed One’s female disciples shines with few concerns and few duties. Announce the purity of intention (*chandapariśuddhi*) for the noble ladies who have not yet arrived.
Having been brought [the message] by the messengers of intention, they should ascend to the end of the senior nuns, perform the proper salutation (*sāmīci*), and say:
"The intention has been brought by us, the messengers of intention; it has been accepted by the noble lady named so-and-so."

96. At the time when the community of monks (bhikṣu-saṃgha) has sat down and the reciter of the Sūtras (sūtroddeśaka) has received the Sūtra: "Let the venerable Saṃgha listen to me. Today for the Saṃgha there is either the fourteenth or the fifteenth day, a conjunction (sandhi), a Poṣadha, or an auspicious lunar mansion (viśuddhi-nakṣatra). So much of the season has passed; so much remains."
"Has the Saṅgha already performed its preliminary duties? The Blessed One’s community of disciples shines when it has few concerns and few tasks.
Venerable sirs, announce the consent and purity of those monks who have not yet arrived, and report back once they have been announced."
Whichever monk is the messenger of the will for the nuns, he should rise, go to the place of the elders, and say:
"I pay homage to the noble Saṅgha. The entire community of nuns, being united, bows its head at the feet of the united [Saṅgha] and requests instruction."
And he accepts the *poṣadha*.
This should be stated a second and a third time as well.
If there is an appointed instructor of the nuns (*bhikṣuṇī-ovādaka*) present there, it should be said: "The instruction has been given."
97. Now, if there is no one at all who is an exhorter of the bhikṣuṇīs, then whoever is endowed with twelve qualities should be formally appointed.
With which twelve? They are as follows:
He dwells restrained by the Prātimokṣa vows, perfected in conduct and sphere of activity;
seeing danger in even the slightest faults, he trains himself having undertaken the rules of training, endowed with pure bodily and vocal action,
and possessed of a completely purified livelihood.
He is learned in the Abhidharma and learned in the Abhivinaya; he is capable of training others in the training of higher ethics (adhiśīla-śikṣā);
he is capable of training them in the training of higher mind (adhicitta-śikṣā);
and he is capable of training them in the training of higher wisdom (adhiprajñā-śikṣā).
He is one whose holy life is uncorrupted.
Grā.
He who is of a nature characterized by abundant patience;
hrā;
and he does not commit a grave offense against the nuns.
He is one whose speech is wholesome and who is endowed with the practice of wholesome speech;
he is possessed of speech that is refined, clear, unambiguous, and capable of making the meaning understood;
and he is twenty years of age, or more than twenty years of age.
A monk endowed with these twelve qualities should be formally appointed by the Saṃgha as the instructor of the nuns.
98. The formal act (karma) must be performed by the officiating officer (karmakāraka):
"Let the venerable Saṃgha hear me: this monk named so-and-so is endowed with the [required] qualities."
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha appoint the monk named so-and-so as the instructor of the nuns by formal authorization. This is the motion (*jñapti*).
Let the venerable Saṃgha hear me: this monk named so-and-so—this Saṃgha appoints this monk named so-and-so as the instructor of the nuns by formal authorization.
For those venerable ones who approve of appointing the monk named so-and-so as the instructor of the nuns by formal authorization through the Saṃgha...
Therefore, he remains silent.
Whoever does not approve, let him speak.
This is the first formal proclamation; likewise the second and the third formal proclamation.

"Venerable sirs, the Saṃgha has authorized the monk named so-and-so as the instructor of the bhikṣuṇīs by a formal act of the Saṃgha. It is pleasing to the Saṃgha because of its silence; thus do I hold it to be so. 99. Now, being thus authorized, that monk must instruct those bhikṣuṇīs neither at an improper time nor in an improper place.
Not in a future time;
not in a past time;
not according to one's own will.
Not distractedly;
not with a retinue;
not with long-winded speech.
One who desires to come should be sent for.
Now, what is meant by "the wrong time"? The wrong time is when the sun has set.
And the dawn has passed.
Why then "not in a public place"? A public place (*adeśa*) means in the vicinity of a brothel or a gambling house.
Near a tavern,
or near a liquor shop,
or near an execution or prison house, or in a place that is too secluded or too exposed.
What, then, is the time that has not yet come? It is the future time, namely the first day of the lunar fortnight or the second.
What, then, is the time that has not passed?
It is the past time, namely the fourteenth or the fifteenth day of the lunar fortnight.
Now, indeed, she should be exhorted starting from the third day up until the thirteenth. Why then not according to one's own will?
The consent (*chanda*) must be given by the nun to the one who exhorts her.
Now, indeed, everyone must come. Why is it that they do not come together? A monk must not exhort a disordered community of nuns.
Then indeed, all of them together should be exhorted:
"Why now is there no exhortation for the assembly?
You must not exhort the assembly yet; today is not your turn to exhort the assembly; today is not your turn to exhort the assembly."
Now, indeed, they should all be exhorted together. Why then are they not exhorted with a long discourse?
Rather, they should be exhorted in brief.
To refrain from all evil, to cultivate the wholesome,
and to purify one's own mind— this is the teaching of the Buddhas.
Sisters, this is the exhortation; the remainder shall be a formal discourse. Whoever wishes to come, let her come; whoever wishes to listen, let her listen.
100. Now, what should be sent for one who wishes to come?
If that monk who is the instructor of the nuns has gone to another region, then those who are his co-residents or pupils should be encouraged by the community of nuns [with these words]:
"Go, bring the noble one's bowl and robe."
Now, as they go and come, there must be no lack of provisions on the road.
When one is approaching, the community of nuns should go out to meet him for a distance of one *yojana* with parasols, banners, and flags.
Having entered whichever monastery [the nuns have come], food must be provided there for both Saṅghas for seven days.
Now, if the Bhikṣuṇī-saṅgha is poor, food must be provided for the Bhikṣu-saṅgha alone for seven days.
At the very least, they must be honored with even a single alms-offering. Furthermore, that monk who instructs the nuns (bhikṣuṇī-ovādaka) should maintain the perception of them as his own daughters.
Those nuns should maintain the perception of their father toward that monk who exhorts the nuns.
101. It is not permissible for that monk who exhorts the nuns to exhort them by stretching out his neck like a horse.
Rather, he should look only as far as the distance of a yoke; they should not be exhorted [if he looks further than that].
If, at some time, there should be [an indication] there by a whorl of hair,
or by arched eyebrows, or by robes that have been beaten and rubbed,
or by a white waist-band.
Or with variegated sandals or shoes. It is not permissible to neglect this;
if she is young, she must be subdued.

"You are not training now in that which is unmanifest and unskillful; when will you train? When you have become aged, decrepit, elderly, and have reached the end of your life's journey, even this assembly of yours, seeing you and following your example, will fall into ruin through such misconduct."
This is good for you, this is fitting for you, that you, being auspicious, virtuous, and desirous of training, apply yourself to yoga in the teaching of the Buddhas.
Now, if she is an elder, it should be said:
"O kinswoman, what has become of you now? What were you like in your youth? You do not train yourself now; when will you ever train?

When you have reached the gate of the assembly hall, even this retinue of yours, seeing you, will fall into imitation and thus come to ruin. It would be well for you, it would be fitting for you [to act otherwise]."
"You are auspicious, virtuous, and desirous of training; you apply yourself to the practice within the teaching of the Buddhas.
102. Now, when that instructor of the bhikṣuṇīs has gone out for alms and sees the bhikṣuṇīs on the street with their hair curled or their eyes painted.
Nor with beaten garments,
nor with a white waistband,
nor with variegated sandals; now it is not permitted to say anything at all.
"Let no one speak in reproach, saying: 'Look, sirs! This little śramaṇa is exhorting his female disciple as if she were his wife!
Rather, you should ask:
'In which dwelling does she reside?'"
Who is her preceptor?
Who is her teacher? It was stated previously that having gone there, she should be instructed.
Yet this nun, out of contempt or disdain, or treating him as a "stunted" monk (*koṇṭa-bhikṣu*), [acts thus].
Whether regarding them as "physician-monks" or "shaveling-monks," or regarding them as "mediocre,
incompetent, unskilled, and ignorant of the proper way," if one does not expect the community of monks to come for the fortnightly exhortation, one transgresses a weighty rule (guru-dharma).
Thus, Gautamī, the community of monks must be expected by the nuns for the fortnightly exhortation every half-month.

She does not expect [to receive] a heavy duty; she does not transgress it. This, Gautamī, is the sixth heavy duty for the bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored by the bhikṣuṇīs as long as life lasts and never transgressed, just as the shoreline is not overstepped by the great ocean.
The seventh heavy duty.
103. Why is it not permissible for bhikṣuṇīs to enter the rains retreat in a residence where there are no bhikṣus?
It is not permissible for bhikṣuṇīs to enter the rains retreat in villages or towns where there are no bhikṣus.
Now, if a bhikṣuṇī is invited by her relatives who dwell in a village...
In this case, if it is the end of the rainy season retreat and there are no monks present there, but the nuns wish to show compassion toward their kinsmen, they should say:
"First, invite the senior assembly.
Then, they might say:
"We have no faith there; we have no serene confidence.
Thus it should be said.
I, too, do not desire it. But now, if a nun possesses wealth and wishes to show compassion toward her kinsmen, [she may do so].
One should personally invite the monks; once they have arrived, one must ensure they lack nothing by way of food. They should enter the rains retreat there.
That nun, having spent the rains retreat there, must expect to approach those monks for the fortnightly exhortation (*ovāda*).
Now, while those monks have entered the rains retreat,
if during the middle of the rains some danger should arise and they rise up and flee, [the nun shall not be held at fault].
Now, it is not permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to go anywhere until the time of the *pravāraṇā*.
If there is safety, then they [the local nuns] should be summoned;
but not those who have arrived as guests.
Now, indeed, they should be invited by means of what has been spoken.
Having honored those who have arrived with food and having clothed them, one should give according to the distribution.
When an invitation has been made, even if he goes wherever his inclination leads him, there is no offense.
105. If that nun, out of contempt or disdain, treating him as a "stunted monk" (*koṇṭa-bhikṣu*),

or treating him as a "physician-monk" (*vaidya-bhikṣu*), or treating him as a "shaven-headed monk" (*cūḍa-bhikṣu*), or treating him as one who is "stupid, old, unskilled, and ignorant of the nature of things," enters the rains retreat in a residence where no monks are present, she transgresses a heavy rule (*guru-dharma*).
Thus, Gautamī, it is not permitted for a bhikṣuṇī to enter the rains retreat in a residence where no bhikṣus are present.

This, Gautamī, is the seventh heavy rule (guru-dharma) for bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored by the bhikṣuṇīs for as long as life lasts, and which must not be transgressed, just as the shoreline cannot be overstepped by the great ocean. The eighth heavy rule.
106. Now, after the rainy season has been spent, the invitation (*pravāraṇā*) must be expected from both Saṃghas.

On the very day that the Saṃgha’s invitation takes place, on that same day the bhikṣuṇīs must perform their invitation. On the following day, at dawn on the first day of the lunar fortnight, they should go out and proceed to the bhikṣu monastery.

If the entire community of monks is assembled, it is not permitted for all the nuns to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony simultaneously from first to last. Rather, one nun capable of presiding over the *pravāraṇā* must be formally appointed as the *pravāraṇā*-leader.
That nun must be competent to conduct the *pravāraṇā*.
107. Then the karma-maker should perform the formal act (karma):
"May the noble Saṃgha listen to me.
This nun, named so-and-so, is capable of conducting the invitation ceremony (pravāraṇā)."
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣuṇī named so-and-so as the one who performs the *pravāraṇā* for the Saṃgha.
This is the motion (*jñapti*). Let the noble Saṃgha listen to me.
This nun named so-and-so is capable of conducting the *pravāraṇā*.
The Saṃgha appoints this nun named so-and-so as the *pravāraṇā*-officer for the Saṃgha.
For those noble ladies who approve of the appointment of this nun named so-and-so as the *pravāraṇā*-officer by the Saṃgha, [let them remain silent].
She who approves of this remains silent;
she who does not approve should speak.
This is the first proclamation of the formal act.

In this way, the second and third formal proclamations (*karma-vācanā*) are to be recited: "Noble ladies, the one named so-and-so has been approved by the Saṃgha as the *pravāraṇā*-officiant for the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha consents to this, since there is silence. Thus do I understand it."
108. Then all [the nuns] should stand at the end of the seniors.
Then that *pravāraṇā*-officer should say:
"The entire community of nuns invites the entire community of monks regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected."

"May the noble Saṃgha exhort us—being desirous of our welfare, seeking our benefit, and compassionate—out of compassion, knowing, seeing, and remembering, so that we may act in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
This is to be said a second and a third time.
Now, if the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha is complete and there are many Bhikṣus present...
It should be said: "The entire community of nuns invites the many monks regarding what has been seen, heard, and [suspected], up to: 'We shall make amends.
A second time, and a third time."

109. Now, if the community of nuns is complete and there is one monk present, it should be said: "The complete community of nuns invites the noble one regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected; we shall make amends. This is to be said a second and a third time as well.
Now, if there are many bhikṣuṇīs and the bhikṣu-saṃgha is complete, they should say:
"Venerable ladies, we, being many, invite the complete bhikṣu-saṃgha for the *pravāraṇā* regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected; we shall make amends accordingly."
In this same way, a second and a third time as well.
Now, if there are many bhikṣuṇīs and many bhikṣus present, it should be said:
A great number of noble ladies invite a great number of noble gentlemen by means of what has been seen, heard, or suspected, up to:
"We shall deal with it according to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya.
Thus a second and a third time.
Now, if there are many bhikṣuṇīs and there is only one bhikṣu,
it should be said:
A great number of noble ladies invite the noble one for the *pravāraṇā*: "By what has been seen, heard, or suspected, we shall deal with you according to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya.
This is said a second time and a third time.
Now, if there is but one [noble lady]...
There is a nun;
and the Saṃgha is in harmony. It should be said:
"I, [name], invite the Saṃgha regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the noble Saṃgha exhort me; I shall make amends. Thus a second and a third time.
Now, if she is alone...
If there is a single bhikṣuṇī and many bhikṣus,
it should be said:
I, [name], invite the many venerable sirs regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
May the venerable sirs instruct me; I shall act according to the Dharma as is appropriate. Thus a second and a third time.
Now, if there is then a single bhikṣuṇī and a single bhikṣu.
One should say:
"I, [name], invite the noble one regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.

May the noble one, desiring my welfare, seeking my benefit, compassionate, and out of compassion, exhort me—knowing, seeing, and remembering—so that, according to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya, I may act accordingly."
In this way, a second and a third time as well. 110.
That nun, whether out of contempt or out of disdain, having treated him as a "stunted monk" (koṇṭabhikṣu):

Whether he is regarded as a physician-monk, or as a shaven-headed monk, or as one who is incompetent, undisciplined, unskilled, and ignorant of proper conduct— if, after having spent the rains retreat, he does not participate in the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) of both Saṅghas, he transgresses a heavy rule (*guru-dharma*).
In this way, Gautamī, the invitation (pravāraṇā) must be requested by the nuns who have completed the rains-retreat from both Saṅghas.

This, Gautamī, is the eighth weighty rule (gurudharma) for the nuns, which must be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by the nuns as long as they live, and not transgressed, just as the shore is not overstepped by the great ocean.

Gautamī, these are the eight *guru-dharmas* for the bhikṣuṇīs, which must be honored, revered, respected, and venerated by the bhikṣuṇīs for as long as they live, and which are not to be transgressed, just as the tide cannot be overstepped by the great ocean. [These are] the *pārājika* dharmas.

111. Sexual Intercourse. Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣuṇīs: "Therefore, bhikṣuṇīs, from this day forward, you shall regard Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī as the elder of the Saṅgha, the senior of the Saṅgha, and the leader of the Saṅgha."
“Blessed One, these four dharmas leading to defeat which have been taught by the Blessed One after direct realization—may we, O Blessed One, be permitted to hear them in detail?
The Blessed One said, “It is permitted, Gautamī.
For a daughter of noble family who possesses faith and perceives five purposes, it is sufficient to point out the discipline.”
Sufficient for maintaining the Vinaya as it is in the Bhikṣu-vinaya.

113. Gautamī, on one occasion the Tathāgata was dwelling at Śrāvastī. Then, indeed, the Elder Śāriputra [asked], up to: "What, O Blessed One, is the cause, what is the reason, by which here some Tathāgatas..."

Into the urinary tract, or into one or another opening of a wound, or into a sexual organ, he inserts his own sexual organ; having caused pain, he relishes it—
he relishes it at the beginning,

finds pleasure in it, or savors the taste, she commits an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
At the beginning it does not taste sweet; in the middle it tastes sweet;
at the end it tastes sweet.
Up to the point that she becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense:
at the beginning she does not relish it;
in the middle she does not relish it.
If she relishes it at the conclusion and brings the tasting to its fulfillment, she becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense;
[if] she does not relish it at the beginning,
nor does she relish it in the middle.

Likewise, if one inserts the genitals into the genitals of one who is asleep or dead and experiences distress;

"In this way it is alluring, in this way it is desirable, in this way it is deceptive, in this way it is intoxicating, in this way it is captivating, and in this way it creates an obstacle to the attainment of unsurpassed security (*yoga-kṣema*).
Just as a man’s touch of a woman, or a woman’s touch of a man, now withers away through constant indulgence."
Now, she did it again and again.
Then that nun was told by the other nuns:

She then said,
"In this way, it is comfortable for me.

She was then called.

consented to the robbing and further robbing of a man who was himself corrupted, [taking] above the knees and below the armpits?"
He replied, "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

"You have acted wrongly regarding the kingdom! I speak of abandonment;
I speak of transcending.
Yet here you are, practicing such an evil and unwholesome state as this.
This is not the Dharma in the kingdom; this is not the Vinaya;
such is not the teaching of the Teacher.
"It should not be done in this way;
for one who acts in this way, there is no increase in wholesome qualities.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:

"Call together, Gautamī, the bhikṣuṇīs— whatever bhikṣuṇīs there are who dwell in dependence upon the city of Kapilavastu. Then the Blessed One, having perceived that the community of bhikṣuṇīs had assembled, related this matter to the bhikṣuṇīs in detail.
... [as before] ...
until they have become completely purified.

If a nun, being lustful, consents to the touching or stroking by a lustful man below the armpits and above the knees, this nun also is one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion. "If a nun" means:
