She saw: "If she pursues me now, then my gain and honor will perish."
She was restrained and expelled by her.
Now, unable to endure her afflictions, she became intimate with the monastery attendants and wandering mendicants;
consequently, she conceived, and her womb became enlarged.
That nun was expelled by the nuns.
Then those nuns said:
"Noble Kālī, do you know that she has become mixed with householders and wandering mendicants?"
He said: "I know;
it was for this reason that they spoke thus."
For what reason did you not inform me? Why do you not speak? I see that had I informed [you], [this would not have happened].
"She will go home;
this gain and honor of mine will be lost.
132. The nuns [reported] this matter to the [Mahā-]bhikṣuṇīs.
They informed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī;
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Call Kālī.
She was called.
Then the Blessed One questioned her about all of that in detail.
He replied, "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
It is a transgression for you, Kālī!
How can it be that you, Kālī, knowingly conceal a nun who has fallen into a grave offense?
This, Kālī, is not the Dharma; this is not the Vinaya.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Gautamī, assemble the bhikṣuṇīs—however many bhikṣuṇīs there are who dwell in dependence upon the city of Vaiśālī. [And so on, until] the training rule was laid down.

If a nun, knowing that another nun has committed and repeatedly practiced a grave offense, conceals it— neither informing others in private, nor in a large group, nor in the midst of the Saṃgha— [she commits an offense].
When that bhikṣuṇī has fallen away from the bhikṣuṇīs— being dead, deceased, collapsed, or having departed from this Dharma and Vinaya—
then she might say to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"I have understood" (*ājñāpanī*).
"Venerable lady, I have committed a grave offense (*duṣṭhullā-āpatti*) that has been habitually practiced by the nun named so-and-so.
I would not reveal this to others; why is this so? [She says: "Because of her..."
"Let others know [it]!"—
this nun becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*). [The rest is] as before.
"Knowing" means she should know it herself, or hear it from another, by means of a formal seeing or hearing.
"A grave offense" means any one of the eight grave offenses that has been committed or practiced;
"she should not report it to others" means she should not speak of it;
"by herself alone" means by one person.
"Among the great multitude" means among two or three;
"in the midst of the Saṅgha" means in a complete Saṅgha;
"fallen away" means she has fallen away from the holy life (brahmacarya).
"Dead" means she has passed away.
"Seated in despair" means she has entered the state of a householder.
"Transgressed from this Dharma and Vinaya" means she has gone over to the sphere of other sectarians.
Then that nun might say this to the nuns:
"Venerable ladies, I indeed knew that such-and-such a nun had committed a grave offense and had habitually practiced it."
She said: "I shall not tell others; why? So that others may not know of this."
This nun also becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
"Beyond" (*pāra*) is said to mean the knowledge of the Dharma. [The rest is] as before.
Up to the formal designation:
133. This nun sees another nun committing a grave offense (duṣṭhulla-āpatti) after dawn has risen, yet she does not form the intention to conceal it.
If, at the time of sunrise, having conceived the intention to conceal [the offense], she conceals it until the dawn has broken, this nun becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
In this manner, two periods and eight permutations are to be applied,
just as in the case of concealment in the *Bhikṣu-vinaya*.

If this nun sees another nun committing a grave offense (duṣṭhulla-āpatti), she must then inform yet another nun. Now, if it is her pupil (antevāsini) or her co-resident (sārdha-vihāriṇī) who sees it, [she must inform her].
If she conceals [the offense] out of attachment, thinking, "If I report this now, the nuns will expel her," she becomes guilty of a *pārājika*.
Now, suppose that nun sees another nun committing an offense;
she then reports it to the other, saying, "I have seen such-and-such a nun commit a grave offense (*duṣṭhula*)."
She did not confess her offense.
I thought, "If she were to report it now, she would be expelled by the bhikṣuṇīs," and so I concealed it.
She too thought, "If I were to report it, both of us would be expelled."
Thinking, "They will conceal it," she conceals it; she too becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
In this way, as many as conceal it, all of them become ones who have committed a *pārājika* offense.
This nun sees another nun committing a grave offense (duṣṭhulla-āpatti). She informs others:
"The nun named so-and-so has committed a grave offense."
She then said,
"You have committed a misdeed by reporting it to me;
lest you report it to another as well," and she incurs a *thūl'-accaya* offense.
If this nun sees another nun committing a grave offense (duṣṭhulla-āpatti),
she must report it to another.
However, if she is fierce or acts with violence, and she sees [the offense], [she must still report it].
"If [she thinks], 'It will not cause an obstacle to his life or an obstacle to his holy life,' she obtains equanimity; there is no offense.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun, knowing that another nun has committed and repeatedly practiced a grave offense (duṣṭhullā āpatti), should conceal it..."
She should not report this to others— whether to a small group, a large crowd, or in the midst of the Saṅgha—
when that nun has fallen away from the nuns, being dead, deceased, gone, fallen, or having departed from this Dharma and Vinaya.
Now, if a nun should say this to other nuns: "I know,
Noble Lady, that such-and-such a nun has committed and perpetrated a grave offense (*duṣṭhullāpatti*)."
Thinking, "I shall not inform others;
let no one else know of this," that nun also becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion.
Pārājika-dharma 8: Following one who has been suspended.
134. For what purpose the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, has appeared in this world—[that purpose...]
Having considered the matter...
[as before] ...wandering through various monasteries, he stayed at Kauśāmbī in the Ghoṣitārāma.
Now the venerable Chandaka was repeatedly committing one or another offense from among the five classes of offenses.
He was addressed by the monks: "Venerable Chandaka, do you see this offense?"
Then he said:
"I do not see him; do you all see him? Let them see that he has passed away."
"What use have I for this wicked woman?
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, if this Chandaka suppresses one or another offense among the five classes of offenses,
and he does not perceive that offense,
let the Saṃgha perform a formal act of suspension against him for his failure to perceive the offense."
The Saṃgha has performed an act of suspension against him;
he does not share in the communal enjoyment of either the Dharma or material goods.
Now, his mother resides in another nunnery.
Having gone there, he said:
"O kinsman, I have been suspended by the Saṃgha;
they do not share with me either the enjoyment of the Dharma or the enjoyment of material goods."
She then said,
"Noble Chandaka,
you are not my equal; I shall share with you the enjoyment of the Dharma and the enjoyment of material things."
She was then living together with him, both in the enjoyment of the Dharma and in the enjoyment of material things.
She was then addressed by the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Noble lady, this noble Chandaka has been suspended by the entire Saṃgha, in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and he has not yet performed the act of atonement."
"Noble lady, do not follow this monk.
The Blessed One said:
"Noble ladies, may there be no harm; as for me, I likewise shall not follow this monk."
Who else will comply?
I shall comply with this monk. For what purpose [should I not comply]? For what purpose should I not comply with him?
Those bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī;
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī reported it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

If this nun Chandakamātā continues to side with the monk Chandaka, who has been suspended by the complete Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and who has not yet performed penance, then go and admonish her three times in private, three times in a group, and three times in the midst of the Saṃgha, for the sake of making her relinquish this matter. Now she is addressed in private: "Is it true, noble lady Chandakamātā, that you continue to side with the venerable Chandaka, who has been suspended by the complete Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and who has not yet performed penance?"
He said: "Are you then called Kuv-egā?
Noble lady, do not follow the noble Chandaka, who has been suspended by the complete Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and who has not yet performed the act of atonement."

"Indeed, noble Chanda’s mother, whatever you do for your friend who desires your welfare and seeks your benefit, that friend of yours has spoken but one word. Two words remain; desist! [She replied: 'I will not desist. Thus a second time, and thus a third time."
In this manner, an inquiry must be conducted among the great assembly in the midst of the Saṅgha until she says, "I shall desist.
135. The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Blessed One:

"Blessed One, the noble Chandakamātā has arrived; she has been summoned three times in private, three times before the great assembly, and three times in the midst of the Saṅgha for the relinquishing of this matter, yet she has not [desisted]."
She desists.
The Blessed One said:
"Call Chandakamātā."
She was then summoned.
The Blessed One said,
"Is it true, Chandaka-mātā?"

"Is it true that you, [name], are eating together with the monk Chanda, who has been suspended by the complete Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and who has not yet performed expiation?
You have been approached three times in private, three times in a group, and three times in the midst of the Saṃgha for the purpose of relinquishing this matter, yet you do not relinquish it.
"It is true, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, Chandaka-mātā!
Indeed, Chandaka-mātā, I have on many occasions censured and spoken in dispraise of obstinacy; yet you, for your part, are harsh, rigid, perverse, and one who grasps things in a contrary way."
"Chandaka’s mother, this is not the Dharma;
this is not the Vinaya; this is not the Teacher’s instruction.
One must not act thus; one must not do thus."
For one who acts in this way, there is no increase in wholesome qualities.
And now, knowing this, you are siding with a monk who has been suspended by the complete Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.

Therefore, it is not permissible for one who knows to side with a monk who has been suspended by the complete Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, as long as he has not performed the act of atonement.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī: "Gautamī, assemble the nuns— whatever number of nuns there are who dwell in dependence on the city of Kauśāmbī—
until the training rule has been prescribed."
136. “Again, ‘a nun’ means one who is fully ordained.
‘Knowing’ means she knows it herself or hears it from another, through a formal basis for seeing or a formal basis for hearing.
‘By a united Saṃgha’ means by one that is not divided.”
By not seeing an offense according to the Dharma and Vinaya, by not making amends for an offense, and by not relinquishing three types of views—
one is "suspended" (utkṣipta), meaning one is made to live apart from the community;
"not restored" (apratikṛta) means one has not been readmitted.
"She should attend upon" means she should associate with him either through the enjoyment of material things or through the enjoyment of the Dharma.
That bhikṣuṇī should be addressed by the bhikṣuṇīs in this way:
"Venerable lady, this bhikṣu has been [suspended] by the complete Saṃgha."
The full passage continues as before: if she should accept that very matter and not relinquish it— namely, that she follows a suspended monk (utkṣiptaka)—
that nun is like Chandakamātā.

"By the nuns" means: she is to be exhorted and admonished by the Saṃgha, by a group of many people, or by a single individual, up to three times—in private with a group of many people three times, and in the midst of the Saṃgha three times.
She is to be addressed in private as follows:

"Is it true, you [so-and-so], that you are following one who has been suspended by the complete Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and who has not yet performed the act of atonement? He says, "Yes.
Then she should be told:

"Noble lady, do not side with this monk named so-and-so who has been suspended by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya. Indeed, what that friend named so-and-so does for you—being desirous of your welfare and seeking your benefit—is precisely what she is doing for you. That friend has [spoken] but one word remaining; desist! Yet she says, 'I will not desist. A second time, and even a third time..."
[The full formula] as before: even in the midst of the Saṃgha, if she should relinquish that matter after a formal proclamation up to three times, that is well;
but if she does not relinquish it, this nun also becomes one who has committed a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.
"Pārājika" is the designation for the manifestation, disclosure, explanation, analysis, clarification, and making public of a pārājika offense.

137. If that nun, being exhorted and admonished three times in private regarding a matter that ought to be relinquished, does not relinquish it, she incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline (vinayātikrama) for each word [spoken].

If, after being exhorted or admonished three times by the great assembly, one does not relinquish a matter that ought to be relinquished, one incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline (*vinayātikrama*) for every word [spoken].
When one consents to the formal motion (*jñapti*) in the midst of the Saṃgha, one incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline.
When the first formal charge has been brought forward, one incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline.
If she has withdrawn [the charge] after the first speech, she incurs a grave offense (thūl'-accaya).

If she has withdrawn it after the second speech, she incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline (vinayātikrama). If she has withdrawn it after the third speech, she incurs a grave offense (thūl'-accaya).
When the third speech has been superimposed, one incurs a grave offense (thūl'-accaya);
when it has been removed, one becomes guilty of a defeat (pārājika). This is when she has fallen into an offense of defeat.

Whatever transgressions of the Vinaya and grave offenses (thūl’-atyaya) there may be—whether committed by individuals, by a great multitude, or in the midst of the Saṅgha—all of them are resolved; only one offense remains heavy:
namely, this Pārājika.
If one renounces it in the interim, one should be made to undergo the formal act regarding the five established offenses.
How, then, is that which is subject to relinquishment to be understood?
How was that which is not subject to relinquishment [understood] when you said,
"I will comply with the monk named so-and-so who has been suspended"?

"I have not followed [him], I do not follow [him], and I shall not follow [him]"—this is what constitutes being worthy of relinquishment. What then is "not worthy of relinquishment"? It is: "I shall follow such-and-such a monk who has been suspended."
"Now, [thinking] 'I have followed him, I do not follow him, and I shall follow him,' and thus [considering it] unworthy of relinquishment—this is how it should be seen as unworthy of relinquishment.
Therefore the Blessed One said:

'If a nun, knowing that a monk has been suspended by a complete Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and has not yet made amends, should continue to follow him, that nun should be addressed by the nuns as follows:'"
"For this noble monk has been suspended by the complete Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and he has not yet performed the act of atonement.
Do not follow after this monk.
Even when addressed thus by the other nuns, if that nun should persist in her course regarding that matter, [she is to be dealt with accordingly].

If she does not desist, that bhikṣuṇī is to be exhorted and admonished by the bhikṣuṇīs up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that matter. If, being exhorted and admonished up to three times, she relinquishes that matter, that is good.
And if she does not desist from it, this nun also becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion.
Summary verse:
Sexual misconduct, taking what is not given, killing, lying, and socializing— these eight things conceal one's faults.
The offense of following one who has been suspended.
The category is fulfilled.
The *pārājika* offenses are concluded. [Now follows] the *saṃcaritra*.

138. Regarding the offense of matchmaking (*saṃcaritra-karman*): for monks, everything is literal; as the Blessed One has said: "If a nun should engage in matchmaking—whether she conveys a woman’s intention to a man, or conveys a man’s intention to a woman, whether for marriage, or for a sexual liaison, or even for a momentary encounter—this rule is one involving an immediate offense (*prathamāpattika*) and is a *saṃghātiśeṣa*."
The Saṃghāvaśeṣa offense is to be resolved by relying upon the Saṃgha itself.
Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharma 2: Groundless.
The two [procedures] for those who speak untruthfully are to be performed exactly as they are for the monks.
... In this regard, the Blessed One said:
"If a nun, out of malice, being angry and displeased, should groundlessly charge a pure nun who is free from offense with a *pārājika* offense."
"Perhaps I might cause her to fall away from the holy life"— if, at a later time,

whether she is being formally examined or not being spoken to [about the matter], this legal case turns out to be groundless and the nun persists in her fault, saying, "I spoke in error," this too, in this category, is an offense involving a formal meeting of the Saṃgha (saṃghāvaśeṣa), entailing immediate confession.
Up to this point;
because of that slight [fault], the Blessed One said:

If a nun, being wicked, out of malice, angry, and displeased, should— on account of some minor, trifling matter that belongs to a different category of legal offense— accuse a nun who is not guilty of a *pārājika* offense with a *pārājika* offense, thinking, "In this way, perhaps I might cause her to fall away from the holy life (*brahmacarya*)," and if at a later time, when she is being examined or interrogated, it turns out that the legal case belongs to a different category and the matter belongs to a different category of legal offense; [then she is guilty of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense].
If a monk has taken up even a mere fraction of a fault, and a nun, standing upon that fault, says, "I speak of faults," it is a *saṃghātiśeṣa*.
Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharma 4:
Speaking with a Hidden Intention.
139. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, that was the site of both a bhikṣuṇī monastery and a heretical lodging,
situated between two walls;
that wall had collapsed.
Now, in that bhikṣuṇī-vihāra,
there was a resident bhikṣuṇī named Sthūlanandā.
She then said:
"O heretics, make this rag-robe!
You are devoid of shame and modesty, having fallen away from shame and modesty."

The noble ladies, being endowed with a sense of shame and dread of blame, will see them entering and exiting through the door at both the proper and improper times, and their minds will become afflicted.
They then said:
"This is the rainy season; when the rains have passed, we shall do it then."
She then said,
"Do it right now!
But they did not do it.
Then she reviled him: "Fallen from life,
lost from life,
with hopes shattered, you have fallen away from the vehicle of the gods."
— “O donkeys, you shall not do so! Why are you naked?”
"Shameless and without modesty, their sense of shame and dread of blame ruined, they hold wrong views and are fallen into ruin.
Make this rag-robe!
They then said, "O daughter of a fisherman, you who are as stout as a *vaḍa* or a *ḍiṅgara*, you wretched ascetic woman!"
"If you die, we shall not make this rag-robe. Then she went and informed [the king] while he was on his throne;
having reported all of this, she said, "Long-lived one, act in such a way that this rag-robe is made."
The attendants were faithful and devout;
they then said, "Call the stewards.
They were then summoned.
The Āsanikas said:
"O sons of a Hetikitikā! You are naked ascetics fallen from the wine-cup, donkeys for vehicles, and those cast down by false views."
"Go and make that rag-robe!
You are shameless and lack fear of wrongdoing, whereas the noble ladies are endowed with a sense of shame and dread of blame.
As you go out and [enter] at all times, both day and night—"

Seeing this, the noble ladies who lead the holy life will experience a change of heart; they are then appointed by those officials and compelled against their will. Day and night they must raise up the wall, while at night the rain falls upon them.
Now, as they were performing their labor for three months, that time passed. They then said:
"We shall do the work of preparing the clay for this daughter of an Itikitika, a female ascetic nourished on *vaḍa* and *ḍiṅgara*."

The lay followers were reproaching [the nuns], saying: "Look, householders! Your female renunciants, who are worthy of offerings, have had us forced to perform labor for three months against our will, on the pretext that 'I have work to do. The lay followers reported this matter to the *kulopika* nuns, and the nuns in turn reported it to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī."
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
"Call Nandā."
She was then summoned.
"Is it true, Nandā?
[and so forth].
Until they have become completely purified.

Furthermore, if a nun should dwell engaging in festive talk with householders or wanderers, for a day or even for a moment, at the very least together with monastery attendants or novice monks, this rule is also one involving an immediate offense.
"Any nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"Should live with contentious speech" means she should engage in quarreling.
"With householders" means with laypeople (*gṛhika*).
"By wandering mendicants" means by those ranging from the Gautamas to the Jaṭilakas.
"Throughout the day" means throughout the day of the sun.
"For a moment" means for that instant, for that brief duration.
"At the very least, with monastery attendants" means with those who serve the Saṅgha.
"With novice monks" means from those fifteen years of age up to those who are seventy.
One may dwell together [with them].
This dharma is also one of immediate offense, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The "Saṃgha" refers to the eight *pārājika* dharmas;
this offense among them is with remainder and requires remedial action.
“Saṃghātiśeṣa” means: the designation for the confession, the disclosure, the explanation, the analysis, the clarification, and the manifestation of an offense that is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If that nun announces it in a royal family or at a court, it is a *thūl'-accaya*;
if she causes it to be proclaimed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If one reports [the matter] to a family of lay followers (*upāsaka*) or to a faithful family (*śrāddha-kula*), there is a transgression of the discipline (*vinayātikrama*). If one causes [the matter] to be reported, it is a fault leading to restraint (*samvara-gāminī*);
even a monk who reports it to a royal household incurs a transgression of the discipline.
She reproaches [one who is] intent on restraint.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Whichever nun, moreover, [having] an excess..."

If one should dwell in discourse with householders or wandering mendicants for a day or even a moment, or at the very least with monastery attendants or novice śramaṇas, it is an offense entailing defeat; this is an offense of immediate transgression.
Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharma 5: Between Villages 141. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, there was a nun named Rāṣṭrā;
her sister, named Rāṣṭrapālā, had been married in a small village,
and she was still unmarried.
She sent word:
"Noble lady, come to Rāṣṭra; if you wish to see me while I am still alive.
She then went there.
She has passed away.
Now her brother-in-law is lamenting:
"Noble Rāṣṭrā, since your sister has passed away, who now will [care for] me?"
"She will look after the boy; who then will attend to this house of mine?
We must attend to the noble Rāṣṭrā.
Then she thought, "Indeed, these are evil winds that are blowing."
Having departed, she came to Śrāvastī and said to the bhikṣuṇīs: "Venerable ladies, I have been made to fall away from the holy life."
They said:
"What or how?
He then related this very matter in detail.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, in turn, reported it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Summon Rāṣṭrā.
She was then summoned,
and she was questioned in detail about all of that very matter.
“Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
“Is it true that you are traveling along a road without a nun?”
Therefore, it is not permissible, up until the point where the training rule has been prescribed. This is the origin of the matter: nuns were traveling along a road.
Now, another nun— graceful, beautiful, young, and full of vitality— having stepped off the path, sat down while breathing in or breathing out.
A caravan of men was approaching,
and they surrounded her.
They then said:
"Noble lady, you are gracious, beautiful to behold, young, and in the prime of youth. [What do you think of] sensual pleasures?"
"They are to be enjoyed.
Why have you gone forth? Or what is your cause for world-weariness?"
She said, "I have gone forth.
They said, "Tell us first, while they surround you and hold you back immediately thereafter."
Meanwhile, those bhikṣuṇīs had gone to another village.
Now, remorse arose within her,
and she reported it to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, it is an offense for one who acts unintentionally."
143. This is the origin of the matter: some bhikṣuṇīs were traveling along a road, and another bhikṣuṇī there was ill.
She crossed over to another village without the bhikṣuṇīs.
She then felt remorse and reported her remorse to Mahāprajāpatī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī reported it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
"There is no offense for one who is ill.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
"Let her assemble [the community], Gautamī. [The usual formula follows.
"Whatever nun should travel along a road without another nun, even as far as to the next village, except at the proper time—here, the 'proper time' is when the nun is unwilling [to go]."
Or one who is ill.
This is the occasion here.
This rule also entails an offense upon its first commission.
"Again, a bhikṣuṇī" refers to the [standard] formula.
A bhikṣuṇī who instructs [others] without a companion.

The journey along the road is three yojanas, two yojanas, or three yojanas; at the very least, it is the distance between villages. "Against her will" means she is obstructed by the carcass of an elephant, the carcass of a horse, the carcass of a cow, or the carcass of a human.
"Regarding 'one who is ill': she is either weak from old age or weak from disease.

There they experience suffering, intense and bitter sensations;
they groan, they cry out, and thus they call for rescue.
The circle of Śākyas, dear to their sisters and kinsmen—
their birthplace is delightful!
Alas, how delightful is Jambudvīpa!
"The Blessed One is a speaker of well-spoken words," they lamented.
At that time, a great multitude of people had gathered. Then the Blessed One, having dressed himself at the proper time and taking his bowl and robe, entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms.
He addressed the Venerable Ānanda:

"Whose mother is this Gautamī? There is a great clamor from a vast multitude of people; indeed, King Virūḍhaka has [dealt with] six Śākyan women, and they are crying out in their wretchedness until they say, 'The Blessed One is a speaker of well-spoken words!'"
"It would be well if the Blessed One, desiring their welfare and out of compassion for his kinsmen, would approach them.
Perhaps, having heard the Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One, they too might go to heaven.
Then the Blessed One directed his attention toward Śakra, the lord of the gods.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed Śacī:
"Śacī, the Blessed One is approaching his kinsmen out of compassion.
Go, Śacī, have those Śākyan women emerge from the moat and sit down with full awareness; have them cover themselves with garments, for the Blessed One will approach."

Then Śacī and those Śākyāyanīs, having lifted them out of the moat, sat them down with full awareness and covered them with garments. Then the Blessed One, having suffused them with the power of the goddess Indrāṇī, caused all their physical and mental states of suffering to subside.
He addressed the monks:
“Be satisfied, O monks, with the Blessed Ladies! For who, O monks, would delight in existence or cling to it, except for foolish commoners who are blind, sightless, and without vision?

Look, monks, at these Śākyan women who, having played, enjoyed themselves, and dallied with the five strands of human sensual pleasure, now experience painful sensations due to the destruction of their kin, the destruction of their wealth, and the manifestation of their karma.”
Then the Blessed One addressed those Śākyan women:
"Sisters, if you think this way: 'Even though your hands and feet have been cut off, do they still feel pain or not?
[They replied: 'Certainly not, Blessed One."
And there is a painful feeling conditioned by that.
For it is so, Blessed One, if you consider that the sister experiences the intrinsic nature of the eye, up to: and there is a painful feeling conditioned by that.
For it is thus, Blessed One;
thus are the sense-bases untrained;
thus are the aggregates and elements.
Thus are the hair, body hairs, and nails;
thus is the entire collection of impurities.

Furthermore, having understood that painful feeling is dependent on another, bound to another, dependent on conditions, and bound to conditions, one is fundamentally transformed through thirty-two aspects.
The aggregate of conditioned formations is to be fully understood.
Therefore, sisters, a noble disciple does not perceive a self in these five aggregates of clinging.
"Having [realized] what belongs to the self, each one attains parinirvāṇa for themselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One,
until those Śākyan women realized the state of non-returning for their daughters.
And the minds of five hundred bhikṣus were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging;
and the Dharma-eye regarding phenomena was purified in many hundreds of thousands of deities.
Then, while that very assembly was present, the Blessed One spoke to the Venerable Vāgīśa.
May it be revealed to you, O Lord of Speech, as much as you have spoken;
for that which is based on mere hearsay is empty,
wherein the one who grasps erroneously is frustrated.
For by thus conceiving "I" and "mine," they repeatedly increase the funeral pyre. [1]
Having understood that the body is empty and essence-less,
and likewise subject to cessation and destruction,
as well as the arising and passing away of the realms of existence—
Who, being disciplined in yoga, would delight in the realms of existence? [2]
Having experienced this suffering and having seen its root, [suffering] arises;
and both body and mind are rooted in suffering.
They strike down Māra, who pursues one who goes with the stream and whose mind is liberated. [3]
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, what evil karma was committed by these Śākyan women in the past, such that they now experience such painful sensations?
The Blessed One replied:
In the past, Ānanda, these Śākya women were six courtesans right here in Śrāvastī.
Right here in Śrāvastī there was a Pratyekabuddha named Kāla.
While he was wandering for alms, he was addressed by those courtesans:
"Now this ascetic enjoys sensual pleasures himself,
yet he speaks in dispraise of sensual pleasures.
With intentions of mockery and intentions of harassment, they reviled him with various ill-spoken words and paths of speech, and even scattered burning coals over him from a brazier.

Then, Ānanda, that Pratyekabuddha, touched by painful feeling and experiencing harsh and bitter sensations, being distressed in both body and life, rose up right there in the air and, without further clinging, attained final nirvāṇa;
and his own previously established fire-element pervaded his body.
Then those courtesans, being terrified, thought: "An evil deed has been accumulated by us;
much demerit has been produced, for such a highly distinguished seer has been harassed."
Therefore, this will result in suffering to be experienced by us.
Know that they have now become remorseful.
Having taken possession of his body, they constructed a stūpa.
They honored him with parasols, banners, and flags;
they honored him with flowers, incense, and perfumes;
and they made this aspiration:
"In the future, may we please such a Teacher as this;
may we also obtain those five qualities which he possesses."
Because they committed those evil deeds, these women were reborn in the hells; there, for many thousands of years, they experienced suffering.
Ānanda, these foolish worldlings committed an evil deed while laughing, the consequences of which they now experience with tearful faces.
That she performed this worship and gave rise to remorse,
and that she made this aspiration for the future: "May we please such a Teacher as he who is the possessor of these qualities."
"We too shall attain those [realms]," they thought,
until they became those who attain parinirvāṇa there through the abandonment of the five lower fetters (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana).
"Blessed One, what is the name of this Dharma-discourse?"
"And how shall I uphold it?
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, Ānanda, you should uphold this Dharma-discourse by the name 'The Great Exposition of Causes' (Kāraṇavaipulya). Thus he spoke.
157. Now, when the city of Kapilavastu was besieged by Virūḍhaka, some of the bhikṣuṇīs remained hidden within the city while others went outside;
thus, the bhikṣuṇīs were separated from one another.
Regarding their remorse,
the Blessed One said:
"In that case, there is no offense for one who is unwilling and whose city is besieged."
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī. Some bhikṣuṇīs were traveling along a road,
and among them there was a bhikṣuṇī who was weak from old age.
"Weak from illness;
we have been separated from our caravan"—
thus spoke the nuns who had passed [the boundary].
Then they became remorseful. Because of that remorse, they informed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī then informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "In that case, there is no offense for one who acts without desire."
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Gautamī, assemble the bhikṣuṇīs, as far as they may be purified.
Whichever bhikṣuṇī should dwell apart from another bhikṣuṇī for even a single night, except on an occasion [when it is permitted], [that is an offense]."
In this regard, the appropriate occasion is when a bhikṣuṇī is ill,
or when she is besieged during a siege of a city;
this is the occasion here.
"Any nun" means one who is fully ordained.
"Without other nuns" means alone, without a companion. "Should she stay apart for even one night" means until the rising of the dawn, except at the proper time.
In this regard, there is this exception: a nun may be unwilling [to go], or she may be weak from old age, or weak from illness, or there may be a siege of the city;
that is to say, the city is besieged by a hostile army.

Even if a nun runs out from within the city to the outside, or enters from the outside into the city— even if she does enter— there is no offense. However, if that nun, while the sun is still up, remains apart from the other nuns and stays away until dawn breaks, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If, after the sun has set, she opens the door without [another] being present, it is a *thūl'-accaya*. In a nunnery or elsewhere, everyone must move within the reach of hand-span (*hasta-pāśa*) of one another.
Three times during the night, they must come together with one another; they must touch each other with their hands,
and certainly not only once.

Furthermore, if he does not grant an interview during each watch— failing to do so during the first watch, failing to do so during the middle watch, and failing to do so during the last watch— he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
In all such cases, there is no offense.
Now, if it is a two-storied building, one person descends by the lower staircase and the other by the upper;
they must descend three times during the night.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should dwell apart from other nuns for even one night, except on an appropriate occasion;
herein, this is the appropriate occasion: when the nun is ill."
When a city is besieged or has been captured—this is the occasion here.
This rule is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense involving immediate transgression (*prathamāpattika*).
*Saṃghāvaśeṣa* Dharma 7: Without permission.
158. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now, in Rājagṛha, there was the wife of another non-military official named Sudinnikā; she was young, gracious, and beautiful to behold.
He has now passed away;
that woman desires a husband, and her brother-in-law wishes to take her as his wife.
That woman said to the women:
"Noble ladies, I have no desire for this man;
yet this brother-in-law of mine wishes to have sexual union with me."
Another woman said,
"I wish to be released. She then said:
"I wish to. She said,
"Go to Śrāvastī."
Now, a nun named Kālī resides there;
she will ordain you.
She has now gone out.
She went to Śrāvastī.
Having gone to the nuns' quarters, she asked:
"Which is the cell of the noble Kālī?"
Another [woman] pointed her out, saying, "This is she.
She approached her and said,
"Noble lady, I wish to go forth."
She was ordained and received full admission by her. Then that man searched for her, thinking, "I will reconcile with her," but he did not find her.
Then he heard:
"In Śrāvastī there is a female ascetic named Kālī;
she has ordained her."
Then that man, having gone to Śrāvastī by stages, asked:
"Which here is the nuns' residence?
Another pointed it out to him, saying, "This is it."
He entered there and asked,
"Which noble Kālī is this? She replied,
"I am."
He then said,
"It is indeed the right time for the Noble One to ordain my wife, whom I have not released.
She then said:
"But from where do you come, long-lived one? He then replied, "From Rājagṛha."
He then said,
"O Caṇḍāyu, you have entered our city.
She replied, "I am called Sāntevāsinī."
"Bring the outer robe; I shall have this Caṇḍāyudherāṭika (Caṇḍāyu-dhare-cāṭika) bound.
Then that man, being terrified, looked on.

"Before this audacious and talkative female ascetic has me bound," that man complained and retreated, until finally going outside he informed the great king (or the great multitude) regarding the nuns:
"Look, sirs! This female ascetic causes my wife—who was not even released by me—to go forth as a nun, and she intimidates me with the threat of imprisonment."
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī reported it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Summon Kālī.
She was then summoned.
All of this was questioned of her in the same manner.
“Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
“It is a transgression for you, Kālī.”
"In this way, you are indeed ordaining one who has not been authorized by those who grant authorization.
Therefore, it is not permissible to ordain one who has not been authorized by those who grant authorization.
The nuns said:
"Behold, Blessed One, how this Kālīya has been liberated through his presence of mind in the moment;
and that man, terrified, has fled.
The Blessed One said:
O bhikṣuṇīs, it was not only now that Kālī was liberated by her presence of mind;
this man, too, was terrified and fled.
On another occasion as well, she was liberated by that same presence of mind.
And this man has fled in fear.
Monks, formerly this very city was Vārāṇasī;
this woman goes at night carrying a girl upon her shoulder.
And a lion appeared before her;
seeing it, the girl began to weep. Then that woman struck the girl with a slap.
"One lion was eaten by you; you even desired to eat this one as well. The lion looked and saw:
"Such as this woman is—carrion-eating and talkative—she devours [me]."
"This is mine," [he thinks].
Terrified, he flees.
A monkey comes before him and asks the lion:
"O son of the king of beasts, where will you go? The lion replied,
"Fear has come upon me."
The monkey asked,
"What kind of fear is it?
The lion explained it in detail.
He said: "You must not speak thus;
you are a lion, O king of beasts."
"Who will strike you? Come here! Turn back! But he did not wish to do so.
A lion was seized by the hair by a monkey who said,
"Come here!
When the girl saw this, she wept.
That woman said, "Do not weep, little girl!
Who brought this to your mother, seizing her by the hair?
Now eat whatever you desire of her!"
The lion sees:
"Lest this become merely a matter of conventional agreement," he brings it again and again and gives it.
She too eats!
Since I have already fled once, why am I turned back yet again?
Then, having shaken off that monkey, he fled.
A deity spoke this verse:
"This wisdom has arisen in the present."
This has not arisen for long;
behold, the fear of the lion has appeared,
yet it has been turned back by eloquence.
The Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣuṇīs, it may occur to you that she was some other woman;
it should not be viewed in this way."
This very woman was that Kālī.
Monks, it might occur to you that she was some other girl;
it should not be viewed in this way.
This very Sudinnikā was that girl.
Monks, it might occur to you that he who was Siṃha was someone else;
it should not be viewed in this way.
This man was a lion at that time;
even then, she was liberated by means of this present eloquence,
and this man, being terrified, fled away.
159. Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
“Gautamī, assemble the bhikṣuṇīs, as many as there are, until they have become purified.
Should any bhikṣuṇī ordain one who has not been authorized by those who should authorize her, this too is a *saṃghātiśeṣa* offense, entailing immediate confession.”
"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasaṃpannā*).
"Without being authorized by those who have the authority to authorize" means: for an unmarried girl, the mother and father are the authorities;
for a married woman, the mother-in-law, the father-in-law, and the husband's brother are the authorities.

"Should ordain" means she should confer full admission (*upasampadā*). If that nun causes one who has not been authorized by the authorizers to go forth, she incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline (*vinayātikrama*);
if she imparts the training, she incurs a grave offense (*thūl'-accaya*).
If she ordains her, it is a *saṃghātiśeṣa* offense. When anyone seeking the going-forth arrives, she must be asked:
"Have you been authorized by your parents?
If she says, "No," [she may not be ordained].
If she is unmarried, she should be told:
"Go and obtain your parents' permission, then come back. If she is married, she should be told: "Go..."
"Having obtained permission from her parents-in-law, the husband's mother and father, saying 'Come,' [she may do so].
Regarding this, the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should ordain one who has not been permitted by those who grant permission, this too is a *saṃghātiśeṣa* offense, entailing immediate confession."
Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharma 8: The Sixteenth [Case], the Story of Vadhyā. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
There was a town named Mallakalya belonging to the Mallas. Now, at that time, the wife of another Malla was committing adultery with another man. He then said:
"O so-and-so, desist!
Therefore there is this fault; therefore, may I not do such and such an unwholesome thing to you."
Now that wicked woman did not desist,
saying, "I shall die;
I will not, however, refrain from this misconduct."
He took her together with the man caught in adultery and brought them before the assembly, saying:
"Sirs, I wish for this woman to be dealt with according to the law of her own people.
But what, indeed, is the law of those Mallas?"

A woman who practices sorcery with another man shall, after having performed the distribution of gifts for seven days, have her skin torn off before the assembly of both her paternal and maternal kinsmen.
The court officials said: [so it must be done].
"Let it be given; receive it according to your own duty.
Then that man, having led her home, said:
"O daughter of Itikitikā, give whatever you have and whatever you do not have."
"For seven days, I shall tear you apart with a cow-horn in front of both assemblies of your kinsmen.
Then, having gathered both assemblies of her kinsmen together and having prepared food, drink, and various kinds of solid and soft delicacies, she wept.
The women said:
"What is the use of weeping? You yourself acted in such a way that you must now experience this suffering.
She then said, "I did not do it."
"I am about to die; rather, I weep because they will tear me apart with a cow-hide knife in front of both assemblies of kinsmen. Thus I weep.
Another said,
"Do you wish to be released? She then replied:
"I wish to go. He said, "Go to Śrāvastī."
There was a nun there named Kālī;
she will ordain you.

Having heard her words, she ran out from among the people who were eating, drinking, and intoxicated, in whatever manner possible, and having traveled by stages through successive inquiries, she arrived at Śrāvastī.
He asks: "Which is the bhikṣuṇī-vihāra here?
It was pointed out by another.
Having entered, she then asked,
"Which one is Noble Kālī?
and was pointed out by another.
"Here she is. She approached her and said,
"I wish to be ordained by the Noble Lady."
She then said:
"Have you been authorized by those who authorize?
She then said:
"Who, moreover, O Noble One, are the authorized persons?
She replied: "For an unmarried girl, they are her mother and father."
When she was married, her mother-in-law, father-in-law, husband, and brothers-in-law said,
"Then I am permitted by her."
"When I was entrusted to the cowherd’s wife, I was well-entrusted.
She said,
"O mother, you who were entrusted are well-entrusted, since you were entrusted to a cowherd’s wife."
She was ordained and received full admission by her;
that man searched for her,
thinking, "I will split her at the ankle," but he did not find her.
Now he hears:
"In Śrāvastī there is a nun named Kālī;
she has ordained her."
Having arrived at Śrāvastī, he asked:
"Which here is the nuns' dwelling?
Others pointed it out to him, saying, "This is it."
Having entered there,
the noble lady named Kālī said:
"What should be done?
It is not right for me to let my wife go forth [into the religious life] when she has not been given up by her husband.
Then she said:
"Where are you from?
He replied, "From Āmalakakalya."
He said: "Caṇḍāyu, you are a thief; you are a robber; you have entered Śrāvastī with the intent to rob.
Do you not know that the people of Śrāvastī and the Āmalakakalyas are eternally at enmity?"
She then called her female pupil:
"Bring me my outer robe first, so that I may have this Caṇḍāyudha, the beggar, bound in the royal palace."
That man saw:
"This female ascetic is indeed so audacious, talkative, and impudent; I shall have her bound."

Now this man is complaining and retreating; that man is now complaining before the community of bhikṣuṇīs and the great multitude: "Look, sirs! These female ascetics are ordaining my wife, whom I have not relinquished!"
And she threatened me with her own imprisonment.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, and so on,
until the Blessed One said:
"Kāli, this was a misdeed of yours!
How is it that you, knowing her to be one who should be executed, known [to be so], and subject to the penalty of her kinsmen, nevertheless ordain her?
Therefore, it is not permissible to ordain one who is known to be one who should be executed, known [to be so], and subject to the penalty of her kinsmen."
161. This is the origin of the name: there was a town of the Śākyas named Śākyavardhana. In this very manner, it should be elaborated in detail.
"As long as there was another, I ordained someone exactly like her;
for that, I received a disciplinary penalty.
Go away, I do not venture to ordain you."
She then stayed close to various other bhikṣuṇīs, but none of them ordained her;
eventually, she was ordained by the heretics.
That man then went searching for her.
"I shall cause her to be expelled by means of a cowherd's wife.
He did not succeed.
Then he heard that she had been ordained among the non-Buddhist sectarians in Śrāvastī.
Then he said:
"Now that daughter of Itikitikā has been slain with a very great slaughter pertaining to this very life,
she who was a laywoman's daughter but was ordained by the heretics."
He did not seek it out nor inquire about it; she, moreover,
was now distressed by that state of being a heretic,
for those heretics were poorly taught and unrighteous.
They drink rice-water;
they drink the rinsings of the cooking-pot.
Naked, shameless, and without fear, even those who lust after women bring about corruption.
That woman said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Alas, our going forth has resulted in delusion; we have fallen into a pit, we have fallen into hell."
I have fallen into a precipice;
save me now! Have compassion for me!
Lift me up!
Have compassion for me!
Let me go forth!
Then they did not wish to accept it. She then approached Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
and Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "It is permissible.
Whatever dispraise there was has been directed toward the non-Buddhists."
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Gautamī, assemble [the nuns]; they shall become purified.
Furthermore, if a nun, knowing that a woman is condemned to death and recognized as having incurred the penalty of her kinsmen, should ordain her—except at the proper time."
In this regard, the exception is when she has previously belonged to another sect.
This rule is also an offense involving immediate transgression (saṃghātiśeṣa).
162. "A nun" means one who has received full ordination (upasampannā).

"Knowing" means either she knows it herself or she hears it from another. "To be killed" means one who is to be executed. "Known" means known by both groups of relatives: the maternal side and the paternal side.
"Subject to punishment by kinsmen" means:

kinsmen (*jñāti*) are those such as Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, Ambaṣṭhas, Vaidehas, Bhaṭanas, Kuṃkumālas, and so forth, up to certain cowherds (*gopāṭika*). They cause [the offender] to be punished.
Some are burned after being wrapped in a worm or a kāliñja insect;
some are cast into water with a jar of sand tied around their necks;
and some have their heads blown off.
The ears and noses of some are cut off;
for some, a heated plowshare is thrust into the opening of their wounds along the course of the stream [of pus];
and the Śākyas and Mallas are split apart with a cow-hide blade.
The Kṣatriyas are wrapped in straw and reeds and burned;
the Abhīras have a jar tied around their necks and cast into the water;
the Śakas and Yavanas have their heads blown off.
Their ears or noses are cut off;
or a heated plowshare is thrust into the opening of their wounds.
"Would ordain" means he would cause him to go forth and confer full ordination upon him.
The Blessed One has withdrawn this phrase "except at the proper time," so there is no offense. What is the proper time? It is when she was formerly a follower of another sect.

"Other sectarians" refers to the Carakas, Parivrājakas, Nirgranthas, Ājīvakas, Tre-daṇḍikas, Mākandikas, Gudugudukas, Gautamas, Dharma-cintakas, Vṛddha-śrāvakas, and Dakatṛtīyakas— up to and including those designated as such. If a nun, knowing and being aware that a woman is subject to execution and has incurred the penalty of her kinsmen, nevertheless allows her to go forth and ordains her, she commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
If she gives instruction, she incurs a grave offense (thullaccaya);
if she confers full ordination, it is a formal act requiring a remnant of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa).
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun, knowing that a woman is condemned to death, recognized as such, and subject to punishment by her kinsmen, should ordain her—
except at the proper time. In this case,
the proper time is as follows:
She has previously belonged to another sect.
This rule is also one involving immediate offense; it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharma, number nine.
One should cross a river alone.
163. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Then, many women were bathing in the river Ajiravatī.
The nun Sthūlanandā went to that very place;
having set down her robes in a secluded spot, she crossed over by swimming with her arms.
Then those women said:
"The noble Sthūlanandā is coming.
Having rested for a moment at Kayadhānaka, she returned once more.
The women said:
This noble lady Sthūlanandā has arrived.
The noble lady acted with excessive haste;
how is it that you are crossing by means of your arms?
Then those women were rebuked.
The nuns heard about this matter and reported it to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī informed the Blessed One, and the Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, Nandā!
How can you cross a river all alone?"
"Therefore, it is not permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to cross rivers without [a companion].
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
'Gautamī, assemble the bhikṣuṇīs until they have all gathered.'"
Whatever nun crosses a river without another nun—this rule is also one of immediate offense.
"Whatever nun" means one who has received full ordination.
"Without another nun" means without a companion.
"A river" refers to one that flows from outside the boundary and reaches the boundary.
"Should cross" means she should go to the further shore.
This rule also constitutes an offense of the first category (pārājika).

To whatever extent these bhikṣuṇīs cross rivers, they must cross within arm's reach [of one another]. If they cross beyond arm's reach, it is a thullaccaya offense. If they become far apart, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Alternatively, if one stands in the middle while others cross, there is a grave offense (*thūl'-accaya*).
