"For the sake of bedding and seating" (*śayyāsanasyārthāya*):
"bedding and seating" (*śayyāsana*) refers to a couch, a stool, a woven seat, a square mat, a grass mat, or a bolster.
"Having requested" means having made known [the need] and having caused [another] to undertake [the task]. "If she causes another to procure" means if she causes it to be known.
If she causes another to procure a bowl, or a robe, or solid food, or soft food, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.

"[Nissargika-pācattikaṃ]" means that having relinquished it to the Saṃgha, the pācattika offense must be confessed. If one confesses without having relinquished it, one incurs a violation of the Vinaya.
Now, if the bedding and seating have become devoid of their original material, [the rule does not apply].
The object must be shown:
"I have received this price for a bed from such-and-such a person;
recognize this as his bed."
Up to the point of [receiving] a *bimboya* vessel— if he does not show that object, he incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline (*vinayātikrama*).

Whether it be for the purpose of making a patch, a repair, or a plastering, or for setting up water-jars, if a monk, having requested [materials] for the sake of bedding and furniture, causes another to fetch them, he incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline.
He reaches it.
Having shown the object, it is permissible to make it broken, crushed, and so forth.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:

Whatever nun, having requested [materials] for the sake of a bed or seat, should cause a bowl, a robe, food, soft food, or medicine for the sick to be purchased for herself, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. This is the twelfth offense of expiation involving forfeiture concerning what was intended for another.
174a. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
A nun named Sthūlanandā was wandering for alms with robes that were soiled and filthy, torn and tattered, and with a bowl that was broken, cracked, and full of holes.
The women said:
"The noble lady has no bowl.
He said,
"She has none."
He said:
"Noble lady, I will give you the price for the bowl;
noble lady, please have the bowl appraised."
Another said, "The noble lady has no robe.
She replied, "There is none."
He said,
"I give the price for a robe to the Noble Lady;
may the Noble Lady cause a robe to be prepared."
She ate and drank, yet she did not cause her bowl or her robe to be washed.
While the nuns were wandering for alms and entering the houses of frequenting families,
those women then said:
"I gave the price for a bowl to the noble Nandā;
she had the bowl made by it.
Then those bhikṣuṇīs said:
"What will that Bhadrāyaṇī know?
She merely eats and drinks.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī also informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
"Call Nandā."
She was then summoned.
"Is it true, Nanda, that you, Nanda, cause another to purchase something intended for someone else?
She replied:
“Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
“It is a transgression for you, Nanda, in that you cause another to be procured by means of what was intended for someone else.”
Therefore, it is not permissible for one to cause another to purchase something intended for someone else.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"If a nun should cause another to purchase something intended for someone else, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pācattika)."
"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained.
"With what is intended for another" means with the price of a bowl or with the price of a robe.
"If she causes another to purchase [something]—whether it be food to be chewed or food to be eaten—it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika* offense.
This is the formal rule (*prajñapti*).
Now, suppose some nun gives money in order to have a bowl, a robe, ghee, or oil purchased.
If he causes [something] to be procured for a specific purpose, that very thing must be caused to be procured:
a bowl for the price of a bowl, or ghee for the price of ghee. If he causes something else to be procured, [he commits an offense].
This is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
Now, if he gives what is indefinite, making known whatever he desires, there is no offense. Then, if he says:
"Take whatever you wish.
If he makes known what he wishes, there is no offense.
For monks as well, it is exactly the same; however, there is an offense consisting of a transgression of the Vinaya.
There is no offense if it was not intended;
or if one takes what [the other] says, "Take whichever you wish," there is no offense.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
If a nun causes another person to purchase something for someone else's sake, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika* offense.
*Niḥsargika-pācattika* Dharma 13: For others.
175. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
A nun named Sthūlanandā, having taken charge of the meals for the Saṃgha, said while searching for a volunteer:
"Prajāpati, give us the *chandaka*!
We shall prepare a meal for the noble ladies. Then those women, as they were giving the *chandaka*, said:
"Noble lady, on whichever day the serving of food takes place,
we too shall go as servers."
Then she ate and drank and had the bowl brought back.
With what remained after she had eaten— whatever kind of food it was that had been prepared—
the female servers then arrived.
They said,
"Noble lady, we have given you much choice food;
but now this meal is coarse and very poor."
The bhikṣuṇīs said,
"What will this Bhadrāyaṇī do?
She merely eats and drinks."
She makes her known [as one who possesses] a bowl and a robe;
moreover, she urinates into her own small water-pot.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Call Nandā."
She was then summoned.
"Is it true, Nanda, that you, having requested [cloth] for the sake of others, cause someone else to purchase it?
"Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said,
"It is a transgression for you, Nanda.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.

“Gautamī, assemble the bhikṣuṇīs, as many as there are, until they have become completely pure. Whatever bhikṣuṇī, having requested [alms] for the sake of others, causes a bowl, a robe, food, drink, or medicinal requisites for the sick to be purchased for herself, that is a *niḥsargika-pācattika* offense.”
Furthermore, if a nun who has received full ordination,

having requested on behalf of others, should request for herself— having first requested from the Sangha— a meal, or a refreshment, or a drink of gruel, or a bowl, or a robe, or food, or eatables, or medicinal requisites for the sake of illness;
Or if she should cause it to be bartered, it is a *naiḥsargika-pācattika*.
Furthermore, she must inform the very person for whose sake she requested [the gift].

Now, if she causes [a gift] to be requested for the purpose of clothing, or for the purpose of food, refreshment, or the drinking of gruel, yet gives it as a divisible portion [of alms], [she commits an offense].
If she provides a bed or seat, or gives [one] for the rainy season or for the winter,
she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
This nun causes the meal for the Saṃgha to be given.
That which has been relinquished, released, and not grasped is to be given.
If there is anything remaining there—whether rice, soup, or even food to be chewed or eaten—it should be pointed out.
If he takes it and departs, one should let him go.
Then, if he says, "I give it to the noble lady," he should be told:
"No, indeed.
Give it to the Saṃgha.
Then he said, "It has been given by me to the Saṃgha."
"I give it to the noble lady.
She accepts it.
There is no offense.
For a monk as well, it is exactly the same; however, it is a transgression of the rule (*vinyātikrama*).
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun, having solicited for the sake of others, should cause a bowl, a robe, food, soft food, or medicinal requisites for the sick to be purchased for herself..."
An offense entailing relinquishment and confession (niḥsargika-pācattika).
The fourteenth offense entailing relinquishment and confession:
the accumulation of bowls.
176. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī. Some visiting bhikṣuṇīs arrived, and those resident bhikṣuṇīs made them rise according to seniority.
Then they said, "Let us pass the bowls along. They began to pass them along before the sun had set;
the moon had already risen, yet the bowls had not been passed completely.
The guests said,
"Noble lady, the dwelling is empty.
They replied, "We shall move the alms-bowls [there] as well."
Then they said:
"How many bowls do the noble ladies have?
Will the noble ladies set up a bowl-market?"
"What is the caste?
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
and Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī in turn reported it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
"Summon those nuns.
They were then summoned.
"Is it true, nuns? The Blessed One questioned them about all of that, and they replied,
"Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"And yet you indeed accumulate bowls!
Therefore, it is not permissible to accumulate bowls."
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Gautamī, assemble the bhikṣuṇīs until they have all gathered.
Whatever bhikṣuṇī should accumulate alms bowls, that is a niḥsargika-pācattika offense."
"Again, a nun" refers to one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).

"Accumulation of bowls" (*pātra-sannicaya*): "bowl" (*pātra*) means a bowl made of *sumbhaka* clay, a bowl made of *upa-sambhaka* clay, a bowl with a rim, a bowl with a curved rim, or a *tiṃkhini* bowl.
The large, the medium, and the small;
the unworthy bowl, the overly worthy bowl, and the accessory bowl.
"Should make a collection" means he should make a hoard; this constitutes a *niḥsargika* offense, as prescribed by the rule.
A bhikṣuṇī should keep sixteen bowls;
she should consecrate one bowl,
and she may distribute three bowls among her friends.
There are four unsuitable bowls,
four excessively large bowls,
and four bowls for personal requisites.
If they keep it beyond that limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika* offense.
This is now the fixed measure for a nun regarding the possession of an alms-bowl.
Even if a monk uses many bowls after having made them available [for use], there is no offense.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should accumulate an alms-bowl, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika* offense.
This is the *niḥsargika-pācattika* rule (15)."
On the accumulation of robes (cīvara-sannicaya), 176a: The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī. Some visiting bhikṣuṇīs arrived.
Those nuns were ordaining [others] according to seniority. They then said, "Let us transfer our robes. So they began to transfer them before the sun had set.
Candrodgata had not yet transferred them entirely.
The incoming monks said,
"Noble one, the dwelling is empty."
They said,
"We shall go as far as the robes extend.
Then they said:
"How many robes do the noble ladies have? Noble ladies, will you open a shop for selling robes?
Or what is your caste?"
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, in turn, reported it to the Blessed One. [The Blessed One] said:
Furthermore, a nun who has [received] five robes must formally designate one;
the other three robes may be shared with friends.
Thus, these are the twenty robes. Should she keep more than this, it is a *nissargika-pācattika*.
This, now, is the fixed limit for a nun regarding the possession of robes.
Even if a monk uses many robes after having designated them as belonging to friends, there is no offense.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should accumulate robes, it is a *nissargika-pācattika*."
The 16th *niḥsargika-pācattika-dharma*: On relinquishing. 177. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
A nun named Sthūlanandā neither washed, nor sewed, nor dyed her robes.
Her outer robe (saṃghāṭī) was now soiled and filthy, torn and rent asunder; she placed it in the dwelling place, saying, "Let whoever wishes take it."
Now there was another nun named Jetā who wore coarse robes. She was addressed by the nuns:
"Noble lady, wash this outer robe, sew it, and darn it, and then wear it."
Then Sthūlanandā said:
"Noble lady, bring this outer robe; it is my outer robe.
Look, noble ladies, there is nothing at all that can be left behind in the lodging."
The entire monastery was filled with those who had been expelled.
Then, that woman—shameless, talkative, and impudent—snatched away her outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*).
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī also informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, if a nun, having either deposited or caused to be deposited an old outer robe (saṃghāṭī) in a nunnery, should say, 'Let whoever wishes take it,' [that is an offense]."
Having spoken thus, if she herself should subsequently take it up, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
"Any nun" means one who has received full ordination; [the rest is] as before.
"In the nunnery" means in the dwelling of the bhikṣuṇīs.
"Saṃghāṭī" means a robe.
"Having laid aside" means having done so oneself.
"Having caused [it] to be deposited" means by another.
"Let whoever desires it take it" means that if she herself subsequently takes it, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
If that nun, having deposited or caused a robe to be deposited in a nun’s dwelling, says, "Let whoever desires it take it," and someone else has taken it, it is not permissible to snatch it away.
If she seizes it, it becomes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Now, if it has not been taken by anyone and she herself needs it, even if she takes it, there is no offense.
Now, if small and miscellaneous requisites have been deposited, if they have been taken by someone, it is not permitted to seize them.
If one seizes [an item], one commits an offense of transgression against the discipline (*vinayātikrama*).

If a monk, having deposited a bowl, a robe, sandals, or even some minor or very minor requisite in a monk’s dwelling, says, "Let whoever wishes take it," then if it has been taken by someone, it is not permissible to seize it back.
If he seizes it, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
However, if it has not been taken by anyone and he himself is the one who needs it, even if he takes it, there is no offense.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun, having deposited or caused to be deposited an old outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) in a nun’s dwelling, says, "Let whoever wishes take it," and afterwards takes it herself,
that is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*niḥsargika-pācattika*). (Nissaggiya Pācittiya Dharma 17)
178. Regarding "let it dry": the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now, another bhikṣuṇī, having washed an old saṃghāṭī that was extremely soiled and stained, and having sewn it up, placed it in the sun and let the wind blow upon it.
Fire broke out and her outer robe was burned. The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
[The full passage continues] as far as the Blessed One said:
"In this way, you have worn out your old outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) and neither repair it yourself nor cause it to be repaired.
Therefore, it must be repaired or caused to be repaired."
And this was the origin of the matter:
those nuns—daughters of the Śākyas, daughters of the Mallas, and daughters of the Licchavis, who were very delicate—were becoming exhausted while washing their heavy outer robes (saṃghāṭī).
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī also informed the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One said: "In that case, I authorize [her] for six or five nights."
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. ... [as before] ... the Blessed One said:

"If a nun, having sewn or caused to be sewn a new outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*), does not join it together herself or cause it to be joined together within six or five nights when she is not ill, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika* offense."
"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*). "An old outer robe" (*purāṇa-saṃghāṭī*) means an old garment (*purāṇa-cīvara*).
"Outer robe" (*saṃghāṭī*) means one consisting of two layers (*dvi-puṭā*).
"Having sewn herself" means by herself; "having had it sewn by another" means by someone else.
"Beyond" means beyond five or six nights; it does not mean five and six [altogether].
Now, indeed, after six nights at most, one should not have it sewn together oneself, nor should one have it sewn together by another. If one has it sewn together, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
[The rest is as before.]
This applies as far as the designation [of robes] is concerned. Now, if a bhikṣuṇī’s outer robe (saṃghāṭī) becomes soiled, if it is light, it should be washed in that very state.
It is not permitted to let it out [to dry].
Now, if it is a *sārikā* (a type of wooden pin or bolt), after letting it out each time, it must be washed;
having applied new pins, it should be placed in the sun.
Having gathered it together, one should place it in a bowl, a basin, or a tray, and then step over it with a piece of wood or a piece of stone.
It is not permitted to pour it out while it is scattered about.
Now, if there is no vessel available, one should step on it in one spot and then set it down using a brick or a piece of stone.
Afterwards, it should be joined back together by a female disciple, or by a fellow student under the same preceptor, or by a nun herself;
or if she is now frail with old age or weak with illness, even if she joins it back together after a long time, there is no offense.
Therefore the Blessed One said:

If a nun, having sewn together or caused to be sewn together old outer robes (*saṃghāṭī*), does not re-sew them or cause them to be re-sewn for more than five or six nights while not being ill, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*;
[this is] the eighteenth *niḥsargika-pācattika* rule,
spoken after addressing the trainee nun (*śikṣamāṇā*).
179. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now, there was another *śikṣamāṇā* who was to be ordained;
she then said to the nun Sthūlanandā:
"Noble Nanda, ordain me.
She said,
"If you give me the robe-cloth."
Then I ordained her. She then gave a robe to that [other] woman, who said:
"Noble lady, ordain me!
She was embarrassed;
she said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
In this very way, as long as she did not become ashamed and did not grant full ordination,
the nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. [The rest is as before.]
As far as the Blessed One said:

"If a nun, having spoken thus to a *śikṣamāṇā*—'If you give me a robe, then I will grant you full ordination'—and having accepted that robe, does not grant her full ordination, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
'A nun' refers to one who is fully ordained."
"A trainee" means one who has been instructed in the training.
[If she says: "If he gives me a robe, then I shall receive full ordination."
"Robe" (cīvara) means: a robe is called a woolen garment, cotton cloth, and so on, up to a side-covering cloth (saṃkakṣikā).
"Intending to provide" means: intending to ordain.

"Having taken that robe" means: as the nun Thullanandā [acted], she should not herself ordain [the candidate] thinking, "I will not ordain her"; [if she does so], it is a niḥsargika-pācattika offense.
This is the formal designation:
first, a nun takes the robe of a trainee (śikṣamāṇā),
saying, "I shall ordain you."
She should be attended by her.
Now, if she is unable to do so—whether due to weakness from old age or weakness from illness—another person should be requested.
She should be told: "Having taken this robe, please attend to her."
Now, if she does not wish for it, that robe must be returned [to her], with the words:
"Go and receive full ordination wherever you desire.
If that nun, having taken the robe, neither provides it nor returns the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika* offense.
A monk also commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya. Regarding this, the Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣuṇī [instructs] a śikṣamāṇā in this very manner..."
Having said, "If you give me a robe, then I will grant you full ordination," if he accepts her robe but does not grant her full ordination, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika* offense.
*Niḥsargika-pācattika-dharma* 19: Heavy Robe.
180. The Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī.
Now, another merchant arrived from the northern road bringing a precious woolen blanket worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
He was then asked by others: "What is its price?"
He said: "It is worth a hundred thousand.
Neither the king, nor the princes, nor the merchants, nor the caravan leaders would buy it.
Then that merchant, having stepped onto the street, sat there plunged into an ocean of anxiety:
"This merchandise is of great value and carries a heavy tax, yet it is not being sold.
Now, another person asked him:
"Your goods have been sold.
He said, "No, you do not wish to sell them."
He said: "I desire it. He said:
"Go; this nun named Bhadrā will buy it.
So then, having placed it on the shoulder of a servant boy, he went to the nuns' convent and asked, "Which is the courtyard belonging to the noble lady Bhadrā?"
It was reported by other bhikṣuṇīs. Having entered, he said, "I pay homage, Noble Lady. The noble lady named Bhadrā said:
"Certainly! What must be done? He said:
"I am selling this precious woolen blanket for sale.
He asked, "What is its price?"
He said, "A hundred thousand.
Then she neither offered it herself nor caused it to be offered.
She said to her female pupil:
"Go and tell Sālohita: 'Have him give me one hundred thousand from the market-stall.
Now, he was questioned by others.
"Your goods have been sold. He said, "They have been sold."
He asked, "By whom was it bought?
He replied:
"This is the female ascetic named Bhadrā;
it was purchased by her.
Then they began to complain.
Even now, this nun is still full of great desire.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
and Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī in turn reported it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
"Call Bhadrā.
She was then summoned.
"All that is so, up to 'Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
'Is it not true, noble lady, that even future generations ought to be taken into account?'"
Therefore, it is not permissible to have a heavy cloak acquired for more than four *karṣas*.
As the Blessed One said:
"If a nun has a heavy cloak acquired for more than four *karṣas*, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika* offense."
"More than four *karṣas*": a *karṣa* is said to be four *purāṇas*;
four *kārṣas* are sixteen *kārṣāpaṇas*.
"A heavy cloak" refers to a precious woolen blanket (*kambala-ratna*).
"Cetāpayed" means "should cause to be known.
If one causes [the robe] to be acquired for more than sixteen *purāṇas*, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika* offense.
This is the formal rule (*prajñapti*).
If this nun wishes to have a heavy cloak woven, it should be made known that its value is four *karṣas*;
or it may be of lesser value, but more than that is not permitted.
Now, if someone, without being asked or informed, gives her something of great value, she may accept it; there is no offense.
Thus, for a nun, there is a fixed limit.
Even if a monk causes something of great value to be made known and then uses it, there is no offense.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun should have a heavy cloak worth more than four *karṣas* made, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
This is the twentieth *niḥsargika-pācattika* rule concerning fine [materials].
181. The Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī.
Now, another merchant arrived from the southern road, bringing with him a cloth marked with the sign of a swan, worth ten thousand [pieces of gold].
Then, being asked by others,
"What is the price? he said:
Ten thousand purāṇas;
yet the king does not buy it at all.
[The rest is] as before.
"In the meantime, there is a female ascetic here named Bhadrā;
she will purchase it.
He then took it and went to the nunnery.
He asked:
"Which is the cell of the noble lady Bhadrā? Another replied: [This is it].
Having entered, she then said:
"I pay homage, Noble Lady; my name is Bhadrā."
He said: "Certainly. What must be done?"
He said:
"This cloth, marked with the sign of a swan, is for sale.
He replied:
"What is the price of this?
He said, "Ten thousand purāṇas.
She neither offered it herself nor caused it to be offered.
He said to his female pupil:
"Go, tell my maternal kinsman: 'Give me ten thousand purāṇas from this shop-front.
Now, when he was asked by others, he replied: "The merchandise has been sold to you."
He said, "It has been sold.
He said.
"By whom was it bought?
"This nun named Bhadrā;
it was bought by her."
They then complained:
"Even now, though she is a renunciant, she still has such great desire.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī also informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One said: "Is it not true, noble lady, that even the last generation of people must be taken into account?"
"Therefore, it is not permitted to purchase a fine robe for more than a value of two and a half *karṣas*.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī: 'Gautamī, assemble the bhikṣuṇīs, as many as there are, until they have become thoroughly purified.'"
If a nun should have a fine robe made for more than two and a half karṣas in value, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
"If a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"More than" means exceeding [that amount].
"Two and a half *karṣas*":
a *karṣa* is said to be four *purāṇas*.
"He should cause it to be paid" means he should cause it to be known [to the debtor].
A *niḥsargika-pācattika* offense: whichever nun causes a fine robe to be made, it should be caused to be made at a value of ten *purāṇas*, or less. This is the fixed limit for a nun.
Now, if someone gives something of great value—whether worth a hundred or a thousand—without being asked or informed, even if one makes use of it, there is no offense.
Even if a monk causes [an object] worth a hundred thousand to be known [as his], there is no offense.
Therefore the Blessed One said:

whoever among us is most thoroughly resolved upon this shall take possession of it."
Śakra, the lord of the gods, recited this verse:
Whether standing or sitting, one finds no comfort on a seat;
But when one lies down, one finds comfort—when desires abandon me. [1]
Mātali, the charioteer, spoke this verse:
"O Lord of Gods, you are happy that you obtain such happiness while sleeping;
but for me, desires always strike at me, even as I stand upon the head of battle amidst the drums."
The divine son Jaya recited this verse:
"Just as there is a continuous succession of waves whenever a drum is struck, so too do sensual desires constantly strike at me, like a current of wood carried along. [3]
The divine son Vijaya spoke this verse:
"When wood is being carried along, it may occasionally become entangled;
but my eyes, like those of a moth, are forever wide open. [4]
The divine son Khāṇu spoke this verse:
"All of you are truly happy, for whom verses come to mind;
as for me, indeed, I do not know whether I live or whether I die. [5]
Those sons of the gods said: "You have made an excellent resolve; let this Bharaṇī be yours as a queen, she who is beautiful in every limb. [6]
The Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣuṇīs, it may occur to you that the apsaras named Bharaṇī was someone else;
it should not be viewed in this way."
She was that very apsaras Bhadrā;
those other sons of gods were these same five Licchavi youths. Even then, their minds were bound to her.
Even now, their minds remain bound to her.
The nuns asked:
"Blessed One, as the ripening of what karma is Bhadrā so pleasing, beautiful to behold, of noble birth, of great influence, of great wealth, and one who attains realization so swiftly?"
Then the Blessed One addressed Bhadrā Kāpileyī:
“May it be inspired in you, Bhadrā, to deliver a discourse concerning your own past lives, relevant to the nuns.”
Then Bhadrā, recollecting her manifold former existences, addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Long ago, sisters, in a past time, there was a city named Vārāṇasī in the kingdom of Kāśī.
There, at that time, there was a woman who was poor."
She was then summoned by a certain merchant’s wife to have her hair dressed.
She began to dress the merchant’s wife’s hair.
Since the Blessed Buddhas do not appear in the world, Pratyekabuddhas do appear.
Then a Pratyekabuddha named Śuṇṭhika, wandering for alms, entered that house for food.
The Pratyekabuddha simply stood there in silence; no one spoke to him or gave him anything.
Then that woman said to the merchant’s wife,
“Give him alms.
The merchant’s wife looked upward and said:
"Who will give alms to one such as this, so ill-favored and of little renown?
She replied,
"These people do not desire those who are unattractive in body."
"These people are pleasing to the mind; I desire them. "I shall give them to you. Then that poor woman said:
"Noble daughter, give me that which is my meal today, for it is yours to give; I shall give it to him.
She was then commanded:
"Take whatever food you receive today and either cast it into the water or give it to him."
She received that food;
having placed it in her hand, she gave it with devotion to that Pratyekabuddha.
That Pratyekabuddha then departed through the air.
Having seen him, she was pleased, elated, and joyful, and entered the house.
The merchant saw that the seer had departed from the house through the air;
then, having entered the house, the merchant asked:
"Has some seer entered here?
He replied, "He has entered."
He said,
"Was anything given to him?
He replied:
"No;
this merchant, to whom such a worthy recipient has entered my house—one for whom this poor woman has given [this gift]—is filled with longing, yet he has not been honored.
Then that merchant said to the woman:
"Give me this merit which has been accumulated by you today;
I shall give you abundant silver and gold. She then said:
"All wealth, grain, gold, and silver are subject to exhaustion."
The fruit of merit given to sages is never exhausted in any way whatsoever. [7]
If I were otherwise than this, I would be called poor by others;
but because such [beings] are not seen and because there is no sharing of enjoyments,
may I be freed from ugliness and possess an abundance of enjoyments.
Do not live dependent on others, subsisting on what is given by others from other families. [9]
And thus, O Hero, you walk this path as no one else walks it;
so too is Sītā free from passion, liberated from the bonds of existence. [10]
Having given food to the seer, I am joyful and delighted, being glad that my provisions for the next world are well-secured and without deficiency. [11]
Having passed away from here, I shall be reborn in the delightful Nandana grove; there I shall roam among the throngs of gods.
At the proper time, I gave a gift of food to the well-disciplined one for the sake of abandoning suffering. [12]
Then that wife was dismissed by the merchant;
that poor woman was established as Bhaṭṭārikā.
"Sisters, you might think she was some other poor woman, but it should not be viewed in this way."
I myself was that poor woman.
Because I honored that Pratyekabuddha with alms-food with a devout heart, through the ripening of that karma, I am beautiful. [The rest as before.]
Moreover, sisters, it was not by this alone that I planted roots of merit such that I am pleasing, beautiful to behold,
and swift in attainment;
on another occasion as well, I planted roots of merit.

189. Sisters, in the past, in a time gone by, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a certain woman placed a copper wheel in a basket, scattered flowers over it, covered it with a cloth from Kāśi, and gave it to the Blessed One Kāśyapa.
Having given it, she made this aspiration:
Having covered the wheel of the chariot, complete with its hub and rim, with a fine cloth, I too shall bear witness to that Dharma which was indeed witnessed by the best of sages.
Now, she, having committed an offense, had been rebuked by her husband for some reason;
she was then filled with longing.
He said:
"Fie upon this female state! The female sex is contemptible."
"I shall go and hang myself.
Taking a rope, she went out;
and seeing the stūpa of the Blessed One Kāśyapa not far from there, she was filled with faith.
Adorned with ornaments, clothed in garments from Kāśī, and her body anointed with sandalwood paste, she thought:
"I shall die;
I shall perform an offering at the stūpa of the Blessed One Kāśyapa."
With a serene mind, she took off those ornaments and scattered them over the stūpa; having covered it with a garment from Kāśī and anointed it with sandalwood, she made this aspiration:
"In a future time, may I please such a Teacher as this;
may he teach me the Dharma, and may I understand the Dharma he teaches."
Having hanged herself there, she passed away and was reborn in the abode of the Thirty-three.
Surrounded by a thousand apsarases, she remained there for the duration of her lifespan; then, passing away from there, she was reborn among humans.

She was born into a brahmin family of the Kāpila clan in Vaiśālī. Her relatives then gave her the name Bhadrā. Having no desire for the five strands of sensual pleasure, she went forth from home and became a renunciant, whereby she brought about the destruction of all taints.
She who, with a devout mind, offers to the Blessed One Kāśyapa garments from Kāśi and fresh ointment—
that daughter of Kapila pays homage at the feet of the Blessed One, the Teacher.
Then the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, indeed, the so-called 'water-cloth' (daka-śāṭikā) should be made.
The bhikṣuṇīs said,
"Behold, Blessed One, how this Bhadrā went forth together with the Elder Mahākāśyapa!"
The Blessed One said:
"It is not only now that these two have gone forth as renunciants."

On another occasion as well, both of these were renunciants; on another occasion too, O Blessed One, there were bhikṣuṇīs. Long ago, O bhikṣuṇīs, in the past, four royal sages took up residence in a potter’s household.
Khāṇuvarṇa was the king of the Kaliṅgas, Bhārgava of the Gandhāras, Nimi the king of the Videhas, and Ugrasena the Kṣatriya. [13]

These four royal sages, of fierce splendor and great strength, arrived to dwell for one night in the family of a potter. Having approached the potter, they asked him: "What have you seen or heard that led you to announce your intention to go forth?"
The great king of the Kaliṅgas, a bull among men, who was the color of a tree stump, being questioned by the potter, spoke these words: [14] ||
The women fastened conch shells set with gold; as they bound them, a second sound arose from where Ramā had come.
Having seen and heard of the fault of association, I practice the conduct of a monk. [15]
The Bhārgava, the great king of the Gandhāras, that bull among men, being questioned by Kumbhakāra, spoke these words: [16]
The female crow, however, is for the sake of the corpse;
though she is alone, many fall [upon it].
They run about for the sake of food.
Having seen that, I practice the conduct of a monk. [17]
Then King Nimi, the great monarch of Videha and lord of Mithilā, being questioned by the potter, spoke these words: [18]
Alas! She who was once like a cloud in complexion,
with limbs as smooth as if anointed with oil,
has now, for the sake of fruit, fallen into a state of ruin.
Having seen this, I am filled with agitation; I shall practice the conduct of a monk. [19]
The great king Ugrasena, a bull among kṣatriyas, being questioned by the potter, spoke these words: [20] ||
In the midst of such splendor, you beheld that bull,
endowed with a body whose color was like a moving hump,
shattered for the sake of desire.
Seeing that it was broken, I practice the life of a mendicant. [21]
All these have gathered here like gods;
like a fire blazing in the night,
I too shall go forth into homelessness.
Having abandoned delightful sensual pleasures. [22]
The potter’s wife said:
"This is the very time; there is no other.
There is no instructor outside of this [place]."
I too shall go forth into homelessness;
my little sons, where will they go? [23]
They do not know the raw from the cooked, nor the salty from the saltless; like birds released from a man’s hand, these young sons, lacking wings and ignorant, [fly away]. [24]
I have gone forth following him who has gone forth; I am wandering as one who follows him who wanders. [25]
King Nimi was the Bodhisattva; Śārisuta was Kaliṅga;
Ugrasena was Maudgalya; Ānanda was Bhārgava; Kāśyapa was the potter; and Bhadrā was that potter-woman. [26]
At that time as well, both of these were renunciants;
even now, both of these are renunciants. [27]
Now, the Blessed One has permitted bathing cloths for the bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣuṇīs are now making bathing cloths from pieces of cloth belonging to the Tathāgata.
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, it is not permissible to make a water-strain cloth from a robe as it was originally received.
Thus the training rule was prescribed.
When a nun has a rain-cloak made, it must be made according to the proper measurements. In this regard, these are the measurements:
In length, it shall be four spans; by the span of a Sugata. In width, two [spans]; if one should have it made beyond that, there is an offense of expiation involving cutting.
"A bathing-cloth" means that which was authorized by the Blessed One.
"Having it made" means she should either make it herself or have it made by another.
"Of standard measurement" means that the measurement here is four spans (*vitasti*).
"By a Sugata-span" means: a Sugata is a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksambuddha; his span is the measure for the two and a half [vitastis] of a bed-leg.
If one causes it to be made more than that—[namely, more than two spans]—then, if they bathe in a secluded spot or a bower without a bathing-cloth, there is no offense.
If a monk also bathes without a bathing-cloth, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Vinaya.
Now, there is no offense for a nun bathing in a secluded grove without a bathing cloth (*daka-śāṭikā*).
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"A nun who has a bathing cloth made should have it made according to the proper measurements."
In this regard, the measurement is as follows:
in length, it is four spans according to the span of a Sugata.
Two spans across;
if one should cause it to be made beyond that, there is an offense of expiation involving cutting.
Pācattika-dharma 76, Kaṭhina 190: The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
The nun named Sthūlanandā was requested by the community of nuns:
"Noble lady, are you able to beg for cloths on behalf of the Saṃgha?
She then said:
"It is possible.
She then went to some poor families and said,
"O you of great merit, are you able to give a cloth to the Saṅgha?"
They said, "Noble lady, we shall know; you will come again. She came again and again.
They said, "We shall know, we shall know.
Then she spoke.
"If you wish to give, then give!
The time for the Saṃgha's robe-offering is passing away.
What shall we do?"—thus you say.
They did not give it,
and the time for the robes passed.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, and so on until the Blessed One said:
If a nun, out of a weak expectation regarding robe-material, should cause the Kaṭhina-suspension of the Saṃgha to be postponed, it is a Pācattika offense.
"If a nun" means one who is fully ordained. "Weak" means lacking sufficient strength.

"With the expectation of a robe" means: "robe" refers to anything from a *kāla* cloth up to a *kṣaumunikā*. "Of the Saṅgha" refers to the one who spreads the *kaṭhina*. "Should let pass" means he should cause it to exceed [the time limit]; this is a *pācattika* offense, as established by the formal rule (*prajñapti*).
Now this nun is being encouraged:
"Noble lady, will you be able to request the kaṭhina for the Saṃgha?
If she is capable, she should take up the task.
Having made an effort, one should not beg from weak families.
Rather, those who are capable—whether father, son, brother, sister, or relatives by birth or kinship through lineage—should be asked.
Once they have been asked, those who are capable of giving should be informed [of the situation].
Then they said, "We shall know, we shall know," but she should have been told:
"Either give [the robe-cloth] or refuse it, for the time for robes is passing away.
Now, if she is unable [to obtain it], that nun should be encouraged for the sake of the Saṃgha's removal of the kaṭhina.

Having encouraged [the donor], if he neither asks for it himself nor causes it to be asked for, nor informs the community of nuns that it cannot be obtained, he incurs a *pācattika* offense. Furthermore, if a monk, due to a weak expectation regarding the robe-material, [does not inform] the community that the *kaṭhina* has been spread...
"If she causes [the kaṭhina] to be passed over for the sake of a weak hope for a robe, she incurs an offense of transgression of the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "If a bhikṣuṇī, out of a weak hope for a robe, should cause the kaṭhināstāra of the Saṃgha to be passed over, it is a pācattika. Phu.
Pācattika-dharma 77:
Concerning the Retention of Robes.
191. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, those bhikṣuṇīs, having come to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One while dressed in their inner and outer robes, were overtaken by a fire as they were departing;
their robes were burned.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
[The usual formula] ... up to: "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
If you do not now maintain this robe as a reserve robe,
then indeed a reserve robe must be maintained.
This is the very origin of the matter.
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī. Now, those bhikṣuṇīs— daughters of the Śākyas, daughters of the Mallas, and daughters of the Kolitas— who had gone forth from delicate backgrounds,
were becoming exhausted while carrying heavy outer robes (saṃghāṭī).
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī... [as before] ...until the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, I allow it for one who is ill.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Gautamī, assemble [the nuns]."
[The full formula] as before, up to:
"Whatever nun who is not ill does not wear her customary robe incurs a *pācattika* offense.
"Whatever nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"A robe for use" refers to [robes] from the outer cloak (saṃghāṭī) down to the bathing cloth (daka-śāṭikā). "While using it" means that it should be taken along wherever one goes.
"Unless she is ill" is a term withdrawn by the Blessed One; there is no offense for one who is ill.
If that nun, being not ill, does not carry her reserve robe, she incurs a *pācattika* offense.
However, if she now pays homage to a shrine, performs walking meditation, or goes within the boundary, there is no offense.
If a monk also does not wear his reserve robe, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun who is not ill does not wear her reserve robe, it is a *pācattika* offense."
Pācattika-dharma 78:
Cooking. 192. The Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī.
Now, daily food was being brought from the family of Bhadrā Kāpileyī’s relatives.
She would cook it in the monastery and eat it.
Then her sons and brothers arrived.
They went to Bhadrā to see her.
She said to the others, "Will you eat?
They then replied, "We will eat."
She gave it to him from there.
He said,
"This is indeed delicious."
"Where did you get this? She replied, "It was brought from your house."
They said,
"In our house, food is not cooked so deliciously.
He said:
"Will you good slave-girls know how it should be protected?
In this very way, they leave the requisites unsheltered."
Having returned home, they beat those slave girls with sticks and whips, saying:
"Daughters of a *iti-kitikā*, we provide you with such extensive provisions, yet you act so callously!
Weeping, the girls said:
"The noble daughter has killed us!
This matter was heard by the bhikṣuṇīs.
Such was the occasion.
[The usual formula] ... until the Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression, noble lady."

Therefore, it is not permissible to cook, have cooked, roast, or have roasted food—whether hard food or soft food—that has been brought from elsewhere. This is the origin of the rule. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now those bhikṣuṇīs, daughters of the Śākyas and daughters of the Kolitas, while wandering for alms, obtained food that had been kept overnight.
Stale rice;
stale soup;
stale vegetables.
They ate spoiled bean soup;
having eaten it again and again, they vomited.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
[The usual formula] ... up to:
"Is it permissible, Blessed One, for a bhikṣuṇī to eat while remaining silent?
The Blessed One said: "It is permissible."

Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī: “...until they are completely purified. Whatever nun, however, having repeatedly cooked or caused to be cooked, or roasted or caused to be roasted, or boiled or caused to be boiled, hard food or soft food that has been brought [to her]...”
Or if one who is not ill should chew or eat [it], it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
"Whichever nun," and so forth [as in the standard formula].
"Brought from elsewhere" means brought from a village or brought from a city.
"Solid food" means solid food; "soft food" means soft food.
"Having cooked" means by oneself; "having had cooked" means by others.
"Having roasted" means by oneself;
"having caused to roast" means by others;
"having boiled" means by oneself.
"Having caused to be woven" means by others.
"Not being ill" is a term withdrawn by the Blessed One; there is no offense for one who is ill. What, then, is intended here by "illness"?

She is either weakened by old age, or weakened by illness, or she vomits after eating, or she experiences discomfort; this is what is intended here by "illness. If that nun, out of greed for flavor, should repeatedly cook or cause to be cooked alms-food that has already been taken away, she incurs a *pācattika* offense.
Now, when it has become cold, it is permitted to warm it;
but not with a large pan or a small pot.
Rather, it should be warmed with a copper vessel, a bronze bowl, or a brass dish.
If a monk cooks for himself, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Vinaya.
However, if he has it cooked by a kitchen attendant, there is no offense.
Furthermore, if the alms-food has become cold and he warms it, there is no offense.
Therefore the Blessed One said:

"If a nun, being not ill, should eat or consume hard food or soft food that has been brought by another, after having cooked it herself or caused it to be cooked, roasted it herself or caused it to be roasted, or boiled it herself or caused it to be boiled, it is a *pācattika* offense. HRĀ.
Pācattika-dharma 79:
[Concerning] a water-fan. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.

Gartodara, Gartodara’s mother, and Gartodara’s father went forth from the home life into homelessness. Gartodara’s father and Gartodara’s mother had gone forth among the Śākyas, while Gartodara had gone forth among the non-Buddhist ascetics (tīrthikas). Gartodara’s father ate his meal while Gartodara’s mother stood before him fanning him and holding a water-pot.
He then began to recount various past deeds of hers that were unpleasant to her;
she struck him on the head with her water-pitcher.
And he was struck on the head with the handle of the fan; you are a fool, an old fool, unskilled, and ignorant of proper conduct— yet even now you speak what should not be spoken!
She was seen by the bhikṣuṇīs,
and they said to her,
"Noble lady, do not do this."
"This foremost assembly cannot be treated in such a manner.
She then said:
"Indeed, this man is incompetent, unskilled, and ignorant of the proper nature of things; even now, he speaks those things which ought not to be spoken."
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. ... [the Buddha] said: "It is a transgression (duṣkṛta), O mother of Gartodara."
This is not the Dharma; this is not the Vinaya.
And yet, you now attend to a monk while he is eating with water and a fan.
Therefore, it is not permissible to attend to him with water and a fan.
The Blessed One said:
"If a nun should serve a monk who is eating with water or a fan, it is a *pācattika* offense.
Regarding the phrase "if a nun": this refers to one who has received full ordination (*upasampannā*).
[The] "peyālaṃ" [is as follows]:
"A monk" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*). [The] "pe" [is as follows].
"Eating" means any kind of food to be chewed or swallowed, whether it consists of the five types of staple foods (*pañca-jātaka*) or is mixed with the five types of staple foods.

"She should attend with water-fanning" means she should hold a water-pitcher or provide a breeze with a fan; [if she does so], it is a *pācattika* offense. This applies as long as the rule has been prescribed.

If that nun carries a water-pitcher but does not fan herself, she commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya. If she fans herself but does not carry a water-pitcher, she commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
If she does both, it is a *pācittika* offense.
If neither [is present], there is no offense.
This offense applies to one monk and one nun;
however, if there are now many monks, there is no offense.
Now, if a monk is the father or brother of a nun, even if he fans her, there is no offense.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should serve a monk while he is eating with water-fanning, it is a *pācattika*."
Pācattika-dharma 80: Eating Garlic 194. The Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha.
There was a garlic merchant named Meghīya.
He invited the community of bhikṣuṇīs to a meal of garlic.
Then the group of six bhikṣuṇīs ate it, crushed it, threw it away, distributed it, and took it with them as they departed.
Then, on one occasion, he went to inspect the garden;
he then saw that the garden had been devastated.
He then said,
"By whom was this enclosure destroyed?
He replied, "I invited the noble ladies."
Now they were eating garlic, crushing it, throwing it away, distributing it, and taking it along as they went.
Then he became displeased and said:
"If they eat, why do they crush [it]?
and so forth.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
As far as the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should eat garlic,
it is an offense of expiation (pācattika)."
"Garlic" means: garlic is called *jātima*, *sevima*, *nāgara*, *kaccharuha*, *pārvateya*, *brahmadeya*, *āvarantaka*, *māgadhaka*, and *kosalaka*.
Whatever other garlic there may be as well—all garlic is not permitted.
It is not permitted raw; it is not permitted cooked.
Liver is not permitted;
nothing whatsoever is permitted for internal consumption.
Now, if a nun has a boil, a carbuncle, a wound, or an injury, she is allowed to smear it [with ointment].
Having smeared it, one must not remain standing in an open area where others may approach;
rather, one should stay in a concealed place until the news has spread.
After washing [the hands], one should depart.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should eat garlic, it is an offense of expiation. (1)
Summary verse:
Transferring [the robe], [71] the ascetic’s robe,
[72] the inner garment, [73].
The *saṃkakṣikā* [74], the *daśaka-śāṭikā* [75], the *kaṭhina* [76], and the *cīvara-pārihārika* [77].
[He] cooks five [things] [78]; [he uses] water and a fan [79]; and he eats garlic [80].
The eighth chapter.
Pācattika-dharma 81: Giving [a robe].
195. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī. A sister of the nun Rāṣṭrapālā had passed away.

Now she would give various kinds of hard and soft foods to those nephews after having eaten them herself. People then complained, saying, "Look, sirs! This nun gives away the gifts of the faithful to householders."
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. [She said:
"Call Rāṣṭrapālā.
She was then summoned.
The Blessed One asks all of that in detail.
He says: "Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, it is not permissible to give hard or soft food with one's own hand to a householder. This is the origin of the rule."
Gartodara, Gartodara’s father, and Gartodara’s mother went forth from the household life into homelessness.
Gartodara’s father and Gartodara’s mother were ordained by the Śākyas;
Gartodara was ordained by the non-Buddhist ascetics (tīrthikas).
When he approached Gartodaramātṛ, she gave him a bowl full of various kinds of snacks.
Taking it, he went to a tavern; he ate some himself and offered some to others. They then said:
"Where did you obtain this? He then said, "Make no noise!"
The female ascetics of the Śākyan clan are worthy of offerings;
we too are worthy of offerings from them;
we too are worthy of offerings from them.
Now people were complaining.
The nuns heard of this matter. This is the case.
[The usual formula] ... until the Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, O mother of Gartodara!"
Therefore, it is not permissible to give hard food or soft food to a householder or a wandering ascetic.
Then the Blessed One— [peyālam]— up to [the usual formula].
Furthermore, if a nun should give hard food or soft food with her own hand to a householder or to a wandering ascetic, it is a *pācattika*.
"If a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"To a householder" means to a layperson.
"Of the wanderer" refers to [anyone] down to the Gautamas and the matted-hair ascetics.
"With one's own hand" means hand to hand,
or vessel to vessel.
"Solid food" means whatever is solid food.
"Soft food" means whatever is soft food.
Should she give it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittika).
Now, if someone comes to a nun—
whether it be a blood relative or a brother—
if she has anything to give him, it is not permissible for her to give it with her own hand.
It should be given to one who makes it permissible.
Now, if there is no one to make it permissible, it should be said:
"Therefore, take it yourselves and eat."
Then, if he sees that this person is greedy for flavor and eats everything,
having had him accept as much as was relinquished, [he may take] the remainder.
He should be told:
"By Gopa.
Then, having placed him on the ground, he should be told.
"Take it and eat.
Now, when a renunciant arrives, it is not permissible to give hard food or soft food with one's own hand;
it must be given through a *kalpiyakāra* (an attendant who prepares what is allowable).
Now, if there is no one to prepare what is allowable, [he says] "Take this very thing and eat it. Then he replies:
"O kinsman, why do you behave toward us as if we were outcasts?"
It should be said:
"In that way, you have gone forth in a poorly proclaimed teaching.
Now, when he goes to another village, it is permissible for him to have a ritual of purification performed.
Therefore, eat yourselves and accept from us as well.
Now, if he knows [that they are] "greedy for flavors"— the rest is as before.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should give hard food or soft food with her own hand to a householder or to a wandering ascetic, it is an offense of expiation."
The Blessed One was dwelling at Kauśāmbī.
The nun Chandakamātā entered the royal harem.
She was skilled in medicinal roots, medicinal leaves, and medicinal fruits.
She then administered enemas to women from royal families, ministerial families, merchant families, and guild-leader families;
she treated those suffering from difficult labors.
She provides collyrium, counter-collyrium, emetics, purgatives, sudation therapy, nasal medication, surgical treatment, and medicinal remedies;
she receives visits, and she obtains food and snacks.
Then those nuns began to complain.
"This is not the life of renunciation; this is the practice of a physician.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, and so on, until the Blessed One said:
"Call Chandaka’s mother. She was then summoned,
and the Blessed One said:
"Is it true, Chandakamātā, that you make your living by the science of medicine? "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Chandaka’s mother, this was a misdeed!
Therefore, it is not permissible to make one's livelihood by means of the science of medicine. Then the Blessed One—
... [as before] ... up to: Whatever nun should make her livelihood by means of the science of medicine, it is a *pācattika*.
"The science of medicine" refers to the science of snakes, the science of poisons, and so forth, up to the movements of the *grahas*.
If she makes her livelihood by that means, it is a *pācattika* offense.
This is the formal rule (*prajñapti*):
it is not permissible for a nun to practice medicine.
It is possible to teach [this]:
if a monk makes a living by means of the science of medicine, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun should make her livelihood by means of the science of medicine, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
Pācattika-dharma 83:
Vācayati 197. The Blessed One was staying at Kauśāmbī.
The Blessed One has prescribed a training rule:
"It is not permitted to practice medical treatment.
Consequently, Chandaka’s mother no longer practiced medical treatment.
"Now people are coming. It would be well, Noble Lady, if you were to treat them. She then said:
"It is not permitted to practice medicine, for a training rule has been prescribed by the Blessed One. Nevertheless, give me something to recite.
She then taught the science of medicine to householders and wandering mendicants.
The bhikṣuṇīs then complained: "This is no true renunciation; it is merely the practice of medicine. Thereupon the Blessed One said:
Whatever nun should teach medical science to a householder or to a wandering ascetic, that is a *pācattika* offense.
"Whatever nun" is as before.
"Householder" means a layperson.
"Parivrājaka" refers to those ranging from the Gautamas to the Jaṭilakas.
"Medical science" (cikitsita-vidyā) refers to the science of snakes, the science of poisons, up to the movements of the planets.
"One should cause the body to be treated with medical science" means one should prescribe it.
Up to the formal designation:
it is not permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to teach medical science to a householder or a wandering ascetic;
however, it is permissible to instruct [them].
If a monk teaches the science of medicine, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should teach the science of medicine to a householder or to a wandering ascetic, it is a *pācattika* offense."
Pācattika-dharma 84: Service for Laypeople 198. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now, Mṛgāramātā Viśākhā had invited the Saṅgha of both divisions for a meal.
Then those bhikṣuṇīs, having arrived early in the morning, said:
"Laywoman, since you have now invited the Saṅgha of both divisions for a meal, what service can we now perform for you, laywoman?"
She then said:
"What benefit will the noble ladies provide?
Recite and study!"
Apply your minds thoroughly;
in this way, you will have rendered me a service. Indeed, it is so; furthermore, we shall likewise render you a service.
Then, having ascended to the upper floor, they took cotton; some treated it,
others carded it,
and others spun it.
Some had torn it apart;
others had cut it. Taking those bundles of thread, they approached the laywoman.
"O female lay follower, a favor has been done.
She said:
"This is no favor to me, that the noble ladies should comb me, or massage me, or pull at my hair, or cut it."

"This is my favor to you, noble ladies: having eaten from me, you should recite, study, and apply yourselves to the yoga of the Buddhas' teaching. When the nuns heard what that female lay devotee had reproached them for, they reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
[The] *peyālaṃ* [continues] until the Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression, O bhikṣuṇīs."
Therefore, it is not permissible to perform domestic service for householders. [This applies] as far as:
"Whichever nun should perform domestic service for householders, there is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
"Whichever nun" means one who has received full ordination (upasampannā).
"Householder" means one who lives at home.
"Service" means he should do such things as spinning or carding, up to and including crushing,
grinding, cooking, or sewing.
Furthermore, if she should perform any other service for a layperson, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika),
as defined by the formal rule:
it is not permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to perform services for a layperson.
Now, when there is an offering of garlands or the application of perfumes,
she says:
"Assistance must be rendered by the noble ladies (*āryamiśrikā*). Even if she grinds perfume or strings flowers, there is no offense.
However, if a monk performs domestic services for a layperson, he incurs a transgression of the discipline (*vinayātikrama*).
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should perform domestic services for a layperson, it is an offense of expiation. (4)
Pācattika-dharma 85:
On Eating Together. 199. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
A nun named Sthūlanandā approached another household at midday when it was overcast.
At that time, a husband and wife, oppressed by passion and perceiving themselves to be in private, desired to engage in sexual intercourse.
She then entered there suddenly, unannounced.

Now that man was agitated and distressed; the king had him guarded by that [woman] because he intended to have this daughter of Itikitikā, the female ascetic, executed. She, for her part, was terrified.
She spoke to the fleeing bhikṣuṇīs: "Noble ladies, I have been made to fall away from the holy life. [The bhikṣuṇīs] reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī;
[the rest is as before].
The Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, Nanda, that knowing it to be a family where food is shared, you approach them during the day without having first announced yourself.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.

“Gautamī, assemble the bhikṣuṇīs. [The usual formula follows] … “Whatever bhikṣuṇī, knowing that it is a family where food is shared, should go there during the day without having previously informed them, there is an offense of expiation (pācattika).”
"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"Knowing" means she should know it herself or hear it from another.
"Family" refers to families such as those of brahmins and so forth.
Where there is a woman and a man, a cooking pot and a small jar, a winnowing basket and a pestle, a broom and a measure of barley—this is the last house.
"Eating together" means a woman is the food for a man, and a man is also the food for a woman.
If, after midday has passed, they have not been informed beforehand—that is, without making a sound.
"If she should approach uninvited," meaning she should enter, it is a *pācattika* offense, as far as the formal rule (*prajñapti*) extends.
Now, when it is known that this is a family where food is shared, it is not permissible for her to approach there uninvited without having first informed them.
If, however, two...
The gatekeeper should be told,
"I am entering.
If he says:
"Do not enter"—thus one must not enter.
Then he says:
"Wait for a moment until I have returned."
If one has entered but does not exit, it is not permitted to enter again.
Now, if there is the sound of "tuṇu-tuṇa," a snap of the fingers should be given, or one should cough.
If, however, it remains silent, it is not permitted to enter.
Now, if they go out to meet them, saying, "Welcome, noble one," and "Please enter," he should enter.
If a monk approaches even when he has been informed [of the arrival], he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun, knowing that it is a family where food is shared, should visit during the day without having been previously informed and without being invited, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
Pācattika-dharma 86: Association 200. The Blessed One was dwelling at Vaiśālī.

Now, that Licchavi daughter Kālīyantrī who had been ordained was living in close association with both householders and those who had gone forth. The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Then the Blessed One said,
"It is a transgression for you, Kālī.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
"Call the nuns together, Gautamī. [The usual formula applies.

"Whichever nun, moreover, should dwell in association with monastery attendants or wandering mendicants for a day or even for a moment—at least [for the duration of time it takes] with monastery attendants or novice monks—there is an offense of expiation (pācattika)."
"Whatever nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*). [The] intermediate [passage] continues as before, up to... [end].
"By householders," that is, by laypeople; "by wanderers," that is, by non-Buddhist ascetics ranging from the Gautamas to the Jaṭilakas.
"She should live in association" means by bodily association, verbal association,
or both bodily and verbal association;
whether for a day, or for a moment (muhūrta), or at the very least for that instant, that fraction of time, or that brief moment.
"By the monastery attendants and novice monks.
The monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) are those who serve the Saṅgha.
The novice monks (*śramaṇoddeśa*) are those from fifteen years of age up to seventy.
If this nun lives in association with either monastery attendants or wandering mendicants, it is an offense of expiation (*pācattika*).
Now, if nuns live in association with one another...
Those who take [pleasure] while being attached must be separated;
they must be made to live apart.
Even three times, a nun [must be separated] from one with whom she has become intimately associated.
She commits an offense of transgression of the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should dwell in association with lay attendants or wandering mendicants, even for a day or a moment, at the very least together with lay attendants or novice monks..."
An offense of expiation. 6.
Pācattika-dharma 87:
Swearing an Oath 201. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
A nun named Sthūlanandā quarreled with the other nuns.
Whenever she was defeated, she would then prostrate herself, saying:
"Homage to the Blessed One! I swear by the feet of the Blessed One!"
I swear by the saffron robes;
I swear by the end of suffering,
if I speak thus.
May I not die while wearing the saffron robes;
may I not bring an end to suffering;
may I not go to the destination of one who has killed his mother.
I go to the destination of one who kills his father; I go to the destination of one who kills an Arhat;
indeed, I go to the destination of one who is ungrateful.
I go to the destiny of one who betrays a friend; I go to the destiny of one who slanders a noble person;
I become a denizen of hell.
"I go to the realm of animals; I become a hungry ghost.
May it be so for that Bhadrāyaṇī who spoke thus to me."
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. [She said: "Go and summon Nandā.
Then the Blessed One questioned her about all of this in detail.
“Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
“It is a transgression for you, Nanda,” and so on, until the Blessed One said:
Whatever nun should dwell using oaths, whether referring to herself or referring to another, there is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
"Whatever nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*). ...
"Should dwell using oaths" means she should make a formal oath.
I swear by the feet of the Blessed One, the Fortunate One;
all as before, until: that nun, with reference to herself or another...
[If] he curses, it is a *pācattika* offense.
A monk who also curses incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline (*vinayātikrama*).
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun should dwell while swearing an oath, whether referring to herself or another, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
Pācattika-dharma 88: Weeping 202. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
A nun named Sthūlanandā quarreled with the other nuns;
whenever she was defeated, she would strike herself with her fists, slaps, and blows to the head, and she would beat her own belly.
Bala-Balā wept.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
and so on until the Blessed One said:
"Is it true, Nandā, that you are quarreling with the bhikṣuṇīs? [Peṭāla] ... up to ... that you are weeping and wailing?"
"Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "It is a transgression for you, Nanda; this is not the Dharma... [and so on]... Therefore, it is not permissible to weep after having struck oneself."
Then indeed, O Blessed One, until they have become completely purified:
if a nun, having struck herself, should weep, it is a *pācattika* offense.
"Again, a bhikṣuṇī" [and so forth]. "Having killed herself" means with sticks, or with stones, or by any other means whatsoever.
"Should she weep," means: if she should shed tears, it is a *pācattika*.
This is the formal rule (*prajñapti*).
That nun strikes herself but does not weep; she incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline (*vinayātikrama*).
If she weeps but does not strike, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
If she both strikes and weeps, she incurs a *pācattika* offense.
If she neither strikes nor weeps, there is no offense.
If a monk, having struck himself, weeps, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun, moreover, having struck herself, should weep, it is a *pācattika* offense. (8)
Pācattika-dharma 89:
Kṣiyati 203. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now, the nun Jetā was praised by the families for the sake of Sthūlanandā.

That nun Jetā approached the families as a virtuous woman, with a pleasing manner in her advancing and retreating, in her looking ahead and looking aside, in her bending and stretching, and in her carrying of the outer robe, bowl, and inner robes;
she was not arrogant, not haughty, not fickle, not talkative, and her speech was not scattered.
She was pleasing to behold, so gods and humans were filled with serene faith;
they performed services for her,
addressed her in greeting, and rose up before her.
They invited [her] with bowls, robes, and medicinal requisites for the sick.

The nun Sthūlanandā was neither accomplished in proper attire nor accomplished in dignified deportment; she wore robes that were filthy, soiled, torn, and tattered, and she was bloated and protruding like a large, swollen corpse.
"Come here! Suck my breasts! Grow fat on my buttocks! Thus she was arrogant, haughty, fickle, talkative, and loose in speech. They paid her no respect nor did they invite her [to meals].
She then said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"See, noble ladies! The noble Jetā, who was praised by my own family, speaks ill of me!
She then replied, "This is not so, noble lady."
"I am not speaking dispraise of the Noble Lady. The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
and so on until the Blessed One said:
It was a misdeed of yours, Nanda!
[The usual formula]... until:
"Is it not so that you, by what was ill-heard and ill-retained, [have acted]?"

"Since you have fallen into the practice of censuring [others] based on what was poorly heard and poorly understood, it is therefore not permissible for you to fall into the practice of censuring others. Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī."
"Call them together, Gautamī, until they have become thoroughly purified.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣuṇī should speak thus to the bhikṣuṇīs: 'When I, noble ladies, approached such-and-such a family...'"

If, out of ill-will toward a certain bhikṣuṇī named so-and-so toward the Blessed One, one should fall into the offense of reproach based on what was wrongly heard or wrongly understood, it is a pācattika.

"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*). "Should speak thus to the nuns" refers to [the case of] the nun Sthūlanandā, who said: "Noble lady, until I [visit] such-and-such a family. A "family" (*kula*) means a Kṣatriya family; a "family" means a Brāhmaṇa family, a Rājanya family, and furthermore, whatever other families there may be.
Then, regarding the phrase "to one named so-and-so," it is as in the case of the nun Jetā.

"Ill-will toward the Blessed One" does not refer to the ten grounds for resentment or the ten occasions for improper anger. "Without cause" means by what is wrongly heard or wrongly understood; it is not by a formal act of seeing, nor by a formal act of a śramaṇa. If she should charge another with an offense of censure (*kṣiyā-dharma*) without ground, she commits a *pācattika* offense.
As long as it is merely a designation, it is not permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to fall into the offense of censure based on what was poorly heard or poorly understood;
she incurs a *pācattika* and commits an offense.
A bhikṣu also, if he falls into the offense of censure based on what was poorly heard or poorly understood, incurs a transgression of the discipline (*vinayātikrama*).
Therefore the Blessed One said:

"If a nun should speak thus to other nuns: 'When I, noble ladies, approach such-and-such a family, [I hear] that the Blessed One has a grudge against the nun named so-and-so,' and should, on account of what was poorly heard and poorly understood, fall into the practice of censuring [the Buddha], it is a *pācattika* offense. (9)
Pācattika-dharma 90:
Regarding stinginess toward families.
204. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
A nun named Sthūlanandā, having dressed herself at the very hour of dawn, took her bowl and robe and stood at the gate-chambers of great families.
To the monks as they were entering, she said:
"Enter, noble sirs; enter, venerable masters! It is for our sake that this is being prepared."
"First, having given a morsel of food to you who are the foremost, he will afterwards eat for himself.
Do not approach other families;
it is not accomplished by others."
Then, being ashamed, they will retreat.
This same procedure should also be applied to the bhikṣuṇīs. Likewise for the Carakas, Parivrājakas, Ājīvakas, and Nirgranthas...
As many as those who contemplate the Dharma entered the hall, she then reviled them as they entered: "O Caṇḍāyus! You are ruined in hope, shattered in hope!"
"You who have fallen from the wine-cup, you who are like donkeys on a vehicle, naked, shameless, lacking modesty, holders of false views, and fallen—enter! For your sake, success shall be achieved.
Having first given you the foremost alms-food, he will afterwards enjoy it himself.
Do not approach other families."
It is not accomplished by other afflictions;
they will now be ashamed and retreat.
Thus [he addresses] all those who wander for alms.
She engaged in quarreling.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. [The rest is as before.]
The Blessed One said:
"Summon Nandā.
She was then summoned.
All of that;
the Blessed One questions him in detail, until [the reply]:
"Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, Nanda, that you should act with such envy toward families.
Therefore, it is not permissible to act with envy toward families."
"Therefore, it is not permissible to practice stinginess toward families.
Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Gautamī, assemble [the nuns]."
[The full passage] as before, up to:
"Whatever nun should practice stinginess toward a family, that is a *pācattika* offense.
"Whatever nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"Family-sparing" means that she should create an obstruction; it is a *pācattika* offense, up to the point of the formal rule.
It is not permissible for a nun to practice family-sparing.
If she does so, she incurs a *pācattika* offense.
If a monk or a nun asks, one should speak of qualities as they truly are.
But if followers of other sects ask, thinking, "Lest they cause these people to adopt wrong views," and one frowns, there is no offense.
A monk [should also act] toward a family...
[If] she acts thus, she commits an offense of transgression of the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Whatever nun should practice stinginess toward families, that is a *pācattika* offense. [End of section. Summary verse:
[81] He gives; [82] he treats medically; [83] he causes to recite; [84] service for a householder; [85] eating together; [86] social association.
[87] He utters curses; [88] he weeps; [89] he dwells in resentment; [90] out of stinginess regarding his family.
The ninth section is completed.
Pācattika-dharma 91:
In the presence of.
205. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Gartodara, Gartodara’s mother, and Gartodara’s father went forth from the household life into homelessness... [and so on] ...until that old man was eating.
Gartodaramātā was serving [the meal].
Then he spoke of certain past deeds of hers—excesses of feminine wickedness—which were unpleasant to her. She then said:
Short-lived;
neither a capable nor an experienced person;
unrefined, unskilled, and ignorant of the nature of things.
Even now you speak what should not be spoken.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. [The rest as before.]
“Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
“It is a transgression for you, O mother of Gartodara.”
[The usual formula.
Therefore, it is not permissible to revile or abuse a monk face-to-face.
Then the Blessed One [proceeded] until they became completely purified.
Whatever nun should revile, provoke, or abuse a monk face-to-face, there is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
"Whatever nun" means one who is fully ordained (upasampannā).
"Face-to-face" means within the range of four eyes.

"Should revile" means: she should provoke with the syllables *a*, *śa*, and *e*, and she should scold and abuse [the monk], saying, "You wretch! You old fool! You incompetent one! You who do not know the nature of things! This is a *pācattika* offense, up to the point of the formal rule. It is not permitted for a nun to revile, provoke, or scold a monk face-to-face.
If she reviles, becomes angry, or abuses [him], it is a *pācattika*. Now, if a monk who is a nun’s father, brother, or kinsman has gone forth,
and he is agitated, arrogant, and unconcentrated, she may then speak to him.
Now, it is not permissible to speak by means of intimidation;
rather, one should make him understand through wisdom.
If he is a youth, he should be told:
"O kinsman, if you do not train now, when will you train?
When you have become worn out and old. Then, when he has become an elder, he should be told: [this].
"Now you do not train; when will you train? When you have arrived at the entrance of the maṇḍala!
It is not permissible for a monk to revile nuns to their faces, saying, "Shaven-headed woman! Prostitute! ... [and so forth] ...
If that nun reviles a monk to his face, it is a *pācattika* offense. 1.
Pācattika-dharma 92:
Less than twelve years. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, the nuns who had been ordained for one year, two years, up to six years were taking on students;
yet they neither exhorted nor instructed them.
They grew like *indrāgava* oxen in a sanctuary.
They grow like [untrained] colts;
being neither endowed with proper decorum nor established in the path of noble conduct,
they do not know how one should behave toward a preceptor-ni.
