Pācattika-dharma 119:
Gardens 233. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now, some bhikṣuṇīs went out to a park together with women. The women were eating and drinking there,
while the bhikṣuṇīs walked about in female attire, looking at the pleasure-houses, the forest-cottages, and the painted pavilions.
Then, having been harassed by men in a secluded place, those nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. ...
[The report continued] until the Blessed One said:
"Within the kingdom" means even within one's own realm; "within the country" (*anta-rāṣṭra*) refers to the same.
If a nun should go there to see pleasure-houses, forest-houses, or picture galleries, it is a *pācattika* offense. "Even within the kingdom" means within one's own kingdom.
"Even within the kingdom" means one's own kingdom.
And therein, "monastery dwellings" refers to these:
namely, *caṃpaka* groves, or *panasa* groves, or *atimuktaka* groves.
"Forest-houses" refers to these:
either groves of *nyagrodha* trees, or groves of grapes, or groves of plantains, or groves of pomegranates, or groves of *mātuluṅga* fruits.
"Variegated houses" refers to these: either assembly halls or gabled chambers.
"She should go for the sake of seeing" means for the sake of looking. It is an offense of expiation (pācattika),
as far as the formal rule (prājñapti) extends.
It is not permitted to go to see a pleasure-house, a forest-house, or a picture-gallery.
If she goes, she incurs an offense of transgression of the Vinaya;
when she has arrived there, she incurs a *pācattika* offense.
Now, if he wanders about right there together with women, there is no offense.
If a monk goes to see a pleasure-house, a forest-house, or a picture-gallery where those who indulge in sensual pleasures sport, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
Whether it be within the kingdom or even within the realm, if a bhikṣuṇī goes there to see pleasure-houses, forest-houses, or picture galleries, it is a pācattika offense. 8.
Pācattika-dharma 120: In Secret.
234. The Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī.
A nun named Sujātā was formerly the second wife of the venerable Udāyin.
She then sent a messenger to him, saying: "Come! It will be my turn to provide lodging;
we shall stay together."

When those bhikṣuṇīs had entered the alms-round, the venerable Udāyin, having dressed and put on his robes at the very hour, took his bowl and outer robe and entered there. Now, they were sitting on a wooden seat behind the monastery, their minds impassioned, gazing intently at one another’s private parts with their own supple organs. At that time, another elder bhikṣuṇī went to the area behind the monastery for the purpose of voiding excrement or urine.
She was seen by her;
she then became ashamed and drew back.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
[The usual formula] ... up to: "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
It is a wrongdoing for you, Sujātī, until [your offenses] have been fully purified.
Furthermore, whichever nun should arrange to sit in private alone with a monk, it is a *pācattika*.
"Whichever nun" means one who has received full ordination (*upasampannā*).
"One with one" means that she is there and another is also there;
[the other] may be asleep, intoxicated, insane, deranged in mind, distracted by pain, lying on his back, non-human, or belonging to the animal realm—
even in such cases, this is "one with one."
"In private" means secretly. "He prepares a seat" means they should sit together.
An offense of expiation (pācattika).
[The] intermediate [passage]. Up to the formal rule (prajñapti).
If this nun sits together with a monk even once, and they remain seated for the duration of the day, she incurs one *pācattika* offense.
If, however, she rises and sits down again and again, she incurs a *pācattika* offense for each such instance.
Now, if there are two people and one enters the dwelling for some purpose, the nun must rise quickly.
Nor should he think, "Now she will not recognize me as one of a thousand [monks], so she intends to harass me.
Rather, he should perceive this:
"I shall rise up."
He said: "For what purpose?
It must be told."
To stand alone with one [woman].
This refers to a novice (śrāmaṇera) who is less than seven years old.
To what extent, within what interval, does an offense occur for the purpose of seduction rather than release?
If, in the meantime, alms are given without having been intentionally prepared;

or if the nuns' quarters are crowded with people and passers-by, and carpenters, builders, and painters come out and enter— even if they remain there while those [items] are being made allowable, there is no offense.
Now, if the gateway to the street is the door and women and men pass through it without interruption, even if the one who prepares the food remains there, there is no offense.
But if the interval is now broken, it is a *pācattika*.
If the one who prepares the food falls asleep, he should be awakened by snapping the fingers.
Now, if there are two [monks] in a place where it is permissible for a preparer to remain, and he sees one or another of the three, there is no offense.
Or, if he sees one or another of the three through the opening of a window, there is no offense.
There is the sphere of visibility, but not the sphere of the ascetic.
There is that which is the sphere of the ascetic but not the sphere of vision;
there is that which is both the sphere of vision and the sphere of the ascetic;
and there is that which is neither the sphere of vision nor the sphere of the ascetic.
Now, what is the case where there is the range of vision but not the range of hearing?
A monk sees with his ordinary eye that "this person is sitting there," whether it be a monk or a nun, yet he does not hear their voice with his ordinary ear.
In this way, the fourfold permutation is to be applied.
As far as this offense extends:
whether in a village or in the forest, by night or by day, in a concealed place or in the open air, for one person and not before a great multitude, neither in their presence nor at a distance.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
If a nun should sit down in private with a monk, one person with one person, it is a *pācattika* offense.
Pācattika-dharma 121, [Section on] Men 235. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now Bhadrā Kāpileyī, having gone to her family home, was staying alone with each of her brothers, nephews, maternal uncles, and their sons.
When the bhikṣuṇīs, while wandering for alms, saw this, they complained:
"How can this woman who has gone forth sit in private, alone with a man?"
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
[The matter was conveyed] until the Blessed One said:
"Summon Bhadrā."
She was then summoned. She was questioned on all of those very points, to which she replied,
“Yes, Blessed One.”
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, it is not permissible for one woman to sit in private with one man," up until the point where the Blessed One said.
Furthermore, if a nun should sit in private with a man, one-on-one, it is a *pācattika* offense.
"Furthermore, if a nun" means one who has received full ordination. "With a man, one-on-one" means that she is indeed alone with him, even to this extent.
"Secretly" means falsely.

"Should arrange a seat" means they should sit together. It is an offense of expiation (pācattika) up to the point of the formal rule. If that nun sits with a man in a secluded place for even a single day, she incurs one offense of expiation.
Thus in detail, just as it was for the monk,
the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should sit in private, one-on-one, with a man, it is a *pācattika* offense."
Pācattika-dharma 122: Upakarṇaka 236. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now Bhadrā Kāpileyī had gone to her family home;
she stood within arm's reach of her brothers, sisters, sons, and nephews, conversing with them and whispering into their ears.
The bhikṣuṇīs then complained.
"What is the use of whispering into the ear of this nun?
She is certainly speaking for our benefit.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, and so forth.
If a nun should stand within arm’s reach of a man, or converse with him, or speak into his ear, it is a *pācattika*.
“If a nun” means one who has received full ordination (*upasampannā*).
“With a man” means with either a layperson or one who has gone forth (*pravrājita*).
"Within arm's reach" means he should stand within the range of an extended arm.
"Converses" means he should speak something. "Speaks into the ear" means he should speak at the level of the ear.
It is a *pācattika* offense, as far as the formal rule (*prajñapti*) extends:
it is not permissible for a nun to stand within arm’s reach of a man, nor to converse with him, nor to speak into his ear.
Now, if there is something that must be said, [she should say it from a distance].
If [the conversation] is within arm's reach, one should speak while standing;
however, if it is now necessary to speak privately, one should speak having placed a wall, a partition, a pillar, a tree, or a curtain between oneself and the other.
If that nun stands or converses with a man within arm's reach, or speaks into his ear, it is a *pācattika* offense.
If a monk also stands within arm’s reach of a woman, or converses with her, or whispers into her ear, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“If a nun should stand within arm’s reach of a man, or converse with him, or whisper into his ear, it is a *pācattika* offense. [1] Summary verse:
An umbrella [1(112)], a couch [2(113)], and a single-layered coverlet [3(114)];
he steps forward [4(115)], he enters [5(116)].
[6(117)] Together with people; [7(118)] on the road; [8(119)] in a garden; [9(120)] in secret; [10(121)] a man;
[11(122)] whispering into the ear.
The twelfth chapter.
Pācattika-dharma 123: Approaching 237. The Blessed One was dwelling at Vaiśālī.

Then Bhadrā Kāpileyī, having gone to her family home, suddenly entered by force while her sons, brothers, and nephews were in private in the dark and unaware. They were terrified there. The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
... [as before] ... "Yes, Blessed One," he replied.
The Blessed One said:
"Thus, knowing that the dwelling contains a man, you approach it in the dark without a lamp.
Therefore, this is not permissible; [this rule shall remain] until it is fully purified.
Furthermore, if a nun, knowing that a dwelling contains a man, should approach it in the dark without a lamp, it is a *pācattika* offense."
"Again, a bhikṣuṇī" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"Knowing" means she should know it herself or hear it from another. "With a man" means where there is a man. "In the dark without a lamp" means where there would be neither an oil lamp nor a torch.
"Should she enter," meaning she should go inside, it is a *pācattika* offense, as far as the formal rule (*prajñapti*) extends.
It is not permissible for a nun to enter a dwelling with a man in the dark without a lamp.
However, if there is some business and there is a loud noise there, she may enter; there is no offense.
Now, if there is no fire, one should make it known;
either a snap of the fingers should be made or a cough should be cleared.
If he says, "Enter," one should enter.
If that nun approaches without even perceiving [the danger] or making a snapping sound, she incurs a *pācattika* offense.
If a monk also approaches a dwelling containing women in the dark without being perceived, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun, knowing that a dwelling contains a man, should enter it in the dark without a lamp, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
Pācattika-dharma 124, Viśoka 238. The Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha.
Now those six group of bhikṣuṇīs went to a mountain-top festival.
Having gone there, they each took separate seats; a dancer performed, and as he danced with laughter, the performance proceeded through its various scenes.
All the people laughed.
Then they stand silent like practitioners of yoga;
when the drama has become tranquil and the performance has concluded,
they let out a loud laugh.
Then everyone became happy;
however, people now complained,
"There is too much laughter among these female ascetics."
Now, having been deprived of their sight, they did not provide a bandage for the forehead; they complained, saying, "We do not receive a bandage for the arm from these female ascetics."

The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. [She reported it to the Blessed One,] up until: "Yes, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: "In that case, it is not permissible to go to see Viśoka."
Then indeed, the Blessed One [spoke] until they became completely purified:
"If a bhikṣuṇī goes to see a performance, it is a pācattika offense.
Regarding the phrase "if a bhikṣuṇī": she who has received full ordination.

"Free from sorrow" means that they go to see performances by actors, dancers, wrestlers, boxers, musicians, and elephant trainers, or even to places where as few as four people have gathered for the sake of amusement;
this is an offense of expiation (*pācattika*) according to the formal rule.
Now, it is not permissible to go for the purpose of seeing Viśoka.
However, if a bhikṣuṇī, while walking for alms, sees a royal procession departing or the king’s harem coming out, she may close her eyes; even if she sees [them], there is no offense.
Now, if she makes an effort, thinking, "I shall look this way," or "I shall look that way," it is a *pācattika* offense.
Now, when there is an offering of garlands to the Blessed One, the laymen and laywomen say:
"The noble ladies must ensure the beauty [of the display]."
"The requisites must be provided"—thus it is permitted to provide the requisites.
Now, if at that time some agitation of mind arises, it is not permissible to remain. Even if a monk goes for the sake of seeing Viśoka, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun goes to see a performance for amusement, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika)."
Pācattika-dharma 125:
Quarreling 239. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

Then indeed, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, acting like a bull among the bhikṣuṇīs who were living in a state of quarreling, brawling, and having fallen into disputes and contention, did not settle their legal cases herself, nor did she cause them to be settled, nor did she exert herself toward their settlement.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One questioned him about everything, until [the monk] replied, "Yes, Blessed One. The Blessed One said:

"Thus, you, acting like a bull-cow, do not yourself pacify the legal disputes (*adhikaraṇa*) of the bhikṣuṇīs who have become quarrelsome, contentious, and fallen into strife and dispute; nor do you cause them to be pacified, nor do you exert yourself toward their pacification.
Therefore, this is not permissible."
Now, indeed, until they have become completely purified: if a nun,

while nuns are living in a state of quarreling, brawling, and having fallen into disputes and contention, acts as a "bull-like woman" (vṛṣabhī samanā) and does not settle their legal cases, does not cause them to be settled, and does not exert herself toward their settlement, it is a *pācattika* offense.

"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*). "Of those who have engaged in quarreling" means those who are engaging in verbal quarreling, such as saying, "It is my way," "It is my way," and so forth. "Of those who have engaged in brawling" means those who are mutually contending with one another.
"Of those who dwell having fallen into dispute and contention," that is to say:
"Dharma is non-Dharma; Vinaya is non-Vinaya;
an offense is a non-offense."
Whether heavy or light, with remediation or without remediation, with remainder or without remainder; whether a legal action (*dharmakarma*),
an illegal action (*adharmakarma*), a united action (*samagrakarma*), or a divided action (*vyagrakarma*)— up to an action that is appropriate to the situation—
for those who dwell [thus], they are like bulls, they are like leaders.
If one does not settle legal disputes oneself,
or does not cause others to settle them,
or does not exert effort toward settling them, it is a *pācattika* offense; such is the formal rule.

Now, when these nuns are engaged in quarreling, brawling, and falling into strife and dispute, it is no longer permissible to neglect them. Rather, they must be pacified and brought to peace. One must exert oneself for their reconciliation; one must hope for their pacification; they must ask one another for forgiveness; they must be reprimanded as is appropriate for the occasion; and they must be made to become harmonious once again.
Now, if she is unable [to settle it], another bhikṣuṇī should be requested or incited [to do so], as should laymen, laywomen, bhikṣus, or bhikṣuṇīs.
If those legal cases (*adhikaraṇa*) are harsh and difficult to settle, she waits for the right time, waits for the right occasion, and waits for the ripening of those very cases.

Having reached the right time, the right occasion, and the ripening, she settles them; there is no offense. This also applies to a bhikṣu who [waits] when bhikṣus have become quarrelsome, contentious, and fallen into strife and dispute.

If a nun, acting as a leader among nuns who are living while engaged in quarreling, brawling, and falling into disputes and arguments, does not settle those legal cases, nor causes them to be settled, nor makes an effort toward their settlement, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, if a nun, acting as a leader among nuns who are living while engaged in quarreling, brawling, and falling into disputes and arguments, does not settle those legal cases..."
If she does not cause [them] to be appeased, or if she does not exert herself toward appeasing them, it is a pācittika offense. ||3||
Pācattika-dharma 126:
Rubbing with ointment, [numbered] 240. The Blessed One was dwelling at Vaiśālī.

Now Bhadrā Kāpileyī was being led to her kinsmen’s family for anointment and bathing; she was being taken there by the housewives who said, "We shall anoint the Noble Lady and we shall bathe her; merit will accrue to us.
Some did so out of devotion, while others desired to see her slender limbs.
She was now gracious and beautiful to behold. Women are by nature curious; they anointed her, who was fond of fine colors, with *kāleyaka*, *tuṃgeyaka*, *svaṅgaka*, and *padmaka* fragrant powders.
She then consented.
Now the nuns were indignant, saying,
"See, noble ladies, even now this woman who has gone forth still has great desire!"
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. [Pe] ...
up to: "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"In this way, you have indeed had yourself massaged by women with ointments, rubbing, and bathing preparations.
Therefore, it is not permissible.
Now, indeed, the Blessed One [will speak] until they become completely purified."

Furthermore, whatever articles are approved for householders for the purpose of rubbing, massaging, and bathing—if a nun who is not ill should have herself rubbed or massaged with such things, it is a *pācattika*.
"Whatever articles are approved for householders" refers to those of Kṣatriya maidens, Brāhmaṇa maidens, and Gṛhapati maidens.
"Approved for rubbing, massaging, and bathing" refers to *kāleyaka*, *tuṅgeyaka*, or *cikkasa* paste.

If a single one of those nuns, while not being ill, should have herself massaged—what, then, is intended here by "illness"? If she has herself massaged when she is weak from old age or weak from disease, there is no offense.
"Should have herself massaged" means she should have herself rubbed; [if she does so], it is a *pācattika*.

Now, if there is a boil or a carbuncle, it is permitted to have it treated with medicinal ointments by rubbing and massaging. If there is a disturbance of bile, it is permitted to smear it with a paste of chickpea flour.
If there is a disturbance of wind, it is permitted to smear it with a paste of wheat flour.
Now, when there is a gathering, one should have her anointed with compounded medicines, massaged, and smeared [with ointment].
Having been smeared, she must not stand in a place where people pass by;
rather, she should stay in a secluded spot.
When it has become soiled,
then, having rubbed it off, one must go out.
If a monk who is not ill should have himself rubbed with oil-cake or have himself massaged, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun should have herself rubbed, massaged, or bathed by householders with substances approved for such purposes, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika)."
Pācattika-dharma 127 (Bhikṣuṇī 241). The Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī.
Now, a training rule has been prescribed by the Blessed One: it is not permissible for nuns to have themselves rubbed or massaged with substances approved for householders’ bathing.
Yet that nun Bhadrā now has herself rubbed and massaged by the other nuns.
Now the bhikṣuṇīs were complaining... [and so on] ...
until the Blessed One said:
Whatever nun, not being ill, should have herself rubbed or massaged by another nun, there is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
"Whatever nun" means one who is fully ordained.
"By another nun" means by one who is fully ordained.
"Non-ill" means: what, first of all, is intended here by "illness"? Is it one who is weak from old age, or weak from disease?
The Blessed One has withdrawn [the prohibition] for one who is ill, [stating]: "There is no offense for one who is ill.
[If she] causes herself to be massaged or rubbed, it is a *pācattika*—as far as the formal rule extends.

If this nun, though not ill, has herself rubbed with unguents by another nun but does not have herself massaged, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya. If she has herself massaged but does not have herself rubbed with unguents, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
If she does both, it is a *pācattika* offense.
If neither [of these] occurs, there is no offense.
If a monk who is not ill causes another monk to rub his body or massage him, it is a transgression of the Vinaya.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun who is not ill should have herself rubbed or massaged by another nun, it is an offense of expiation. || Phu ||
Pācattika-dharma 128:
It is exactly the same for a female novice; there is no difference.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun who is not ill should have a female novice rub her body or massage her, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika). || Phu ||
Pācattika-dharma 129: This very same [rule] applies to a *śikṣamāṇā*.
A *śikṣamāṇā* is one who trains for two years according to the eighteen rules. Regarding this, the Blessed One said:
"If a nun who is not ill causes a *śikṣamāṇā* to have her body rubbed with unguents or massaged, it is a *pācattika* offense. [End of section].
Pācattika-dharma 130:
This very [rule] applies to a female householder.
There is no difference.
"Gṛhiṇī" means a householder's wife;
therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun who is not ill should have herself rubbed or massaged by a householder woman, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika). || hrā ||
Pācattika-dharma 131:
Regarding living together in purity, [rule] 242. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now the bhikṣuṇīs had assembled for the poṣadha ceremony;
a bhikṣuṇī named Jetā was not coming.
She sent a messenger, saying:
"Noble lady, please come; the nuns have assembled for the formal act of the Poṣadha.
She then said:

The Blessed One has prescribed the purity-uposatha for those who are pure. Since I am one who is pure, yet I do not go to any of those [assemblies], the bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī... [and so on].
"Up to: 'Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
'It is a transgression for you, Jeta.'"
And yet you do not honor the *poṣadha*.
Who else will honor it? And what is the honoring of the *poṣadha*?
One who is not ill must go [to the assembly].
A formal consent (chanda) must be given by one who is ill;
indeed, the Blessed One has said that this should continue until they have become completely purified.
Furthermore, if a nun who is not ill does not attend the half-monthly meeting for the sake of communal purity, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained.
"Every half-month for the sake of pure association" means from the fourteenth day to the fourteenth day,
or from the fifteenth day to the fifteenth day.
"One who, not being ill, does not attend to the Poṣadha ceremony—
what now is intended here by 'being ill'? It means she is either weakened by old age, or weakened by disease, or has had a vein lanced, or is suffering, or has drunk medicine."
Or it may be that she has drunk ghee;
the *chanda* (consent) must be given.
This nun, though not ill, does not go to the *poṣadha*.
If one who is ill does not give their consent, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
If a monk who is not ill neither goes to the Poṣadha ceremony nor gives his consent, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun, being not ill, does not attend the half-monthly *viśuddhi-saṃvāsa* (ceremony of communal purity), it is a *pācattika*. Summary verse:
She approaches [1(123)].
Quarrel [3(124)]; freedom from sorrow [2(125)]; anointment [4(126)].
The bhikṣuṇī [5(127)]; the śrāmaṇerī [6(128)]; the śikṣamāṇā [7(129)].
[8(130)] By means of a householder’s wife;
[9(131)] by means of pure co-residence.
The thirteenth chapter is completed.
Pācattika-dharma 132:
Approaching for exhortation and the purification Poṣadha.
243. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī. The elder monks were exhorting the nuns in turn.
Now, those venerable ones of the group-of-six did not receive their turn to exhort.
They then said:
"These [elders] will not grant you the turn for instruction. To whom, then, shall we go for the turn of instruction?"
They then said:
"The Venerable Śāriputra is both stubborn and gentle.
[This was told] at length until the Blessed One had prescribed the training rule.
"It is not permissible for a monk who has not been formally authorized to exhort the nuns.
Let us go outside the boundary and authorize one another.
Then, having gone outside the boundary and authorized one another, they dressed and robed themselves at daybreak and went to the nuns' quarters, where they said:
"Sisters, assemble; there will be an exhortation.
Those who belonged to the group of six (ṣaḍ-vargiṇīyo) assembled, but those nuns who were practitioners of yoga (yogācārāyo) did not assemble.
They said,
"For what purpose shall we undergo instruction from these undisciplined ones?
Then, having spent a brief moment with them, they departed, breaking off like a flight of crows.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra, having dressed at the proper time and taken his bowl and robes, set out together with the Venerable Ānanda as his attendant monk, and so forth, until he said:
"Gather together, sisters; there will be an exhortation."
Those bhikṣuṇīs who were practitioners of yoga desired to assemble,
but the group of six bhikṣuṇīs did not come.
The elder asked:
"The community of bhikṣuṇīs is indeed complete.
They replied,
"No one is missing."
The group of six nuns said,
"A messenger has been sent to them: 'Come, sisters, there will be an exhortation.'"
Then they said:
"We will not come;
we have been exhorted by the noble group of six (ṣaḍ-vargika) with an improper exhortation."
Then the Venerable Śāriputra, thinking that the community of nuns was distracted, rose from his seat and departed.
The Blessed One, knowing full well, asked: "Gautamī’s mother, why have you returned so quickly?
Have the nuns been exhorted?"
He said:
"Blessed One, after I had dressed myself at the proper time, I entered the nuns' quarters to give them exhortation. I said, 'Assemble, sisters; there will be an exhortation.
Those nuns who were practitioners of yoga assembled as they were requested."
The group-of-six bhikṣuṇīs did not assemble. I said, "The bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha is unanimous.
They replied:
"No, who is not coming?
They replied, "The group of six."
A messenger was sent to them,
saying, "Come, sisters, there will be an exhortation.
They replied:
"We shall not come; we have already been exhorted by the noble ladies of the group of six with an exhortation different from that [proper] one.
"I too, Blessed One, thinking 'the community of nuns is busy,' rose from my seat and departed."
The Blessed One said,
"Summon the group of six bhikṣuṇīs.
They were then summoned.
The Blessed One questioned him about all of that in detail, [to which he replied],
"Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
This was a misdeed for you, O group of six, until [the rules] have been fully clarified.
Whatever nun does not honor the visiting of the community of monks for exhortation every half-month commits a *pācattika* offense.
"Whatever nun" refers to one who has received full ordination (*upasampannā*).
"Every half-month" means: from the fourteenth to the fourteenth, or from the fifteenth to the fifteenth.
If one does not show respect for approaching the community of monks for instruction, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika), as defined by the formal rule.

Now, if she is weak from old age, or weak from illness, or has consumed ghee, she should say: "I give my consent for the exhortation three times. If that nun, though not ill, does not go to the place of the exhortation, or if she is ill but does not give her consent, she incurs a *pācattika* offense.
When the Poṣadha day arrives, the female messengers of consent (chandahārikā) should go to the monks' monastery and say:
"The united Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha bows its head at the feet of the united Bhikṣu-saṃgha; it receives the Poṣadha and requests instruction. This should be requested three times.
If there is anyone who serves as the instructor of the nuns (bhikṣuṇī-ovādaka), he should be informed.
"Sisters, this instructor will arrive.
Now, if there is no one among you who is endowed with the requisite qualities, he should be formally appointed.
If there is no such person, it should be said."

"Sisters, there is no instructor of the bhikṣuṇīs; therefore, you should accomplish [your practice] with heedfulness, attend to the confession of offenses and the poṣadha ceremony, and be respectful toward the elder, middle-ranking, and junior bhikṣus.
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
If a nun, moreover, does not attend the half-monthly purification *poṣadha* ceremony, it is an offense of expiation (*pācattika*).
Pācattika-dharma 133:
Boils or Abscesses.
244. The Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha.
A boil arose in a private part of the nun Jetā.
While her female disciples had gone out for alms,
a physician of the Hiṇḍika caste arrived.
She then said,
"Long-lived one, can you perform surgery on me?
He then replied:
"Certainly. So he then cut it open, washed it, applied a bandage, and departed.
Those bhikṣuṇīs arrived.
Then they saw that place smeared with pus,
and they said:
"Noble lady, what is this?"
He said,
"Surgical treatment was performed.
They replied:
"A rash act has been committed by this noble lady, having had a surgical procedure performed in a cramped place.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī... [as before] ...up until: "Yes, Blessed One."

The Blessed One said: "In this way, you indeed cause the Saṅgha to perform surgical treatment upon yourself— above the kneecaps and below the armpits— without having first performed the preliminary ritual and without having consulted [the Saṅgha], whether it be for a boil, a carbuncle, a wound, or an injury."
Therefore, it is not permissible. [The usual formula applies] ... up to ...

Furthermore, if a nun, without having first performed the preliminary act and without having examined the Saṃgha, [treats] a boil, a carbuncle, a wound, or an injury above the knees and below the armpits, [she commits an offense].
If she causes a man to wash, or to rinse, or to soak [the robe], it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
"Again, a bhikṣuṇī" means one who has received full ordination.
"Above the two knee-circles" means above the thighs and the navel.
"Below the two armpits" means below the breasts and the abdomen.

Without having first performed the preliminary rites—whether for a boil, a carbuncle, a wound, or an injury—a nun intending to have surgical treatment (śastra-karma) performed must say: "I am going to have surgical treatment performed.
Without having sought permission from the Saṃgha, she must seek permission in the midst of the Saṃgha:
"May the noble Saṃgha hear me. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha permit that the nun named so-and-so undergoes surgical treatment."
The Noble Saṃgha shall cause the nun named so-and-so to have surgical treatment performed.
It is pleasing to the Saṃgha since there is silence; thus do I understand this.

"By a man" means by one who is either a householder or a renunciant; "should have it cut, or have it washed, or have it bandaged"—as in the case of the nun Jetā, it is a *pācattika* offense, up to the point of the formal rule (*prajñapti*).

Now, if in a confined place there should be a boil, a carbuncle, a wound, or an injury, it must be reported to one who has confidence—whether it be a female disciple, a fellow pupil under the same preceptor, or a fellow student under the same teacher. [One should report:
"I have been pierced by a thorn or by a fingernail."

It should be caused to be applied with medicine, or she should be made to smear it. Now, if there is a boil, a carbuncle, a wound, or an ulcer below the knees or above the armpits, and a man causes her to heat it, wash it, or apply a poultice; or likewise, if he causes a vein to be lanced—whether it be the vein on the forehead, the arm, or the ankle—it must be stepped upon by another nun.
Thus said the Blessed One.

If a nun, regarding a boil, a carbuncle, a wound, or an injury above the knees and below the armpits, should have it lanced, washed, or treated with an ointment by a man without having first performed the preliminary duties or without having obtained the permission of the Saṃgha, it is a *pācattika* offense.
Pācattika-dharma 134:
Regarding those who have entered the rains retreat.
245. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, a nun named Kālī, having entered the rains retreat, departed on a journey after securing a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī... [as before] ...up until: "Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, Kālī, that you set out on a journey while having entered the rains retreat.
Therefore, it is not permissible for one who has entered the rains retreat to set out on a journey."
Then indeed, the Blessed One [spoke] until they become completely purified:
"If a nun who has entered the rains retreat should go on a journey, it is a *pācattika* offense.
"If a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"Rainy season" means the rainy season night.
"Has entered" means she has entered either the earlier or the later period of the rains-retreat.
"Should set out on a journey" means she should go elsewhere, even to another village; this is an offense of expiation (*pācattika*), as far as the formal rule (*prajñapti*) extends.
If this nun stays apart for even one night, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).

Now, if there should be fear of a king, fear of an army, fear of a foreign invader, or if there should be a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (brahmacarya), she may go even if she does so; there is no offense.

There is no formal act of authorization (avalokanā-karma) for a nun, nor for seven days. However, if a monk, having performed the act of authorization, should remain empowered for seven days and then go, there is no offense.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun who has entered the rains retreat should set out on a journey, it is an offense of expiation. (3)
Pācattika-dharma 135:
Regarding those who have spent the rains retreat.
The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, the nuns who had spent the rainy season retreat at Śrāvastī arrived at Vaiśālī.
They entered the family circle of Bhadrā Kāpileyī’s relatives,
and those women said:
"Where did the noble ladies spend the rains retreat? They replied, "In Śrāvastī."
They asked:
"What is Śrāvastī like? They replied:
And such and such [trees], thus delightful with groves;
thus is the Jeta Grove.
Thus is the Fragrant Chamber;
thus does the Blessed One dwell;
thus do the noble ones Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
If this is true renunciation, then this noble daughter of ours— who was born right here and raised right here—
does not go anywhere at all; she remains like a frog in a well, never venturing forth.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
and so on until the Blessed One said:
"In that case, a bhikṣuṇī who has completed the rains retreat must set out on tour."
As far as the Blessed One said:
"If a nun who has completed the rains retreat does not set out on a journey, it is a *pācattika* offense.
Regarding the phrase "if a nun": this refers to one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).

"Having spent the rains" means: during the three months of the rainy season, one should not set out on a journey, even as far as to another village; [if one does so], it is a *pācattika* offense, according to the formal rule (*prajñapti*).
If that nun sets out even for a night, it is a *pācattika*.
Now, if she is weak from old age or weak from illness and is not capable of traveling, there is no offense even if she goes.
If a monk who has completed the rains residence does not set out on a journey, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun who has completed the rains residence does not set out on a journey, it is a *pācattika* offense. [Nka]
Pācattika-dharma 136:
Udvaheya 247. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
The nun Jetā was prevented from going to Rājagṛha by the nun Sthūlanandā, who said, "The noble lady must observe the rains retreat here. She [Sthūlanandā] had praised her among the families,
saying, "The noble lady Jetā is excellent, virtuous, devoted, and well-restrained."

“Exert yourselves in her service. Now she approaches families with a pleasing demeanor—whether in advancing or retreating, looking ahead or looking aside, contracting or extending her limbs, or in carrying her outer robe, bowl, and inner robes; she is self-restrained, not arrogant, not fickle, not talkative, and does not speak incoherently.
Because she is so pleasing, gods and humans are inspired with faith.
They performed services for her; they greeted her, rose up for her, and invited her [to accept] alms-bowls, robes, and medicinal requisites for the sick.

The nun Sthūlanandā was not perfected in proper appearance nor perfected in deportment; she wore robes that were soiled and filthy, torn and tattered, while her breasts were large, pendulous, and hanging down like those of a cow.
With her buttocks grown large, she was arrogant, haughty, fickle, talkative, and loose-lipped;
they showed her no respect nor invited her [to meals].
Now, she bore a grudge against them in both body and speech.

The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. ... [The Buddha] said: "Call Nandā. She was then summoned, and she was questioned about all of that, to which she replied, "Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "It is a transgression for you, Nanda," and so forth.
"If a nun, having spoken thus to another nun—saying, 'Noble lady, you must dwell here for the rains'—should afterwards herself move away or cause her to move away, it is a *pācattika* offense.
"If a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).

If she says to a nun, "Noble lady, you must dwell here for the rains," and having spoken thus for three months and having restrained her, she subsequently causes her to move away— either by herself moving her through body or speech,
or by causing another to move her through body or speech— it is a *pācattika*. This is as far as the formal rule extends.

It is not permissible to marry her after having previously rejected her; however, if she becomes lax, or indulgent, or unwilling to train, or quarrelsome, and one perceives that if she remains here she will cause a schism in the community,
then even if one marries her, there is no offense.
If this nun takes up with another nun, it is a *pācattika*.

If she takes up with a *śrāmaṇerī* or a *śikṣamāṇā*, it is a transgression of the Vinaya. At the very least, if she takes up even with a housewife, she incurs a transgression of the Vinaya regarding one who is proceeding toward restraint.
If a nun, having spoken thus, saying, "Noble lady, one must dwell here for the rains," should afterwards move away herself or cause another to move away, it is a *pācattika* offense. (3)
Pācattika-dharma 137:
Regarding one who has already arrived [first].
248. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now there was a nun named Kālī.
She approached [the assembly],
but those [nuns] had gone to another village for the rainy season retreat.
She arrived when the bhikṣuṇīs had already assembled;
there, the bhikṣuṇīs had already assigned the dwellings and assigned the lodgings. She then said:
"Noble lady, please give me a dwelling.
She did not obtain a dwelling. They said:
"Where has the noble lady Varṣopanāyikā gone?
She was quarreling.
Now, there was another nun who was a practitioner of yoga (yogācārā).
She said, "Noble lady, this is my dwelling. Bring your bed into it; we shall live together."
She caused a cot to be brought in there; it was a wooden frame where she inserted the branches. Then she said:
"Noble lady, do not cause trouble in the monastery. She then said, "Bhadrāyaṇī, was the monastery built by you? Was it sold by you?"
"Why does she not enter the monastery belonging to the Saṅgha?
She [acted] both with her body and with her speech.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
"Call Kālī. She was then summoned.
All of this was questioned of her, to which she replied, "Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, Kālī.

Whatever nun, knowing that another nun has already arrived, should subsequently come and either herself drive her out or cause her to be driven out, whether by body or by speech, it is a *pācattika* offense."
"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"Knowing" means she should know it herself or hear it from another.
"A nun who has already entered [the rains retreat]" means one who has entered during the earlier period of the rains-retreat (*purimikā varṣopanāyikā*).
"Having come afterwards" means in the western [direction]. "Or she should carry it up" means either by herself or by having someone else carry it.
"Or" means: if she [acts] toward another with body or speech, it is a *pācattika* offense, up to the point of the formal rule (*prajñapti*).
If she supports a nun, it is a *pācattika*.
If she supports a female novice (*śrāmaṇerī*) or a trainee (*śikṣamāṇā*), she incurs an offense of transgression of the discipline that requires confession (*deśanā-gāmi-vinayātikrama*).
At the very least, even if one marries a householder woman, it is a transgression of the discipline regarding the observance of restraint.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"If a nun, knowing that another nun has already arrived first, should afterwards come and marry her, or cause her to be married, whether by body or by speech, it is a *pācattika* offense. || Phu ||
Pācattika-dharma 138:
Vighasaṃ 249. The Blessed One was dwelling in Kāśī.
Now, another nun, without first inspecting her chamber-pot, threw it onto the street.
At that moment, another brahmin, having bathed his head and wearing fresh, clean garments, was passing along that street.
The chamber-pot fell upon his head;
his head and his clothes were ruined.
And the people mocked him, saying, "O Brahmin, you are well-bathed and well-anointed!"
Then he reviled her, saying:
"O daughter of a slave-girl, O female ascetic! Do you not see that my head and my clothes have been defiled by excrement?"
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. [Pe] ... "Is it so, Blessed One? "It is so, Blessed One," they replied.
The Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you that you discard [something] without first examining it. Therefore, it is not permissible to discard anything without having examined it.
Furthermore, the Blessed One [taught] until they become completely purified."
Whatever nun, without first looking, should discard excrement, urine, spittle, snot, food scraps, or refuse over a wall, it is a *pācattika*.
"Whatever nun" refers to one who has received full ordination (*upasampannā*).
"Through a wall" means through a fence; "excrement," "urine," "spittle," "nasal mucus," "food scraps," "refuse," "laundry water," "dishwater," or "hair" or "nails.
"Without having inspected" means without having looked.
"Choreyā" means "one should discard.
It is an offense of expiation (*pācattika*) up to the point of the formal rule (*prajñapti*).
If one wishes to discard anything, it must be inspected first.
If the streets are crowded with many people and passersby, one should wait until they have cleared away.
But if they are not crowded, even if one discards it, there is no offense.
Nevertheless, it is not permitted to discard it without making a sound; rather, one must snap one's fingers or clear one's throat.
If that nun neither examines [the area] nor discards it after snapping her fingers, she incurs a *pācattika* offense.
If a monk also discards it without examining it and without snapping his fingers, he incurs an offense of transgression against the discipline (*vinayātikrama*).
Therefore, the Blessed One said:
If a nun should, without first looking, throw away excrement, urine, spittle, snot, food scraps, or refuse over a wall, it is a *pācattika* offense. [End of Chapter] on Throwing Over a Wall.
Pācattika-dharma 139 and 140: [digging] in green grass or water.
250. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now, King Prasenajit of Kosala had a park named Pūrvakoṣṭhaka, which was well-provided with lotus ponds;
it was open to the monks and nuns, but closed to other people.
Then the king said to the park-keeper: "Ho there, my good park-keeper! Have the eastern enclosure of the garden sprinkled and swept;
tomorrow I shall go out together with the ladies of the harem."

Now the group of six heard that tomorrow the king, together with his harem, would go out to the park grounds. Having gone there beforehand, they ruined the place covered with green grass by defiling it with their own spittle and mucus, and [they disposed of] their excrement upon lotus leaves.
Having tied them in bundles, they set them adrift in the lotus pond.

Now, having spent the day there breaking up the flocks of crows, they entered the city at the time of evening. King Prasenajit of Kośala had gone out from the city on that very day accompanied by his harem;
those women of the harem, somehow or other released from their confinement, were wandering about as if they felt themselves liberated from the cauldron.
Some were seated, some were lying down;
some ran here and there, seeking an opening, and wandered about upon the grassy carpet.
Now, their clothes had been ruined by that cooked phlegm and cooked snot.
They descended into a lotus pond to bathe,
and there they saw the lumps floating on the surface.
The sons of good family had heard that tomorrow the king, together with his harem, would enter the park; thinking, "These packets of perfume have been sent by them," they took them.
However, they were soaked with water and nibbled at by excrement, for the lotus leaf is naturally delicate.
As soon as it was taken, it melted away.
"Alas! Alas! they cried, and having approached the king, they said, "Great King, such is his condition. The king said, "Summon the monastery attendant."
He was then summoned.
The king said, "Ho there, my man! Monk-attendant, by whom has the park been laid waste?"
The six groups of female ascetics went away after breaking their wooden staffs all day long.
The king laughed and said:
This shall be the offense for those who are undisciplined.
The nuns reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, and Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī in turn reported it to the Blessed One. ... up to [the point where the Blessed One said:]
If a nun should void excrement, urine, spittle, or nasal mucus upon green grass, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
If a nun should void excrement, urine, spittle, or nasal mucus in water, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika).
"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained.
"Excrement" means feces. "Urine" means urine.
"Phlegm" (kheṭa) means mucus. "Snot" (siṃghāṇaka) means dried snot. "On green grass" (harite tṛṇe) means on a verdant lawn that has not been cut or mown. "Water" (uda) refers to ten kinds of water.

If one should void excrement or urine in a river, a pond, a well, a pit, a stream, rainwater collected on the ground, water drawn from a source, water from the sky, melted snow, or the sea, it is a *pācattika* offense, as prescribed. Now, during the rainy season, when the entire ground is covered with a carpet of green grass, one should do so only in a place where there is very little vegetation.

Now, if there is no green vegetation available— neither in a basin, nor on a brick, nor on a stone, nor on dry grass, nor on a piece of wood, nor where excrement has been deposited by another, such as by an ox,
nor where it has been deposited by another person— one should defecate there. If, however, even this is not possible, one must at least prick one's smallest finger and defecate upon it.
One should act in such a way that it falls first upon that [spot].
Now, when walking in meditation, it is not permitted to discharge phlegm onto green grass;
rather, one must discharge it onto a mat or into a leaf-cup.
Therefore the Blessed One said:

"If a nun should void excrement, urine, spittle, or snot upon green grass, it is an offense of expiation (pācattika). Furthermore, if a nun should void excrement, urine, spittle, or snot into water, it is an offense of expiation."
Pācattika-dharma 141:
Group-gain 251. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Then the group of six nuns went to ask for consent.
They said, "Prajāpatī, give us your consent; we shall provide a meal for the noble ladies."
Then those women gave [their consent]. They said, "Noble lady, on the day you provide a meal for the Saṅgha, please inform us as well;
we too will come as servers."
They then invited the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Revata, Kapphiṇa, Śroṇa-koṭīviṃśa, Upavāna, the venerable Rāhula, and the group of six monks. They then prepared two seats.
One [portion] was for the elders, the other for the group-of-six monks.
Then, at the very time of the meal, the monks entered after having dressed and put on their robes.
Thereupon, for the Venerable Śāriputra, there was to be given rice-gruel with rice, a soup of mung beans, ghee, and curd.
For the venerable Maudgalyāyana there was barley-gruel, bean soup, and oil; for others there was sixty-day rice with soup;
and for others there was kodrava-grain gruel.
To some the condiments were given, but the rice was not given;
to others the vegetables were given, but the rice was not given; to others the rice from the field was given, but the condiments were not given.
When those women took some greens and various kinds of food and drink for the venerable Rāhula and went there, they asked:
"Where are those noble ladies?"

Now, having concealed the elder monks, they showed the group-of-six monks [to the donors]. Consequently, rice-gruel was given to them—rice, bean soup, ghee, fresh butter, water, sweet things, jaggery, curd, white curd, and milk; whatever was required, as much as was required, was given.
Whatever food, whether hard or soft, drink, or warm refreshment was considered choice, they caused it to be given to the group of six monks.
These venerable monks, having finished their meal and being fully satiated, rose repeatedly and approached to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One.
Knowing [the situation] already, the Blessed One asked:
"Moreover, Śāriputra, [it was] in the month of Śobhana, whether it was pure, or excellent, or abundant.
The Elder said:
"O Blessed One, the function of food has been fulfilled by means of this meal."
A second time, and a third time,
the Blessed One spoke;
the Elder spoke.

"Lord, we have obtained rice from śāli paddy, soup of mung beans, fresh butter, water, sweet side dishes, jaggery, curd, and milk; and for whatever purpose these are required, they are given as much as needed, all for the sake of the sisters who are full of faith and confidence. What is this, [is it] for the acceptance of those sisters? The Blessed One said: [The Blessed One said: "Monks, that is not a gift of faith, nor is it a gift of confidence. Monks, that is a gift of fear, a gift of servitude, a gift of slavery, a gift of subjection, a gift of dependence, a gift of being under the power of others. Monks, one should not accept such a gift. Whoever should accept it, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, I allow you to accept a gift of faith, a gift of confidence. Monks, that is a gift of love, a gift of affection, a gift of respect, a gift of reverence, a gift of honor, a gift of esteem, a gift of devotion. Monks, one should accept such a gift. Whoever should accept it, there is no offense. Then the venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage at his feet, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: "Lord, what is the distinction, what is the difference between a gift of faith and a gift of confidence? The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, a gift of faith is when one gives with a mind of pure faith, thinking: 'This person is virtuous, of good character, and worthy of offerings; may my gift be well-placed. A gift of confidence is when one gives with a mind of pure faith, thinking: 'This person is virtuous, of good character, and worthy of offerings; may my gift be well-placed, and may I too in the future become like this, virtuous, of good character, and worthy of offerings. This, Ānanda, is the distinction, this is the difference between a gift of faith and a gift of confidence."
Who was the elder of the Saṅgha there? The Venerable Śāriputra.
The Blessed One said:
“Śāriputra, he spoke the truth. “Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
“Śāriputra, you have misused [the gift]; for you thus remain indifferent while the community of monks is being harassed.
For one whom the Blessed One declares to have ‘misused’ [the gift], that [gift] might remain for an eon or the remainder of an eon, and would never undergo decay.
Having been given the “crow’s mouth” by the Elder, he vomited everything up with a retching sound.
The Blessed One said:
"Call the nuns. They were called, and they were questioned on this very matter.
They replied, “Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, “It is a transgression for you, O bhikṣuṇīs, that knowing this to be so, you divert a group’s gain to another group.”
Therefore, it is not permissible.
Now, indeed, [the rule shall remain] until they have become completely purified.
Furthermore, if a nun, knowing that a gain intended for a group has been dedicated to a group, should divert it to another group, it is a *pācattika* offense.
"Again, a nun" means one who is fully ordained (*upasampannā*).
"Knowing" means she should know it herself or hear it from another.
"The gain of a group" refers to the group of monks (*bhikṣu-gaṇa*) and the group of nuns (*bhikṣuṇī-gaṇa*).

"Gain" refers to the eight kinds of gain, ranging from what is received at the proper time to what is received at the improper time, and from what is allowable to what is unallowable. "Dedicated" means fully accomplished. If one should dedicate it to a group, it is a *pācattika* offense; such is the formal rule.
Now, suppose someone comes wishing to give a gift.
He said:
"Noble lady, if one wishes, it should be accepted as being accepted.
The Prātideśanika Dharmas 1–8.

252. Clarified butter, oil, and so forth. Now those monks of the group-of-six (ṣaḍvargika), having requested clarified butter from ghee-sellers, oil from oil-sellers, molasses from molasses-sellers, honey from honey-sellers, fish from fishers, meat from meat-sellers, milk from milk-sellers, and curds from curd-sellers, ate them.
Now people were complaining:
"Look, sirs! The ascetic Gautama praises fewness of desires in many ways, yet he has laid down a rule of training [that contradicts it].
Therefore, Gautamī, the bhikṣuṇīs must train in this very matter."
This is the origin of the matter:
At one time, Gautamī, the Tathāgata was staying among the Śākyas. Then the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
"Call together the bhikṣuṇīs, Gautamī, until they have all become purified.
Whatever bhikṣuṇī, not being ill, for her own sake requests ghee from families, or causes it to be requested, and then eats or consumes it, that bhikṣuṇī must confess it:
'Venerable ladies, this which was not to be done, a *prātideśanika* offense, I have fallen into; I confess that offense.'"
This is an offense requiring confession (*prātideśanika*):
likewise with ghee [1],
and molasses [4].
Milk [5], fish [7], and meat [8].
Furthermore, "a nun" refers to one who has received full ordination.
"For one's own sake" means having directed [the thought] toward oneself, having focused one's attention upon oneself.
"Not being ill" is a term specifically excluded by the Blessed One; there is no offense for one who is ill. What, then, is intended here by "illness"?
Whether weakened by old age, weakened by disease, having drunk a purgative, or having had a vein bled; whether due to phlegm or a derangement of the humors (*sannipāta*);
"in families" means in Kṣatriya families, Brāhmaṇa families, or whatever other families there may be;
"ghee" refers to ghee from cows, buffaloes, goats, sheep, or camels.
"Having requested" means having requested it oneself.
"Having caused to be requested" means having caused another to request it. "Should eat" refers to that which is solid food (*khādanīya*).
"Solid food" means whatever constitutes solid food.
That nun must confess it; this is a *prātideśanika* (to-be-confessed) offense.
Now, if there is a disturbance of bile, she is permitted to request ghee, and so forth.
Now, while wandering for alms-food, if he sees ghee being sold, he must not say:
"May long-lived one obtain gain; may it be abundant;
and once obtained, may it remain stable."
Then he said:
"What is needed for the Noble Lady? [She] replied: "I am going on alms-round."
Then he said:
"If the noble lady has need of ghee,
she should say, 'I have need [of it].'"

If he receives even a full bowl, there is no offense. Now, if there is yet another [person] present, it is permissible for him to say, with reference to those already there, "Give this one some as well."
This is regarding oil.
If there is a disorder of wind (*vāta-vikāra*), one may request oil; however, in that case, he must not request it from oil-pressers.
Now, if while wandering for alms he sees oil being measured out, he may take even a full bowl; there is no offense.
As long as it is possible to say, by means of present application, "Give me this too," so it is with honey. If there is a disorder of phlegm, it is permissible to request honey;
however, it is not now allowable to request it from honey-killers.
The same applies to molasses.
If she is ill and the physician says, "Noble lady, make use of jaggery," it is permissible to request jaggery.
The same applies to milk.
It is permissible to drink milk.
Now, when one is walking for alms and sees cows being milked in the houses, one should not say:
"May there be great gain; may the cows graze in safety."
They said:
"By what means is there need for the noble lady?
It should be told."
"I am going for alms.
They said:
"If a noble lady requests a bowl even when it is already full of milk, there is no offense, provided that one may say 'give this to her' based on a present application [of the mind]."
Now, he wishes to learn the Śvetamaya [text],
but there is no Śvetamaya;
do you desire milk?
He said: "I wish for it.
Even if he receives a full bowl, there is no offense.
Now, if one has a nasal catarrh,

and the physician says, "Perform the function of curd," it is permissible to request curd. Furthermore, if while wandering for alms one sees curd being poured out, it is permissible to request the whey.
Then he said:
"There is no whey; do you want curd? He replied: "I want it."
If she accepts even a full bowl, there is no offense. Now, if a nun wishes to perform emesis or purgation, and a physician says, "Noble lady, drink plenty of fish broth," [she may accept it].
As long as it is not permissible to request [food] from fishermen,
then while wandering for alms, it is permissible to request sour gruel (*āmbūkāñjika*).
Now, if there is a bloodletting to be performed...
She became a purgative-drinker.
The physician said,
"Noble lady, consume meat broth."
It is permissible to request meat broth;
however, it is not allowable for those who raise poultry.

If one who is ill requests [food] and one who is not ill eats it, there is an offense of transgressing the Vinaya. If one who is not ill requests [food] and one who is ill eats it, there is no offense. If one who is not ill requests [food] and one who is not ill eats it, it must be confessed.

[The same applies if] what is prepared as wholesome is prepared as unwholesome, or what is prepared as unwholesome is prepared as wholesome.

There is no offense when one's livelihood depends upon others.

Honey, molasses, milk, curd, fish, and meat; furthermore,

Bhikṣuṇī Prakīrṇaka 1: Concerning Sitting (Niṣadyā). 255. This is the beginning of the Bhikṣuṇī Prakīrṇaka of the Noble Mahāsāṃghika Lokottaravādins.
The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Now, those bhikṣuṇīs were sitting for their evening meditation in the svastika-paryaṅka posture.
Then, a long worm entered through the opening of a wound in another bhikṣuṇī, following the direction of the hair.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī reported it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Go and give her such-and-such medicine; then that *dīrghaka* will come out.
She then gave him that medicine for him to drink.
That *dīrghaka* came back with the current, yet he did not die.
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, you sit in the auspicious cross-legged posture (svastika-paryaṅka).
Therefore, it is not permissible to sit in the auspicious cross-legged posture."
Concerning the practice of sitting:
it is not permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to sit in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka).
Rather, she should bind her legs in the half-lotus posture with only one foot [crossed over].
The wound-mouth must be covered with another heel-cloth.
If that nun sits in the svastika-paryanka posture, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya. This is called that which is connected to sitting.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 2, connected with the kaṭhina: 256. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now those nuns, having placed their robes on the *kaṭhina*, were sewing them.
Another nun caused blood to flow from a wound made by a bamboo splinter.
This is the case.

Then, indeed, having spread out mats in the assembly hall, or in a palace, or in the meditation hall, one should sew after having laid out the robe-cloth.
If even that is not possible,
one should sew after having laid it out upon a bench or a couch.
If even this does not suffice, she should sew it after placing it upon her knees.
If that nun sits on a wooden board (*kaṭhina*), she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
This is called the section connected with the wooden board. ||2||
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 3: Concerning the Veṭhaka. 257. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

Now the nun Sthūlanandā, having gone with many women to the Ajiravatī River, set aside her robes in a secluded spot and entered the water to bathe. Having emerged first, she wrapped her body in a turban and said to the women,

"Do I look beautiful or not?
They then said,

"We do this for the sake of honor, so that we may be enjoyed for our desires and become most beloved to our householders. "Noble one (or noble lady), what is the use of that?"
What had been spoken by those women was now heard by the bhikṣuṇīs.
This is the case. ... [as before] ... "Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "It is a transgression for you, Nanda. [He continued] up to: "Therefore, it is not permissible to wrap the body with a turban. [This concerns] the turban."
If this nun wraps her body with a turban or a cloth band, she commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Now, if she wraps her body with a strip of cloth or iron,
it is not permitted to wrap it even twice or even thrice.
Now, it should indeed be wrapped with a single fold.
Furthermore, if one's side is seized by wind,
or if there is a boil, a carbuncle, a wound, or an injury, even if one wraps the body with a cloth bandage, there is no offense.
This is called that which is connected with the binding. ||3||
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 4: Concerning the hip-ornament, 258. The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī.
Just as with Veṭhaka, so too should the origin of the matter be understood.

These are what are called "hip-ornaments":

whether they be spiral-shaped, or *śirikā*, or *pīluka*, or coral, or *akṣarakṣā*, or made of gold or silver, or made of jewels, or *prakālakā*, or at the very least a string-bead (*sūtra-maṇika*); if she fastens them and thereby seeks to dispel her desire for hip-ornaments, she commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
This is called that which relates to the hip-cushion. (Ṇka)
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 5:

This is the origin of the matter: [it occurred] until a nun, having tied on household ornaments, [was rebuked], whereupon the Blessed One said:

Or head-coverings;

Or patches,

Or necklaces,

Or conch shells, or anklets, or finger-rings.
Furthermore, whatever else may be householders' belongings, none of it is permitted. If that nun fastens on householders' ornaments, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
However, if she fastens on medicinal items or a fever-thread, there is no offense.
This is called that which is connected with the household utensils. (Section 3)
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 6:
Concerning the Adornment of a Householder’s Wife 260. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now those Śākyan maidens, Koliyan maidens, and Malla maidens who had gone forth from great families were taking their ornaments with them;

People then began to murmur in disapproval.
"This is not the life of renunciation; this is trade.
This is the context.
[The rest] as before, up until the Blessed One said:
Therefore, it is not permitted to wear the ornaments of a householder.
If a certain householder woman goes forth into homelessness and possesses any ornaments, she should be told: "Discard them.

Now, if she perceives that there might be a famine, or that alms-food might not be obtained, or that she will become weak from old age, or weak from illness, or that some sickness will arise, or that gains will be few—[then she may keep them].
"Lest women be hindered," [it is said];
having had their hair clipped, they are to be ordained.
If that nun ordains someone without having them relinquish ornaments, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
This same rule applies to a monk as well.
This is called that which pertains to the ornaments of a householder. Phu.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 7:
Concerning a Prostitute 261. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, those bhikṣuṇīs—daughters of the Śākyas, daughters of the Koliyas, and daughters of the Mallas who had gone forth from great families—were going forth while taking their maidservants with them.

"This is not the life of renunciation; these are courtesans.

Therefore, it is not permissible [to attend upon] a courtesan."
To maintain [her].

This is called the section concerning prostitutes. [End of] Chapter.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 8: Concerning the Female Attendant. 262. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now the Blessed One has laid down a rule of training:
"It is not permissible to ordain a courtesan.
Now those daughters of the Śākyas, daughters of the Mallas, and daughters of the Kolitas were going forth from great families.
Now they were taking on female monastery attendants for their own private use.
These female attendants were so beautiful that people began to complain:
"This is not the life of a renunciant; this is a courtesan!"
The nuns heard this matter... [as before] ... "Yes, Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
"In that case, it is not permissible to maintain a park-keeper as one's own personal attendant."
It is not permitted for a female monastery attendant; it is not permitted for a female servant;
it is not permitted for a ritual specialist.
That nun who causes a private female attendant of the monastery to be appointed incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
This is called the section concerning the female attendant of the monastery. Hraḥ.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 9: Concerning the Saṃkakṣikā. 263. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now there was another nun who was graceful and beautiful to behold. As she walked with full breasts, her robe was lifted up. She was then mocked by the people.
The nuns heard this matter... [as before] ... "Is it so, Blessed One? "It is so."

The Blessed One said: "Therefore, one must make what is called a *saṃkakṣikā*. When putting on the *saṃkakṣikā*, it should be worn in such a way that the breasts are covered. If a bhikṣuṇī does not provide herself with a *saṃkakṣikā*, she commits an offense of transgressing the discipline (*vinayātikrama*)."
If one does not wear it when it is available, there is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya; this is called that which pertains to the *saṃkakṣikā*. || 0 ||
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 10:

Now, an origin for the rule concerning Bhadrā Kāpileyyā must be established. Thereupon the Blessed One said:

One should bathe using a bathing cloth.
Regarding the matter of the bathing cloth:
it is not permissible to bathe naked in a river, a torrent, a lotus pond, or a lake.
One should bathe with a bathing cloth.
If one bathes naked, it is a transgression of the Vinaya.

Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 11: Concerning the Striking with the Palm. 265. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 12:

A "lacquered dildo" (*jatu-maṭṭhaka*) means: having fashioned a phallic image out of lac, iron, tin, lead, brass, ivory, cotton, or clay, one inserts it into one's own organ and thereby dispels lustful passion; she incurs a grave offense (*thullaccaya*). Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 13 and 14:

267. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

The Blessed One said:
"It is permissible [to wash] that which is connected with washing and that which is connected with entering.
When a bhikṣuṇī is washing, she should wash after inserting a single finger-cord."

It is not permissible to cause [the robe] to enter [the mouth] too far. If one causes it to enter too far and thereby dispels lustful desire, one incurs a *thūl'-accaya* offense. This is called that which is connected with washing and connected with causing to enter. ṇka ||

Now, as those bhikṣuṇīs reached their season month after month, their blood stained the bedding and seats. Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Venerable Sir, is it permissible to wear an *ānīcola* for the purpose of protecting one's bedding and seating?

When her season arrives and blood flows, she should wear a menstrual pad made of strips of cloth. It is not permissible to insert it too deeply, nor is it permissible to insert it too far, so that she might thereby dispel sensual desire.
Now, it should indeed be inserted into the opening of the wound when it is relaxed.
If that nun inserts it too far or inserts it too deeply such that she experiences sensual passion because of it, she incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
This is called the section concerning the *ānīcolaka*. 3.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 16:
Concerning the bathing place for women, 269. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

This is the case;

Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 17:

270. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

"In the same way, it should be done at a washerman's bathing place.
The Blessed One said:

Those pads should be dried when the season has not yet returned, and then they should be given back again.

Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 19:
Concerning the Stream of Water 272. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

Bhikṣuṇī-parikīrṇaka 20:
Connected with the Flow of Water, 273. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 21:
Concerning Deformity 274. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 22:
