275. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, a formal act of suspension (*utkṣepanīya-karman*) was being performed against another monk.
There was no one there skilled in performing such acts;
therefore, the act was performed by a nun.
Now she felt remorse, thinking:
"Is it indeed permissible to do this, or is it not permissible?
Because of her remorse, she informed the nuns.
The nuns reported this to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
and so on until the Blessed One said:
"This is the foremost assembly."
It is not permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to perform a formal act (*karma*) for a bhikṣu.
It is not permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to perform a formal act connected with a formal act for a bhikṣu.
However, if there is currently no one who is thoroughly skilled in performing formal acts, it is allowable for a bhikṣuṇī to instruct a bhikṣu.
Now, if one performing the ritual action forgets it, it is permissible for a nun to provide assistance.
If that nun performs a ritual action for a monk, there is a transgression of the Vinaya.
However, even if a monk performs a ritual action for a nun, there is no offense.
This is called that which is connected with action.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 23:
Concerning Silk.
276. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.

Now Bhadrā Kāpileyī, dressed in a silken robe, was going to her kinsmen’s home when a heavy rain fell. The silken robe became soaked; clinging to her body, her body appeared like polished crystal. A crowd of people gathered, desiring to see Bhadrā’s slender form.
She then sat down in a crouching posture, surrounded by her female disciples.
This was the background of the matter.
Up to the point where [the monk] replied, "Yes, Blessed One," the Blessed One said:
Therefore, it is not permissible to [use] silk.
That which pertains to silk:
"silk" refers to both that which is natural and that which is artificial.

If that nun wears one made of natural [silk], she commits an offense of transgression of the Vinaya requiring confession (*deśanā-gāmī-vinayātikrama*). If she wears one made of artificial [silk], she commits an offense of transgression of the Vinaya requiring restraint (*samvara-gāmī-vinayātikrama*). Even if a monk wears both, there is no offense.
This is called that which is connected with silk. ||3||
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 24:
Concerning the covering of a tumor.
277. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
A nun named Sthūlanandā was walking back and forth on the open terrace of the monastery wearing only a single *saṃkakṣikā*.
As she walked, her large breasts bounced up and down.
People mocked her, saying, "Look, sirs! This female ascetic is crossing the river as if with a gourd-bowl!
The nuns heard this matter... [and so forth].
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, one should make what is called a 'boil-covering' (gaṇḍa-praticchādana). It is connected with the boil-covering."

It should be drawn down over the *saṃkakṣikā* so that the swellings are covered. If that nun does not wear the garment for covering swellings (*gaṇḍa-praticchādana-paṭa*), she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya. Now, it is no longer permissible for her to remain in an open place wearing only a single *saṃkakṣikā*.
Now, it is not permissible to walk in a public place wearing only a single *saṃkakṣikā*.
However, if one walks in a secluded part of the monastery while wearing a single *saṃkakṣikā*, there is no offense.
This is called that which is connected with the concealment of a tumor (*gaṇḍa-praticchādana*).
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 25:
Concerning Female Ornaments 278. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now those Śākya maidens who had gone forth from great families were capable of adorning themselves with supernormal powers.
Whenever young girls were being married off, or new brides were being brought home, they would adorn them; they were led from house to house while thus adorned.
They receive food and drink in order to adorn themselves, and by means of that they provide their livelihood.
Now people are complaining:
"This is not the true life of renunciation; these women are merely decorators."
The nuns heard this matter... [as before] ...until the Blessed One said:
"In that case, it is not permissible to adorn oneself."
[This refers to] that which is connected with the ornaments of women.

If this nun adorns her head, or applies collyrium to her eyes, or powders her face with face-powder, and makes her livelihood by means of that, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Now, if there is pain in the eyes or a headache...
Or one may obtain *ardhāvabhedaka* [ointment] to apply to the eyes or to cleanse the head.
This is called that which is connected with the adornment of women. 3.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 26:
Concerning the Lotus-Sower, 279. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, those Śākya maidens, Koliyan maidens, and Malla maidens who had gone forth from great families were planting and selling blue lotuses,
and they made their livelihood by that means.
People then began to complain.
"This is not the life of renunciation; this is a lotus pond.
[The full] context, including the *peyāla*, continues until the Blessed One said:
Therefore, it is not permissible to sow blue lotuses, nor anything connected with the sowing of blue lotuses.
If a nun sows them and sells them, and makes her livelihood thereby, she incurs an offense of transgressing the Vinaya.
However, if she sows them for the sake of a *caitya* or sows them for the purpose of making an offering to the Blessed One, there is no offense.
This is called the account concerning the lotus-planters.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 27: Concerning the planting of *sumanā* flowers. 280. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
In this very way, the sowing of *sumanā* flowers should be performed; this concludes what is called the section connected with the sowing of *sumanā* flowers.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 28:
Connected with the Utpala-granthikā, 281. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now the Blessed One has laid down a precept:
"It is not permissible to cultivate *sumana* flowers.
Thereupon, those Śākyan girls, Koliyan girls, Malla girls, and Licchavi girls, having strung together blue lotuses (*utpala*), were selling them.
Now people were complaining:
"This is not true renunciation; this is merely a performance.
The monks heard this matter from the nuns.
[The usual formula] ... up to: "Yes, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
Therefore, it is not permissible to string together blue lotuses.
This concerns the stringing of blue lotuses:
that nun, having made garlands of blue lotuses, or garlands of jasmine, or garlands of *āraṅgaṇa* flowers, sells them.

And if they make their livelihood by means of that, it is a transgression of the Vinaya. Now, if there is an offering of garlands, or a festival for the birth [of the Buddha], or a festival for the Enlightenment, or a festival for the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma, or a festival for Ānanda, or a festival for Rāhula, or a five-year festival, or a great five-year festival.
Now people said: "The noble ladies should adorn themselves. Even if a nun weaves a garland of blue lotuses, or a garland of jasmine, or a garland of *āraṅgaṇa* flowers, there is no offense.
This is called the section connected with the lotus-knot. Hraḥ.
Bhikṣuṇī Prakīrṇaka 29:
Concerning the *sumanā* flower garland-maker.
In the same manner, having fashioned various types of *sumanā* flower garlands—whether as knotted strings, wound strands, wreaths, or flower-baskets—and sells them.
If one makes a livelihood by means of that, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
This is called the section concerning the *sumanā* flower and the knot.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 30: Concerning Spinning. 282. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now those nuns—daughters of the Śākyas and others who had gone forth from great families—being conceited, were weaving thread and selling it.
People then complained:
"This is not the life of one who has gone forth; this is merely a cotton-carder."
The nuns heard this matter... [as before] ...until the Blessed One said:

Therefore, it is not permissible to engage in weaving. If a nun weaves wool, cotton, linen, silk, hemp, flax, or any other material, and then sells it, making her livelihood thereby, she commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
She obtains it.
Now, if a nun’s robe is worn out or exhausted, it is permissible for her [to obtain another].
(Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 31)
"I am one who has violated proper conduct (ācāra-vikopanā). I have been made to fall away from the holy life (brahmacarya).
She said.
"By whom? She said,
"My brother-in-law makes me drink it."
He, wishing to lead me away, said:
"Mother, sit down; go."
"We shall protect you. She then said, "I will go to the presence of the Noble Lady; the Noble Lady will protect me.

Then she had her anklets fastened, her earrings put on, and her bracelets slipped onto her arms. Adorned and dressed in protective garments dyed with red ochre, she was veiled and surrounded by four or five female attendants.
Then that man stood at the door and watched her,
thinking, "When she goes out, I shall seize her. He saw her as she was departing.
The thought occurred to him: "This woman deserves to be the wife of a householder;
she is not that nun. Then, when that nun went to her dwelling, she was seen by the other nuns.
They said,
"Noble lady, this Sudinnā has run back toward us.
She said:
"I did not run out against him; rather, it was my husband's brother who desired to run out against me. Out of fear of him, and with the intention of protecting [him], I acted in this way.
[The rest] is as before, up to this very point.
The Blessed One asked everything. "Yes, Blessed One," [he replied]. The Blessed One said:
And yet you violate the proper conduct!
Therefore, it is not permissible to violate the proper conduct.
When that nun violates the proper conduct with a mind that has abandoned and released [its restraint], she ceases to be a nun.
Now, if one who intends to protect [herself] violates the proper conduct, it is a transgression of the Vinaya;
yet she does not cease to be a bhikṣuṇī.
Likewise, if a bhikṣu violates the proper conduct for the sake of protection with a mind that is neither renounced nor liberated, there is no offense.
This is called that which is connected with the violation of proper conduct. ||1||
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 32:
Concerning the Concealing of the Alms Bowl.
284. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
The nun Sthūlanandā was wandering for alms.
She then entered another large household for alms; in that house, there was a woman with a restless fetus.
She said,
"Noble lady, abandon this boy.
She replied:
"Venerable lady, please set it aside;
I will give something to the venerable lady.
She said:
"I will not abandon him.
She said,
"I shall give this much and that much to the Noble Lady."
The greedy woman said,
"Give it here in this bowl.
Having covered it, she went out.
Now the Elder Mahākāśyapa entered for alms. It was the Elder’s vow: "Whatever first alms are obtained, that shall be established for a monk or a nun."
Then she was seen by her;
she said, "Bring the bowl."
She pulled it away, covered it, and did not show it.
The Elder said,
"Bring forth the bowl."
She was addressed by that elder, who was of great renown and like a teacher himself.
Then, terrified and trembling, she extended her bowl toward him;
it was seen by the elder.
He said,
"Alas, the Dharma has declined!
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa then informed the monks of this matter.
The monks informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
"Call Nandā before me."
She was then summoned. She was questioned on this very matter, to which she replied,
"Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"It is a transgression for you, Nanda; this is not the Dharma, this is not the Vinaya...
and yet you indeed cover over the bowl."
Therefore, it is not permissible to cover the bowl.
Regarding the matter of covering the bowl:
it is not permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to go for alms with an uncovered bowl; she must go having covered it.
When she receives alms, she should receive them with [the bowl] uncovered.
If she sees a monk on the street, she should show [the food] to him with [the bowl] uncovered.
If that nun wanders about with her bowl uncovered, she commits an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
If, upon seeing a monk, one does not uncover [the bowl] to show it, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
This is called that which is connected with the concealment of the bowl.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 33: Concerning the latrine. 285. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now those nuns sat down in a latrine that had a closed-off chamber for excrement.
A woman’s miscarried fetus had been thrown into the latrine,
and outcastes were dumping excrement from painted jars into it.
They saw that boy;
seizing him by one arm, they complained:
"A female ascetic has given birth in the latrine!"
The nuns heard this matter... [as before] ...therefore, it is not permissible to sit upon a covered latrine.
Concerning the restroom:
it is no longer permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to have a covered restroom constructed;
rather, one must have it constructed with open sides.

It is not permissible to cause a toilet to be made with water flowing into it. It must be caused to be made without water flowing into it. If a nun sits down in a covered privy where water flows into it, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
This is called that which pertains to the latrine hut.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 34: Concerning the Jentāka (Steam-bath). The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now, while those Śākya maidens, Licchavi maidens, and Malla maidens were bathing in a bathhouse with that nun,
some young men of good family entered and caused them to fall away from the holy life.
The nuns heard about this matter.
[The usual formula] ... until: Therefore, it is not permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to bathe in a steam bathhouse (jentāka).
However, if she is now ill, she may bathe after having sweated in a dwelling and having anointed her limbs with oil.
If that nun bathes in a sauna, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
This is called the section concerning the sauna. 3.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 35: Concerning Lodgings in the Forest. 287. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
At that time, at that period, forest lodgings for the bhikṣuṇīs had not yet been prohibited, nor had those in the vicinity of villages been established.
Now, at that time, about five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, headed by Mahāprajāpatī, were residing in the Royal Park.
These women—daughters of the Śākyas, daughters of the Licchavis, and daughters of the Kolitas—were gracious and beautiful to behold.
Now those women had been seduced by the sons of good family;
they sat down for the meditation session during the first watch of the night, and the sons of good family stayed close by, thinking, "We shall seize them."
They rose up into the air and flew away.
Those sons of good family were despondent.
Then, during the middle watch and likewise the final watch, they sat down for the practice of meditation.
And the sons of good family, thinking "we shall take hold [of them]," were then led there by those who quickly attain meditative absorption;
and those upon whom drowsiness had not descended rose up into the air.
As many as were in meditative attainment, and those into whom sleep had descended, were seized and harassed by the sons of good family.
This is the account;
[and so on] as before.
Therefore, it is not permissible to dwell in a forest dwelling (*āraṇyaka-śayanāsana*).
Now, if it is a crossroads frequented throughout the night and laymen and laywomen are passing by, it is permissible to dwell there;
yet even there, it is not permissible to dwell in a secluded place.
If this nun takes up residence or dwells for the rains in a forest lodging, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
This is called the section concerning forest lodgings. 3.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 36–41;
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 36, 37:
288. That which is an *āstāra* for the bhikṣus is not an *āstāra* for the bhikṣuṇīs.
Whatever is an *āstāra* (formal proclamation) for the bhikṣuṇīs that is not an *āstāra* for the bhikṣus. [End of] section.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 38, 39:
Whatever is a suspension (uddhāra) for bhikṣus that is not a suspension for bhikṣuṇīs. [End of section].
That which is a suspension for bhikṣuṇīs is not a suspension for bhikṣus. || 0 ||
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 40, 41:
Whatever is an offense for monks that is not an offense [for them], that is [an offense] for bhikṣuṇīs.
Whatever is an offering for the bhikṣuṇīs that is not an offering for them is [likewise] for the bhikṣus. ||ḻ||
The Fourth Chapter.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 42–48;
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 42, 43:
289. Whatever food is unallowable for the bhikṣus [is likewise for the bhikṣuṇīs].
That is not allowable for the bhikṣuṇīs.
Whatever food is unallowable for the bhikṣuṇīs is allowable for the bhikṣus. ||2||
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 44, 45:
It is permissible for a monk to accept [gifts] from a bhikṣuṇī, with the exception of gold, silver, and what is fit for fire. || 3 ||
It is permissible for a bhikṣuṇī to have things accepted by a bhikṣu, with the exception of gold, silver, and what is fit for fire. [Nka]
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 46.
290. There are three things that cause a monk to cease being a monk.
What are the three?
[1] She renounces the training with a mind that has abandoned and released it; [2] the Saṃgha no longer dwells in that place;
[3] or her female gender appears.
These three things cause a monk to cease being a monk.
That monk must go to the nuns' quarters;
it is not permitted for him to stay even for a single night or in a single enclosure with the nuns.
Now, indeed, one must dwell where the range of movement has been cut off.
When the marks of a monk appear again in him, then he must come to the monks' residence.
That itself is his full ordination; that itself is his seniority by rains. Tṛ.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 47:
There are three things that cause a woman to cease being a bhikṣuṇī.
What are the three?
[1] He violates the rules of conduct with a mind that has abandoned and released its restraint;
[2] the Saṃgha dwells in that place and does not depart from it;
[3] or the male organ appears in him.
These three things cause a nun to cease being a nun, exactly as in the case of a monk. Phu.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 48:
There is no superfluous formal act for a bhikṣuṇī. Rule.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 49: Concerning Jewels 291. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
Now there was another family that had been ruined by the royal court;
royal guards surrounded it and kept watch over it.
A nun named Sthūlanandā, while wandering for alms, entered there.
That woman said to her:
"Noble lady, this family has been struck down by the royal house; its hair is disheveled and matted.

Noble lady, let this [child] be brought out, so that if we are released alive, it will be ours; we shall provide for the noble lady’s livelihood, and this [child] will belong to the noble lady. She then presented her with the bowl, saying, "Give this to me!"

Having filled a bowl with various kinds of jewels—pearls, gems, crystal, musāragalva, and red coral—it was given to her. She then departed after covering it; and she was seen by the guards, who then said:
"Bring it; what is this?
She tried to conceal it and would not show it. Trembling all over and terrified, she showed it to him.
The bhikṣuṇīs heard this. They reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
until she had her summoned.
That very point was asked:
he replied, "Yes, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "In that case, it is not permissible to conceal a jewel,
nor anything connected with a jewel."
Now, this great family does not become subject to the royal court as long as a written record has not been made,
nor has a formal decree been issued.
If they give anything, it is permissible to take it away.

Now, if a legal document has been drawn up, or protection has been established, or if the house is surrounded by soldiers, he says: "This house has been seized by the royal family; if we are released while still alive, it will belong to us, and it will belong to the Noble Lady alone. Therefore, it is not permissible to evict her.
It should be said:
"The training rule has been prescribed by the Blessed One; it is not permissible to expel [the person]. Then he said:
Whether it is given for a *caitya*, or given for the Saṃgha, or given specifically for a noble lady (*āryā*), it must be accepted.
Having accepted it, it is not permissible to take it away by concealing it;
having made it public, it should be taken away.
Then he is asked, "To whom does this belong? [He replies: "To the shrine," "To the Saṅgha," or "To me.
If it is released, it is well for Nanda. But if it is cut off, it must be given.
If that nun conceals a bowl full of jewels, she incurs an offense of transgression against the Vinaya. This is called the section concerning jewels. Hraḥ.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka 50: Regarding the Order of Seniority, [Section] 292. The Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī.
On both banks of the river Ajirāvatī, there was a meal for the Saṅgha.
The monks went there by boat,
but the bhikṣuṇīs were not permitted to board.
The monks said,
"Sisters, do not mount;
a training rule has been prescribed by the Blessed One."

"It is not permissible for a monk to board a single boat together with a nun. Now, when those monks were crossing at a landing place, even a single boat became crowded with just one monk; it became crowded with two or three.

When those monks had crossed over, the nuns were then ferried across by a boat that could carry only one person at a time. As they were calculating their seniority according to the date of their full ordination (*varṣāgra*), it became incorrect because of the delay. Then, in the evening, when her great elements were exhausted from fatigue, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī approached the Blessed One to pay homage at his feet.
The Blessed One, though already knowing, asked:
"Gautamī, by what have your great elements been exhausted?
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī reported all of that to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"In that case, eight bhikṣuṇīs should sit according to seniority;
the remaining ones may sit as they please."

Now, when there are meals, or refreshments, or drinks of barley-gruel, or even during the annual or great five-yearly festivals, eight seats must be set out for the eight *bhikṣuṇīs* according to seniority.
Having first prepared eight empty-handed hands [as a signal], one may then depart.
If those *bhikṣuṇīs*, having had the eight seats set out, sit down [without waiting], they commit an offense against the Vinaya.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Eight bhikṣuṇīs should sit according to seniority; the remaining ones may sit according to their arrival."
The Fifth Chapter.
Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka (Concluding Supplement) 293.
[1] Parivāsa; [2] Garlic.
An umbrella [3],
a vehicle [4],
and likewise surgical procedures [5].
[6] Sandals;
[7] a bed;
[8] a seat.
The ninth examination [9]. These nine phrases have been extracted from the *Prakīrṇaka*.
All other nine phrases, without omission, are to be inserted there once again.

Wherever there was a parivāsa, one should burn it along with a transformation of a living being; wherever there were sandals, one should burn them along with a transformation of a tree; wherever there was garlic, one should burn it along with a transformation of wood.
Where there is a bed, one should indicate a transformation of flowers;
where there is a vehicle, the wise person should indicate a transformation of fruits;
where there is sitting together, one should designate an umbrella as being of a single color.
Where there is an offense, there the wise one should point it out;
where there is the act of punishment, there he should point out that offense.
Where there is the vision of freedom from sorrow—that is, the counteraction of the offense—there the wise one should point it out.

By this much, the extractions from the *Prakīrṇaka* and those that were omitted have been set forth. Having extracted the twelfth section, there are nine items; furthermore, for the *Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka*, everything is rejected [from the *Bhikṣu-prakīrṇaka*], and thirteen sections are to be made.
And five other sections are to be added, as in the *Bhikṣuṇī-sūtra*.

The forest-dweller’s practice; the sauna; the restroom; and the removal of the wooden frame—these remaining matters are to be handled in the same manner as before. These are the rules of proper conduct.

All of that has been compiled again into eighteen sections by the Self-Existent One in the *Prakīrṇaka*. Having compiled the *Bhikṣuṇī-sūtra* and the *Ubhaya-sūtra*, the collection of training rules (*śikṣāpada*) is presented exactly as it is:
five hundred [rules] not lacking, and another thirty-four items.
The Bhikṣuṇī-prakīrṇaka of the noble Mahāsāṃghikas, the Lokottaravādins, is completed.
